title:
From Ledgers, to Options, to Latency 
A History of Trading, Mathematical Finance, and the Quant Profession
affiliations: Imperial College London - Department of Mathematics

detail.title:
From Ledgers, to Options, to Latency 
A History of Trading, Mathematical Finance, and the Quant Profession
detail.abstract:
The quantitative finance profession is often narrated as a late-twentieth-century consequence of option-pricing theory, electronic markets, and the migration of mathematicians and physicists to Wall Street. That account is correct but incomplete. The modern quant is the latest expression of a much longer co-evolution among five systems: institutions of exchange, mathematical representation, information technology, organisational specialisation, and regulation. This paper develops that thesis from the prehistory of money and markets to machine learning and large language models. It treats merchant accounting, bills of exchange, bourses, joint-stock companies, organised derivatives markets, telegraphy, the stock ticker, and the formation of specialised trading desks as genuine antecedents of quantitative work rather than as decorative prehistory. It then follows the mathematical line from Bachelier through axiomatic probability, stochastic calculus, portfolio theory, asset pricing, no-arbitrage valuation, volatility modelling, market microstructure, optimal execution, and modern computational statistics. Parallel to this intellectual history, it traces the professional line from mathematically sophisticated merchants and actuaries to portfolio "quantifiers," derivatives quants, systematic hedge funds, electronic market makers, quantitative developers, risk quants, data scientists, and AI-assisted researchers. 
      The paper also argues that the profession cannot be understood by following theory alone. Each wave of quantification depended on a matching substrate of market data, computing, communication, and institutional demand. Conversely, mathematical models reshaped the markets in which they were deployed, while crises and regulation repeatedly redirected quantitative labour toward new problems such as value-at-risk, counterparty exposure, xVA, capital, liquidity, execution quality, and model risk. The result is a history in which the quant is not a single occupation but a family of roles occupying the interface between formal models and executable decisions.

title: How Large Should a Strategic Petroleum Reserve Be? Three Optimization Problems for a Landlocked, Single-Supplier Economy

detail.title: How Large Should a Strategic Petroleum Reserve Be? Three Optimization Problems for a Landlocked, Single-Supplier Economy
detail.abstract: We ask how large a strategic petroleum reserve a landlocked country with a single overland supplier should hold. The standard theory, built for large maritime importers, assumes a world market, a price shock and a consumer welfare loss; all three fail for Mongolia. We pose the question instead as three optimization problems. Problem A asks how large a shock the system absorbs. Taking survival to be the radius of the largest ball inscribed in the polyhedron of viable states gives a linear program whose solution saturates: past a finite reserve, stock no longer moves the nearest face and the radius stops responding. That reserve is sufficient, and defining it needs no probability. Problem B asks how much fuel private importers bring in; under an administered price that is a Nash equilibrium, not a constant. We show the ceiling leaves the payoffs concave, so an equilibrium exists, and compute it by a reduction whose gap function certifies a global solution. Where the ceiling binds through the kink, the equilibrium set is a continuum on which total supply is pinned and the allocation is not. Problem C asks what reserve minimises expected cost, and is a stochastic dynamic program containing Problem B. Pass-through of a release is exactly zero while the ceiling holds total supply at the kink and exactly one once the ceiling has driven importers out, so the reserve is least effective in ordinary months and fully effective in the state it exists for; treating imports as exogenous, as the standard model does, overstates the reserve the state needs by about 32 per cent. Under an illustrative calibration built on Mongolia’s administered price of 3,040 MNT per litre, the two reserve calculations bracket a ceiling of 105 to 180 thousand tonnes, well below the ninety-day international norm. But at that cap the binding face is importer solvency, not physical cover, so only about 21 days is usable. The instrument that raises the survival radius is the pricing rule, not the stockpile.

title: Clarifying Monopoly Broth

detail.title: Clarifying Monopoly Broth

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None

detail.abstract:
U.S. v. Microsoft describes a type of Section 2 Sherman Act claim known as “monopoly broth”: a “series of acts, each of which harms competition only slightly but the cumulative effect of which is significant enough to form an independent basis for liability.” Broth is once again on the menu in important government monopolization cases against the world’s largest technology, energy, and pharmaceutical companies. But in the twenty-five years since Microsoft, monopoly broth claims have simply lurked in and around monopolization cases; they never been closely scrutinized or clarified in judicial reasoning. This has left courts and defendants conflating the cognizability of monopoly broth claims with other legal and factual issues, in ways that confuse judicial reasoning, weaken legitimate plaintiff claims, and fuel unnecessary appeals in the modern wave of litigation.

This article picks up where Microsoft left off to clarify monopoly broth. It examines the features that define monopoly broth claims to disentangle them from related, though at times overlapping, concepts. The article offers five key clarifications: 

(i) not every course of conduct claim under Section 2 is also a monopoly broth claim—broth claims are standalone counts, not just enhanced effects findings for other violations, 

(ii) monopoly broth claims must allege synergistic or cumulative effects on competition from the defendant’s acts, 

(iii) existing law does not prohibit otherwise-lawful acts as an “ingredient” in monopoly broth claims—and there are reasons why the law should stay this way, 

(iv) Section 2 is open-ended and effects-driven in its prohibitions, and that means the ingredients in a broth claim is not limited to recognized forms of misconduct, like refusals to deal or predatory pricing, and 

(v) recent monopoly broth claims have failed because they lack plausible allegations of anticompetitive effects, but this pleading failure is being misconstrued to argue that monopoly broth claims are not legally cognizable. 

These clarifications suggest that when properly understood, monopoly broth claims are rarer than represented, but also that distinct issues are improperly clouding the assessment of whether broth claims are legally viable under Section 2.

title:
Turning a Tontine into Real Income 
Clearing, Reserve and Scale in an Inflation-Protected Mortality Pool

detail.title:
Turning a Tontine into Real Income 
Clearing, Reserve and Scale in an Inflation-Protected Mortality Pool
detail.abstract: A household can buy protection against living too long, or protection against inflation, but not both at once: an annuity is a nominal promise on an insurer's balance sheet, and an index-linked bond ladder eventually runs out. Pooled payout vehicles exist that supply the first without the second. We ask what it takes to supply both: a pool that guarantees nothing, holds only government debt, writes claims on one life or on two, and re-rates income by a published rule instead of promising it. Two rules make such a pool fair, up to a residual that shrinks as it grows. Balances left by the dead are divided on the risk each surviving position brings, not on its size; we extend that rule to claims on two lives, which shed liability at the first death as well as the last. And income is quoted below what the mortality table supports, so that a margin accumulates in members' own balances and returns to each of them as their balance runs ahead of their liability. How large that margin must be is almost entirely a question about the mortality table. Pooling noise falls with the inverse root of an effective membership count, not of a headcount, which lets the threshold for re-rating be written in closed form; above roughly eight hundred members it calls for no margin at all. A seasoned pool can match roughly ninety-nine per cent of a liability running to age 110 with an inflation-linked ladder. What will not diversify is being wrong about how long members live: some five per cent of income for every year of unanticipated longevity. Priced against a live annuity quote, the pool costs about what the annuity costs. That near-parity is the useful finding and not a disappointing one, because it turns the case for the structure from a claim about cost into a choice: what stands behind a household's income, what currency that income is paid in, and where the prudence margin goes when it turns out not to have been needed.

title: Schumpeterian Demographic Trap
affiliations: Hitotsubashi University

detail.title: Schumpeterian Demographic Trap
detail.abstract: Fertility decline can first support modern growth and later become a source of stagnation. Motivated by Schumpeter (1942), I model capitalist rationalization as a persistent weakening of the family motive that lowers fertility. In the modern-growth phase, lower fertility raises the working-age share and innovation, reinforcing investment in child quality. Once fertility falls below a unique threshold, smaller working cohorts shrink the demographic base of innovation, and further fertility decline lowers growth. If the family motive becomes sufficiently weak, the economy converges to a stable low-fertility, low-growth equilibrium—a Schumpeterian demographic trap. The trap features higher saving, capital deepening, and a lower real return.

title: Bank Specialization within Production Networks
affiliations: , Tilburg University and KU Leuven - Department of Accountancy, Finance and Insurance (AFI)

detail.title: Bank Specialization within Production Networks
detail.abstract: Using firm-to-firm transaction and credit registry data from Belgium, we show that banks' common lending to supply chain partners is persistent and widespread. To study the benefits and costs of this lending specialization along supply chains, we develop and estimate a structural model of credit demand and supply in imperfectly competitive markets, where firms are connected through the production network. Our estimation results reveal that firms prefer to borrow from the same bank as their suppliers or customers, which gives common lenders market power and enables them to charge higher markups. At the same time, the network effects of common lending give banks an incentive to offer lower interest rates to maintain their role as common lenders. Exploiting the closure of a large manufacturing plant as an exogenous shock, we show that common lending also creates costs: the shock propagates through the production network, reducing credit demand along the supply chain and among common lenders, with banks more exposed to the affected network experiencing significantly larger declines in lending. A simulated counterfactual shows that the preference for borrowing from common lenders shapes how the losses are distributed across banks, concentrating them on the banks that lend directly to the disrupted firm and have a high exposure to the network.

title: Resources, Nations and Laws in the Making of Artificial Intelligence (A Comprehensive Study of the Major Countries, Legal Frameworks, and Systems of Power Driving the Global Expansion of AI)

detail.title: Resources, Nations and Laws in the Making of Artificial Intelligence (A Comprehensive Study of the Major Countries, Legal Frameworks, and Systems of Power Driving the Global Expansion of AI)
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is commonly regulated as software, data processing or automated decision-making. This article argues that such approaches capture only part of the legal object. Advanced AI is also a geographically distributed infrastructure system whose operation depends on critical minerals, semiconductor fabrication, lithography equipment, cloud platforms, labour, submarine cables, electricity networks, water systems and territorial regulatory permissions. Using a cross-jurisdictional infrastructure map, the article traces these dependencies through the Democratic Republic of Congo, Taiwan, the Netherlands, the United States, China and India, before examining the cable, energy, water and jurisdictional layers that connect them. Its central claim is that AI governance is also infrastructural governance: states and private actors exercise power over AI not only by regulating models or data, but by controlling mines, processing capacity, fabrication plants, export licences, cloud regions, labour supply chains, cable landings, grid connections and water permits. The article develops the concept of jurisdictional chokepoints to explain why legal authority over an upstream or supporting layer can shape downstream AI capability far beyond the regulator's territory. It further shows that responsibility is fragmented across the same chain: environmental, labour, security and distributional costs often arise in jurisdictions different from those capturing the highest-value economic returns. The article's contribution is therefore a legal-infrastructural account of AI power that connects fields usually studied separatelymining, trade, export control, labour, maritime, energy, environmental, data and technology law-and argues that effective AI governance must address the physical conditions that make computation possible as well as the behaviour of the models that computation produces.

title: The AI Investment Boom and Housing Wealth: Evidence from Data Centers
affiliations: , , Chapman University - The George L. Argyros College of Business and Economics and China Europe International Business School

detail.title: The AI Investment Boom and Housing Wealth: Evidence from Data Centers
detail.abstract: Data centers are the largest corporate-investment boom of the current era. Using a new facility-level database of U.S. data centers in a staggered difference-indifferences design, we examine who captures the financial windfall. Data center counties expand their tax bases and return part of the gain to residents: property-tax rates fall, and the cut capitalizes into homes, households' most valuable asset, whose price rises 4.5%. Capitalization is insignificant where the tax base is riskier, as for speculative crypto facilities, and the cuts are larger where local government is less transparent, consistent with officials paying the surplus as the "price of consent." The estimates survive entropy balancing, a cancelled-project placebo, and a border county-pair design. In aggregate, data centers have created over $100 billion in housing wealth while delivering little to renters, bondholders, or schools. The paper is among the first to show how technology investment and its risks are transmitted into household portfolios.

title: Private Credit and Leveraged Loan Markets: Similarities, Differences, and Substitution
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, , Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and Independent

detail.title: Private Credit and Leveraged Loan Markets: Similarities, Differences, and Substitution

publicationDetails.journalName: Board of Governors: Finance & Economics Discussion Series (Topic)

detail.abstract: Private credit (PC) and leveraged loan (LL) markets are two key sources of financing for below-investment-grade middle-market firms, typically those with revenues between $10 million and $1 billion). Although these two markets have different structures and rely on different lenders, they have become increasingly interconnected in recent years, with some firms seeking financing in both markets.

title: Reviving Statutory Hope in U.S. Antitrust Law

detail.title: Reviving Statutory Hope in U.S. Antitrust Law

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None

detail.abstract:
This essay is a rallying call for renewed hope in U.S. statutory antitrust. It tracks the striking disappearance of Congress from antitrust lawmaking over the last half century, then makes the case for why we urgently need to revive that statutory role. For years now, there has been strong, bipartisan support for antitrust reform in the U.S. Yet we have seen no legislative change of  significance. Antitrust legislative reform is unusually stalled and plodding relative to this momentum.  

This essay argues that there is an insidious reason for this stalemate that has not yet been identified in the literature: antitrust thinkers retain a deep-seated, widely-held skepticism toward the legislature’s role in U.S. antitrust law. Despite the dramatic foment around antitrust reform, American antitrust continues to be viewed almost exclusively as a construct of the common law.

The essay challenges this common law dogma, using the novel framework of “hope” in philosophy and psychology literature. It explains how the various schools of antitrust law have lost the two constitutive elements of hope in statutory reform—belief and desire. Some no longer believe it is genuinely possible, while others do not truly desire statutory change. This missing hope is undermining reform efforts; it pushes change agendas toward other modalities, like case-by-case litigation and agency-led reform, that are slow, and in the case of agency action, far less viable than just a few years ago due to Supreme Court decisions in administrative law.

The essay then makes the case for reviving statutory hope in antitrust law. It argues that a belief in the potential for statutory reform has instrumental value in achieving that change, because it drives thought and action that make such reform more likely to occur. Next, it contends that a desire for statutory change makes sense across the political spectrum. The essay identifies three widely-supported antitrust reforms that can only be achieved through statutory amendment, making it logical to desire: the renewal of monopolization liability against big tech after decades of judicial narrowing, the continued viability of the FTC as an institution in the face of the Supreme Court’s attack on the administrative state, and the repeal of archaic antitrust exemptions that are costing consumers dearly in industries like shipping and rail. It is time to become antitrust statutory optimists, to make these changes a reality.

title: Pricing Transient Carbon Shocks in Bitcoin An Instrument Variable Approach
affiliations: Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge

detail.title: Pricing Transient Carbon Shocks in Bitcoin An Instrument Variable Approach
detail.abstract: In equity markets, separating environmental salience from carbon transition risk is a central identification challenge, as carbon pricing attributed to investor preferences may instead reflect hedging of future carbon liabilities. I address this problem by exploiting cryptocurrency markets, where investors do not face any carbon liability. Utilizing an empirical strategy that instruments Bitcoin's seasonal changes in its carbon footprint with monsoon precipitation cycles over the hydroelectric watersheds of China, I isolate a nature-driven, exogenous shock to network carbon intensity. I show that investors ignore its predictable changes and do not price seasonal changes to its carbon footprint. In sharp contrast, a within-exchange difference-indifferences analysis reveals that investors react severely to sudden attention shocks. This paper develops a novel instrument variable approach to price transient carbon shocks in Bitcoin. These findings demonstrate that when regulatory risk is absent, voluntary environmental preferences do not continuously price transient carbon externalities but instead express themselves episodically through transient salience shocks.

title: Future of a Hands-On Businesses Balanced Approach in Transformative Leadership, Education, and Modernity
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Future of a Hands-On Businesses Balanced Approach in Transformative Leadership, Education, and Modernity
detail.abstract: As defined by rapid technological advancement, shifting cultural landscapes, and evolving organizational demands, the future of hands-on businesses hinges on a balanced approach that integrates transformative leadership, modernized education, and cultural sensitivity. Central to this vision is the ability to maintain trust and accountability without over-reliance on a leader’s constant presence. Through effective delegation, trust-building systems, and a willingness to relinquish control, organizations can foster resilience and shared responsibility, ensuring long-term sustainability. Transformative leadership, when grounded in strategic communication, participatory decision-making, adaptive practices, and emotional intelligence, can remain visionary while staying attuned to the everyday realities of employees. This dual focus cultivates engagement, innovation, and organizational trust. To prepare leaders for the complexities of modernity, education and leadership training must be restructured to emphasize critical thinking, adaptability, and ethical reasoning. Problem-based learning, experiential opportunities, ethics-centered curricula, and technological integration are essential to developing leaders capable of navigating uncertainty and making principled decisions. Furthermore, reconciling traditional cultural expectations with the demands of modernization requires culturally intelligent and inclusive leadership. By embracing ethical responsibility, adaptive change management, and strategic use of technology, leaders can drive transformation that respects cultural values while advancing innovation. The future of hands-on business lies in a holistic leadership paradigm—one that balances strategic foresight with grounded engagement, modern competencies with ethical integrity, and innovation with cultural respect. By adopting these integrated approaches, organizations can thrive in complexity, foster trust across all levels, and build sustainable success in an increasingly interconnected and dynamic world.

title: When Does Sentiment Predict Volatility?
affiliations: ,  and University of New South Wales (UNSW), University of New South Wales - Australian School of Business

detail.title: When Does Sentiment Predict Volatility?

declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by the UTS Business Doctoral Scholarship and UTS International Research Scholarship.

detail.abstract: Can media sentiment improve volatility forecasts when price-based dynamics fail? We study this question using daily realised volatility for DJIA stocks and media-based sentiment measures from the Thomson Reuters MarketPsych Indices. Augmenting standard HAR models with sentiment yields only modest average improvements, consistent with prior literature. However, this average masks strong state dependence. We show that sentiment becomes materially more informative in the upper tail of the volatility distribution and, more importantly, during periods when volatility persistence weakens. Using a fractional integration framework to measure persistence, we find that sentiment-based predictors deliver their largest gains precisely when lagged volatility becomes less informative. Out-of-sample, these gains are concentrated in regimes characterised jointly by high volatility and low persistence. Our findings suggest that media sentiment does not provide a generic forecasting enhancement, but instead supplies forward-looking narrative information when standard price-based volatility models are least reliable.

title: Government bond-backed repo markets: between resilience and vulnerability
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Banque de France, , International Monetary Fund (IMF), De Nederlandsche Bank and European Central Bank (ECB)

detail.title: Government bond-backed repo markets: between resilience and vulnerability

publicationDetails.journalName: Board of Governors: Finance & Economics Discussion Series (Topic)

detail.abstract: This paper synthesizes the literature on vulnerabilities in government bond-backed repo markets, focusing on the features that contribute to both the fragility and stability of these markets. The literature shows that the same features that enable efficient liquidity provision, including short-term funding, dealer intermediation, extensive collateral reuse, and low haircuts, can also create channels for rapid transmission of stress. The review documents tight linkages between repo and government bond markets, highlighting how repos are key to the build-up of leverage and can propagate stress across funding, cash, and derivatives markets, particularly through dealers and nonbank financial intermediaries such as investment firms, hedge funds, and money market funds. Evidence from recent stress episodes illustrates how these vulnerabilities materialize in practice. The review also examines post-crisis regulatory reforms and central bank interventions, identifying how these measures have enhanced market resilience while also creating trade-offs for market dynamics, with implications for liquidity and collateral availability.

title: The Effect of AI Writing on Governance: Evidence from a $3.5 Billion DAO
affiliations: and

detail.title: The Effect of AI Writing on Governance: Evidence from a $3.5 Billion DAO
detail.abstract: We study the extent to which online deliberation aggregates information before collective votes. Our setting is Arbitrum DAO, a decentralized organization controlling a $3.5 billion treasury, where token holders debate proposals on a public forum before each binding vote. Forum activity predicted vote closeness before March 2024 but became uninformative after, coinciding with language models capable of producing indistinguishable governance prose. Interestingly, we observe that the degradation of the forum's signal (the elimination of the correlation between posting volume and margin-of-victory) takes place at a time when relatively few posts are A.I. generated, relative to the end of the sample period where A.I. posting volume grows rapidly. A model of endogenous posting, reading, and voting-derived from primitives-shows this is a general phenomenon: the signal value of a forum collapses at a discrete tipping point at a realized A.I. share strictly below the level that would mechanically destroy reading value, and the collapse is hysteretic: reducing A.I. volume afterward does not restore the forum. Calibrating to the data, the forum generated net social benefits equivalent to saving at least 858 words of research effort per delegate per proposal (under a stated non-redundancy assumption)-all destroyed at the tipping point. Delegates who rely on AI hold far less voting power than those who do not, which is inconsistent with power capture by insiders. Our results suggest that the mere availability of indistinguishable AI writing can degrade the governance capabilities of economically important organizations, even when such AI is rarely used in equilibrium.

title: Gold, Power, and Crisis: The Panic of 1893

detail.title: Gold, Power, and Crisis: The Panic of 1893
detail.abstract: In the spring of 1894, Jacob Coxey, an Ohio businessman whose own fortunes had been damaged by the Panic of 1893, led a march of unemployed workers toward Washington, D.C. Known as “Coxey’s Army,” the group sought federal intervention to create public jobs and stabilize the economy. Though the marchers were dismissed and Coxey himself was arrested, their presence revealed a growing expectation that the federal government should respond to economic crises, an idea that had not yet been fully established in the 19th century. While commonly overshadowed by the 1929 crash, the Panic of 1893 was a significant turning point in American economic history. This severe economic depression exposed the dangers of decentralized finance, rigid gold dependence, and the control of the wealthy over national liquidity. The crisis's resolution by private financiers marked the unofficial beginning of centralized banking in the United States which set the stage for the Federal Reserve and fundamentally altered how the nation manages financial panics. The end of the 19th century saw brilliant industrial growth, increased migration, and a growing national GDP. Yet beneath the gilded veneer lay financial weaknesses that led to a largely forgotten economic depression: the Panic of 1893. This downturn, spanning several years, made the unemployment rate soar to approximately 11.7%, led to the downfall of tens of thousands of businesses, and bankrupted nearly 575 of 3,800 banks. The Panic of 1893 saw the highest bank failure rate of any panic in U.S. history, at 1.28 percent of all banks. When President Grover Cleveland turned to Wall Street titan J.P. Morgan to replenish federal gold reserves, private capital effectively supplanted public authority. By examining the context, causes, and aftermath of this crisis, one can better understand the foundations and motives of modern central banking in the United States.

title: Robust Signal Maximization in Spillover Experiments
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley, Brown University and The University of Chicago

detail.title: Robust Signal Maximization in Spillover Experiments
detail.abstract: We study the optimal design and analysis of experiments for estimating spillover effects. Assuming a known (e.g., linear) exposure mapping, we characterize the treatment-assignment distribution and regression-based estimator that minimize worst-case asymptotic variance against a broad class of distributions of unobservables. The design problem yields an intuitive solution in which the planner trades off spillover signal strength against diffusion of spillover variation. The analysis problem yields a simple recentered instrumental variable estimator to best leverage this variation. This framework produces natural solutions in several benchmark cases-such as clustered exposure-and suggests computationally tractable approximations for general networks, including bipartite settings. We illustrate these new tools in semi-synthetic experiments based on two applications from development economics. Our approach yields large standard error reductions in both experiments, increasing effective sample sizes by 50-100% or more.

title: Poverty beyond Reduction: Toward a General Theory of Regenerative Human Development
affiliations: African Research Network (ARN)

detail.title: Poverty beyond Reduction: Toward a General Theory of Regenerative Human Development
detail.abstract: The global struggle against poverty has achieved substantial gains, yet progress has slowed and the persistence of deprivation increasingly reflects interactions among economic insecurity, inequality, climate vulnerability, institutional weakness and unequal access to productive capabilities. This article argues that these conditions expose a conceptual limitation in conventional approaches to poverty reduction. Reducing an observable deprivation does not necessarily transform the systems through which vulnerability is reproduced. The article therefore develops the concept of regenerative human development, defined as the capacity of individuals, communities and societies to restore, sustain and expand the economic, social, institutional, ecological, cognitive and technological conditions necessary for human flourishing across generations. Drawing on contemporary scholarship on human development, multidimensional poverty, capabilities, resilience and sustainable development, the article distinguishes poverty reduction from poverty transformation and regeneration. It proposes that poverty should be understood as a dynamic process involving deprivation, vulnerability, capability erosion and the reproduction of unequal developmental conditions. Regenerative development interrupts this cycle by strengthening the capacities through which wellbeing can be continuously generated. The article argues that this perspective is particularly relevant to Africa, where poverty increasingly intersects with demographic change, ecological pressures, structural inequality and emerging technological opportunities. Regenerative human development consequently provides a theoretical bridge between poverty studies and broader debates on sustainability, resilience, institutional transformation and human flourishing.

title:
The Digital‑Economy Resilience Curve: 
How Digital-infrastructure Density Reduces Climate-shock Volatility in Emerging Markets

detail.title:
The Digital‑Economy Resilience Curve: 
How Digital-infrastructure Density Reduces Climate-shock Volatility in Emerging Markets
detail.abstract:
Digital infrastructure has become a decisive, yet under‑recognized, determinant of how emerging‑market economies absorb climate shocks. While physical adaptation reduces the hazard, digital‑infrastructure density reduces the volatility that hazards transmit into output, consumption, and welfare. Drawing on evidence from information systems, mobile‑money networks, digital‑ID platforms, and logistics coordination, this report formalizes the Digital‑Economy Resilience Curve: climate‑shock volatility declines as digital‑infrastructure density rises—steeply at low density, then at a diminishing rate as saturation approaches.

The mechanism operates through five channels: information and early warning, financial continuity, labor‑market flexibility, state‑capacity and social‑protection delivery, and supply‑chain coordination. Early increments of digital density unlock multiple channels simultaneously, producing disproportionately large resilience gains. Case studies from Bangladesh, Kenya, and India demonstrate this dynamic: cyclone mortality collapses as warning systems scale; mobile‑money networks absorb drought‑driven income shocks; digital‑ID and payment rails enable relief delivery to hundreds of millions within days.

Using a four‑layer Digital Infrastructure Density Index (DIDI)—connectivity, financial rails, identity/data, and compute/platforms—the report maps density variation across emerging markets and shows its negative association with climate‑shock vulnerability. It argues that digital infrastructure should be classified and financed as climate adaptation, not merely as a growth input, and that investment sequencing should prioritize low‑density economies where marginal resilience returns are highest. The report concludes with a research agenda to empirically estimate thresholds, refine volatility measures, and quantify delivery‑speed effects.

title: Who Runs First? Higher-order Learning and Financial Fragility

detail.title: Who Runs First? Higher-order Learning and Financial Fragility
detail.abstract: Financial coordination depends on both how many investors are informed and how well they know who else is informed. We study these two dimensions-informational breadth and epistemic depth-in a coordination model motivated by bank runs. Increasing the informed share first weakens panic among uninformed investors but, once that panic disappears, facilitates coordination among informed investors. Fragility can therefore be minimized at an intermediate informed share. We then allow informed investors to observe social signals about the fraction of investors who are informed. These higher-order signals have opposite effects depending on whether coordination is sustained by uninformed panic or informed investors. Dynamically, informed investors may delay an irreversible Attack while waiting to learn who else is informed. Because uninformed investors respond only indirectly through strategic complementarity, stronger prospective higher-order learning can reduce informed Attack more sharply and reverse who attacks first in the dynamic equilibrium.

title: Meta-extraction A Foundational Definition

detail.title: Meta-extraction A Foundational Definition

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No competing financial or personal interests to declare.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This paper is a theoretical and analytical work drawing on published secondary sources and public disclosures; it does not involve new data collection from human participants.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding or financial support.

detail.abstract: This short paper states, in fixed and citable form, the definition of meta-extraction-the capacity of sufficiently powerful actors to extract not merely wealth or resources, but the public's ability to recognize, contest, and respond to extraction itself. The term is introduced and applied at length in two companion working papers on the creation-extraction distinction in political economy; this note exists independently of both, so that the definition can be cited precisely, without requiring citation of either full-length argument. The paper distinguishes meta-extraction from ordinary (first-order) extraction, specifies its mechanism across four sites of institutional control, states a falsifiable evidentiary standard-including a confirming case and a constitutive boundary case-situates the term against its nearest neighbors in the existing literature (agnotology, cultural hegemony, instrumentarian power, testimonial injustice, manufactured doubt), and closes with four testable propositions offered for empirical or critical engagement.

title: External Demand and Local-income Housing-price Responsiveness: A Conditional Comparative-static Extension

detail.title: External Demand and Local-income Housing-price Responsiveness: A Conditional Comparative-static Extension

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not apply
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This technical note develops a narrow comparative-static extension of the equilibrium housing-price exposure framework established in Sintes (2026). It distinguishes between the primitive effect of local income on local buyers’ willingness to pay and the equilibrium transmission of that effect into housing prices. The note then studies how this transmission changes when a positive external-demand shock relocates the market-clearing equilibrium. The main result is that local-income housing-price responsiveness declines only when the external component’s contribution to aggregate demand slope grows proportionally faster than the local component’s contribution along the induced equilibrium path. This condition can be decomposed into an equilibrium-relocation channel, reflecting differences in local demand-slope geometry, and a direct shift-induced change in the external demand slope. External-demand expansion therefore does not mechanically weaken local-income anchoring: attenuation, invariance, and amplification are all possible depending on how the perturbation changes the relative slope composition of demand at the new equilibrium.

title: Reshaping Southern Africa: Post-Mugabe Zimbabwean Development through Youth Empowerment
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Reshaping Southern Africa: Post-Mugabe Zimbabwean Development through Youth Empowerment
detail.abstract: In the wake of Zimbabwe’s four 20th century historical phases—British Colonial Rule, 1965 white minority rule of Rhodesia, 1980 Zimbabwean independence seeking black majority rule, and Mugabe’s aggressive 2000 Fast Track Land Reform Program, which plunged the nation into economic crisis—marked by youth (age 15-25) unemployment reaching over 30%—Zimbabwe in 2026 distinctly lags neighbors Botswana and South Africa in poverty alleviation. Notably, Botswana’s poverty rate—as measured by % of people living under $3/day in earnings—stands at 21.37% and South Africa’s at 17.44%, as compared to Zimbabwe’s 49.2% (2021 PPP). This analysis argues for proposed solutions for Zimbabwe drawn from successful programs in Botswana and South Africa: (1) Stabilizing the independent currency to support the nation’s population and international investment, (2) strengthening youth economic mobility through government-assisted programs fostering market-relevant skills, and (3) reinforcing existing agricultural and technological industries to cultivate economic development. A uniting theme is that a more prosperous Zimbabwe lies in youth empowerment—through mentorship, entrepreneurial programs—to reduce talent migration away from Zimbabwe, mimicking similar programs in Botswana and South Africa. Through comparative research, local primary source interviews, and discussions with senior commercial investors in Africa, this analysis sets forth ways in which similar measures can be introduced or enhanced in Zimbabwe.

title: Financial Engineering at the Sovereignty Frontier: De-risking Debt-for-Climate Swaps with Layered Carbon Markets
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Financial Engineering at the Sovereignty Frontier: De-risking Debt-for-Climate Swaps with Layered Carbon Markets
detail.abstract: Heavily indebted sovereign nations face a compounding, closed-loop crisis where financial insolvency and ecological collapse actively dismantle one another. Mandatory debt servicing drives severe budgetary austerity, forcing immediate fiscal suffocation of long-term conservation projects, while attempting to borrow out of this funding gap triggers punitive, junk-grade interest premiums. Furthermore, the nation’s valuable natural infrastructure remains financially unmonetized due to an idle-asset paradox, leaving standing ecosystems unrecognized as viable collateral. This austerity-driven neglect feeds back into a macroeconomic degradation loop, structurally weakening the country’s long-run creditworthiness and leaving it vulnerable to catastrophic climate shocks. Traditional debt instruments cannot break this cycle; unlocking it requires structural liability re-engineering through market-driven Debt-for-Climate Swaps. By utilizing credit guarantees from Multilateral Development Banks (MDBs), these instruments execute a cost-of-capital arbitrage that artificially lowers sovereign interest rates and locks the resulting savings into legally binding local conservation funds. Layering Article 6 carbon-market revenue on top monetizes these idle natural assets, creating a self-renewing income stream that transforms a one-time fiscal relief event into an ongoing source of environmental capital. Consequently, this paper analyzes these instruments strictly as institutional risk-transfer engineering driven by quantifiable financial returns rather than moral gestures, focusing on stakeholder incentive alignment and the rigorous Article 6 rules required to prevent double-counting.

title: The Dynamic Distribution in the Fixed Cost Model: An Analytical Solution
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City

detail.title: The Dynamic Distribution in the Fixed Cost Model: An Analytical Solution
detail.abstract: I derive an analytical solution to the Kolmogorov forward equation for fixed cost models. This is a challenging PDE because the dynamic distribution depends on the flow of resetting agents, which is endogenously determined by the distribution itself. I show that there is a shortcut that allows the reset flow to be derived without first finding the entire distribution of agents. This shortcut is also valuable because many aggregate variables can be written in terms of the reset flow alone. Steady-state conditional adjustment behavior recovers the entire marginal reset-flow response to a common state shift. As an example, I solve an investment model with fixed costs of adjustment and study the effects of increased productivity growth. Aggregate dynamics can be derived from a one-dimensional weighted distribution of capital gaps. Because of adjustment frictions, the shock causes a boom-lull investment pattern whose shape depends on the shock size.

title: Net Margin Proportional Representation Incorporating Negative Vote into Proportional Representation

detail.title: Net Margin Proportional Representation Incorporating Negative Vote into Proportional Representation
detail.abstract:
Net Margin Proportional Representation (NMPR) extends proportional representation to elections conducted under Negative Vote, in which each voter casts a single YES or NO vote for one party or candidate. Conventional proportional representation allocates seats on the basis of positive support alone and therefore cannot translate net political mandates into parliamentary representation. NMPR instead allocates seats according to each party's Net % Active Votes, defined as the difference between YES and NO votes as a share of all active votes cast for qualifying parties. 

The paper derives a unique continuous allocation rule that preserves pairwise differences in Net % Active Votes while satisfying the standard constraints of proportional representation, including fixed chamber size, statutory qualification thresholds, and whole-seat allocation. The framework is illustrated with survey-based evidence from Taiwan and with hypothetical applications to Israel and Germany. NMPR offers a theoretically consistent method for incorporating Negative Vote into proportional representation while preserving one person, one vote.

title: Local Market Power, Ownership, and the Incidence of Fiscal Policy
affiliations: University of South Carolina - University of South Carolina - Darla Moore School of Business - Department of Economics

detail.title: Local Market Power, Ownership, and the Incidence of Fiscal Policy
detail.abstract: Firms with local market power charge markups that differ across cities, so the same goods cost more in some places than in others. This paper asks who bears those markups, who receives the revenue, and whether fiscal policy can offset the difference. I add spatially varying markups to an estimated spatial equilibrium model with heterogeneous households. Households pay markups in proportion to what they buy but receive the profits in proportion to what they own, and ownership is far more concentrated than earnings. The result is a transfer of $14 billion a year from non-college to college households in the United States, four times the deadweight loss of the federal income tax and running the other way. Assuming instead that profits track wages, as is standard, leaves the aggregate cost of markups unchanged but reverses who gains from removing them. Almost all of the spatial variation in goods prices survives conditioning on local rents, wages and population, so place-based policies cannot target this burden.

title: Climate Adaptation Economics : Water Insecurity Metrics, Biodiversity‑Linked Financing, and Land‑Cover Transitions for Sustainability‑Linked Loans

detail.title: Climate Adaptation Economics : Water Insecurity Metrics, Biodiversity‑Linked Financing, and Land‑Cover Transitions for Sustainability‑Linked Loans

keywords: and Land-Cover Transitions for Sustainability-Linked Loans

detail.abstract: This report examines the economic dimensions of climate adaptation, focusing on how regions, industries, and governments can reduce vulnerability to climate‑related risks while sustaining long‑term growth. It evaluates the costs and benefits of adaptation strategies, models projected economic impacts under multiple climate scenarios, and identifies policy mechanisms that improve resilience and resource allocation. The analysis highlights the importance of early investment, cross‑sector coordination, and adaptive governance frameworks to mitigate losses and capture emerging opportunities in a changing climate. Findings emphasize that adaptation is not only a defensive measure but a driver of economic stability and innovation.

title: The Corporation as an Evolved Organizational Design
affiliations: University of Connecticut

detail.title: The Corporation as an Evolved Organizational Design

declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: Legal institutionalists correctly emphasize that corporations are constituted by law rather than merely by private contract, but many wrongly conclude that shareholders do not own corporations and that corporations themselves cannot be objects of ownership. This paper argues instead that the Hansmann-Kraakman conception of the corporation-centered on legal personality, asset partitioning, transferable shares, delegated management, and investor ownership-is both compatible with legal institutionalism and superior as an account of the corporation's economic role. The paper reconceptualizes the corporation as a modular legal architecture designed to cope with complexity, arguing that incorporation functions as a system of encapsulation and information hiding. By legally partitioning assets and defining organizational boundaries, the corporation creates a protected module within which rich, complex, and difficult-to-price interactions can occur. Corporate law thus operates as a set of abstract design rules that reduce the knowledge burdens associated with large-scale cooperation. This modular organizational form evolved gradually from medieval ecclesiastical corporations and chartered trading companies into the modern public corporation through the emergence of increasingly abstract and general legal rules of incorporation. The paper concludes that stakeholder and managerial theories ultimately rest on epistemic assumptions incompatible with a world of uncertainty and decentralized learning. The shareholder-owned corporation, embedded in external capital markets and disciplined by transferable ownership claims, evolved precisely because it is an effective institutional response to complexity, experimentation, and economic change.

title: The Two Yardsticks: Heterogeneous Valuation and the Generalized Product Frontier

detail.title: The Two Yardsticks: Heterogeneous Valuation and the Generalized Product Frontier
detail.abstract: The product theorem says that under relative-gains preferences a settlement both parties prefer to conflict exists if and only if λ_R·λ_U ≤ 1, and its proof chains one party’s acceptance condition into the other’s — a step valid only when both parties measure the stake with the same index. This paper characterizes feasibility when they do not: each party i evaluates every share through its own increasing index v_i. Four results follow. First, the feasibility frontier in weight space is an exactly characterized decreasing curve λ_U = Φ(λ_R), computable from the two indices and the conflict values, which reduces to the hyperbola λ_U = 1/λ_R under a common index; verified against an oracle on 2,973 randomized heterogeneous instances with no disagreement. Second, the product theorem survives in generalized form: feasibility holds if and only if λ_R·λ_U ≤ Δ(x*), where Δ is a cross-valuation distortion — a ratio of the two parties’ exchange rates between own gain and rival gain — evaluated at the marginal acceptance point; Δ ≡ 1 exactly when the indices agree up to positive affine transformation on the relevant range. Third, a pivot theorem: when the conflict positions are symmetric, the point (1,1) lies on the frontier for every pair of indices whatever — heterogeneity rotates the frontier around the common-index pivot rather than shifting it — while under asymmetric conflict positions the threshold moves in both directions, rising when valuations are complementary (each party relatively prizes what it receives) and falling when they are rivalrous, with degradation linear in the divergence of the indices. Fourth, a measurement result that converts the elicitation protocol’s principal contamination into information: the product of willingness-to-pay answers elicited at the conflict allocation equals the true product times a local version of Δ, and in 2,932 randomized heterogeneous instances the elicited product predicted feasibility correctly 96.6 per cent of the time against 90.6 per cent for the true product. The distortion that curvature inflicts on the measurement points, on average, in the direction of the truth, because it partially encodes the yardstick divergence that actually governs feasibility. We close with the reading the series requires: memory policy is yardstick policy, and mutual sacralization of the same object is the configuration that lowers the threshold below one.

title:
The FTX-Alameda Research Fraud: Anatomy of an $8.9 Billion Collapse 
A Comprehensive Analysis of Corporate Structure, Fraud Mechanics, Regulatory Failure, and Legislative Aftermath
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title:
The FTX-Alameda Research Fraud: Anatomy of an $8.9 Billion Collapse 
A Comprehensive Analysis of Corporate Structure, Fraud Mechanics, Regulatory Failure, and Legislative Aftermath

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study is based on publicly available documents and did not involve human participants
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding

detail.abstract: This paper presents a forensic analysis of the FTX Trading Ltd. and Alameda Re- search fraud, the largest cryptocurrency fraud in history, resulting in an $8.9 billion shortfall in customer deposits. Drawing upon court filings, SEC and CFTC com- plaints, bankruptcy examiner reports, and trial testimony, this study examines the corporate architecture that enabled systematic misappropriation of customer funds through a coded backdoor (allow_negative), fabricated balance sheets, and circu- lar collateralisation of the proprietary FTT token. The paper analyses the catalytic role of the CoinDesk exposé and Binance CEO Changpeng Zhao’s divestiture an- nouncement in precipitating a $6 billion bank run, evaluates why regulatory frame- works and investor due diligence failed to detect the fraud, and assesses the legal outcomes including Sam Bankman-Fried’s 25-year prison sentence and the evolv- ing legislative response encompassing the EU’s MiCA regulation and proposed U.S. legislation. The analysis concludes that the FTX collapse represents classical embezzlement enabled by regulatory arbitrage, absent corporate governance, and the deliberate cultivation of political and reputational capital.

title: Funding Strategic Asset Accumulation: A Post-Keynesian Stock–Flow Theory
affiliations: Hanyang University

detail.title: Funding Strategic Asset Accumulation: A Post-Keynesian Stock–Flow Theory

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This theoretical study involved no human participants or animals.
declarations.funderStatement: The author received no specific funding for this work.

detail.abstract: Strategic asset-stock theory explains how investment flows build hard-to-imitate productive stocks. We use Post-Keynesian economics (PKE) to explain which planned flows remain funded through time. Under fundamental uncertainty, banks can create credit, but liquidity preference and shared financial conventions shape its allocation and renewal. A convention change can redirect unchanged aggregate new bank lending before firm-specific technical evidence changes. Accumulation–funding fit describes the ex ante correspondence between an asset path’s timing needs and its funding terms. Committed-horizon coverage, payment rigidity, and refinancing exposure determine which paths are interrupted. Dierickx and Cool’s accumulation properties explain why resulting stock gaps can persist after funding returns. The theory identifies a monetary source of strategic-asset differences that can support advantage when value and rent conditions hold.

title: Calling off the Dogs: Enforcement Threat and the 2025 Presidential Inaugural Fund

detail.title: Calling off the Dogs: Enforcement Threat and the 2025 Presidential Inaugural Fund
detail.abstract: The theory of rent extraction (McChesney 1987), that politicians profit by threatening harm and selling forbearance, has gone largely untested for four decades because the transaction is typically invisible. However, the 2025 presidential inaugural fund supplied a clean record of the payments: corporate donations, publicly disclosed, collected while an incoming administration's threats were live and its favors were still promises. In a sample of 665 firms coded for threat status using only pre-inauguration information, firms facing active federal enforcement donated at 38.6 percent against a 14.3 percent base rate, while firms in industries the administration had promised to help, and firms facing only industry-wide harm, donated like everyone else. Within sectors, enforcement threat raises the probability of donating by 30.6 percentage points, an estimate that survives seven logged re-estimations and a firm-size control. The evidence that payment bought better case outcomes is suggestive but underpowered. Payment followed jeopardy, not hope: the pattern protection predicts, and the opposite of what favor-buying would predict here.

title: Nowhere Else to Put It: Institutional Distrust, Constrained Investment Choice, and Empty Housing in Emerging Asia
affiliations: Saki Partners

detail.title: Nowhere Else to Put It: Institutional Distrust, Constrained Investment Choice, and Empty Housing in Emerging Asia
detail.abstract: This paper asks why household and elite savings across emerging Asia flow so overwhelmingly into residential real estate, and why so much of that real estate is deliberately left empty. It argues that this concentration is not primarily a matter of cultural preference but of constrained choice under institutional distrust. Working through the hierarchy of stores of value available to an ordinary saver, it shows how each rung has been compromised: bank deposits by negative real returns and by catastrophic failure, epitomised by the collapse of Saigon Commercial Bank; equity and corporate-bond markets by manipulation, weak enforcement and extreme concentration in a single family conglomerate; and the physical hedges of gold and diamonds by counterfeiting, state-monopoly embezzlement, certification fraud and the price-collapsing rise of laboratory-grown stones. With trusted alternatives eliminated, real estate becomes the residual asset by default, attracting both legitimate savings and the darker pools of corruption and tax evasion, for which vacancy is a feature rather than a cost. The paper traces how this capital is parked in empty units, trapped by resale restrictions and title limbo, and exported to destination markets such as Australia, before documenting the resulting bubble risk and setting out five recommendations for policymakers.

title: Measuring Spite: Invariance, Elicitation, and What Survives Curvature

detail.title: Measuring Spite: Invariance, Elicitation, and What Survives Curvature
detail.abstract: Every result in this series turns on a matrix of relative-gains weights that has never been measured. This paper shows that it can be, and states precisely how much of it survives the standard objection that utility is not linear in payoffs. The instrument is one question: how much of your own payoff would you give up to prevent a gain of one unit to that person. Under a common payoff index v, the weight this recovers at profile x is not λ_ij but λ_ij·v′(x_j)/v′(x_i), so the elicited matrix is a positive diagonal similarity transform of the true one. The consequence is a sharp identification result. Λ is identified exactly up to positive diagonal similarity and no further, so a function of Λ is recoverable by an experimenter ignorant of v if and only if it is invariant under that transformation. What is invariant turns out to be exactly the part of the theory that decides whether peace is possible: every directed-cycle product, hence the bilateral product λ_R·λ_U; the spectrum, hence the spectral radius; and the zero pattern, hence which parties are resented by nobody. What is not invariant is the row sum — the attention budget on which the social-preference results rest — which is recovered only under linearity or at an equal-payoff profile. The paper proves the invariance, reports 14,376 numerical tests against twelve payoff indices confirming that the feasibility threshold does not move, identifies the two hypotheses that do bind (continuity and a common index), quantifies the finite-stake bias and removes it by extrapolation from two stake sizes, and sets out the resulting protocol, including a column-wise screening procedure that makes the unresented-party criterion operational and a synthetic-validity study that fixes the estimator, the grid and the equivalence margin the protocol should pre-register. It closes by restating what each prior result in the series predicts once the parameter is observed rather than assumed.

title: Where Did the Gold Go? Bolivia's Mining, Mercury, Law, and Forecasts

detail.title: Where Did the Gold Go? Bolivia's Mining, Mercury, Law, and Forecasts

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, identifiable personal data, animals, clinical interventions, or the collection of primary data requiring ethical approval. The research relies exclusively on publicly available and/or secondary data. Therefore, institutional ethics approval and informed consent were not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant or financial support from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The research was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: Bolivia’s recorded gold exports collapsed after 2023 while gold prices rose and the Banco Central de Bolivia (BCB) developed a domestic purchasing and export-administration channel. This paper separates extraction, commercialization, regulation, pollution, and prediction using 413 monthly gold-export observations (1992–May 2026), a 3,496-observation mineral panel, 80 interrupted-time-series specifications, temporal placebos, automatic break searches, two independent pre-policy counterfactuals, negative-control outcomes, local projections, orthogonal machine learning, regime models, and strict rolling-origin forecasting. All 80 policy-sequence specifications produce a negative post-level coefficient, and the two counterfactual models place observed post-policy exports near 30% of conditional counterfactual levels. Yet temporal randomization gives 𝑝 ≈ 0.059, the globally preferred one-break date is 2012, and the 2023 intervention is a compound sequence rather than an isolated treatment. A non-gold production negative control does not reproduce a comparable collapse. The legal analysis adds DS 5076 and the June–July 2026 BCB rules that tie export certification and quotas to the domestic BCB channel; because these rules post-date the outcome sample, they create a genuine distribution shift for forecasts. The environmental analysis maps sixteen distinct pathways spanning elemental-mercury vapor, methylmercury, fish and human biomonitoring, sediment, turbidity, channel change, forests, biodiversity, occupational exposure, and broader mine-waste risks. The strongest conclusion is therefore a change in the recorded gold commercialization regime, not a proven collapse of extraction and not a quantified national pollution dose-response.

title: Under the Radar: How Predatory Policing Distorts the Reporting of Violence against Women
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley and

detail.title: Under the Radar: How Predatory Policing Distorts the Reporting of Violence against Women
detail.abstract: A fundamental component of citizenship includes seeking protection from crime and violence. How do citizens make such claims to law enforcement when the police themselves are often predatory? The core argument is that police predation (1) discourages citizens from reporting crimes directly to the police while (2) shifting reporting towards intermediated channels. We argue that trust is the mechanism driving this reporting behavior. To test our theory, we focus on the reporting of violence against women (VAW) in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. We build an original database of reports to the police and to an intermediary (an independent hotline), then conduct descriptive and causal tests to show that exposure to police violence redirects reporting from the police to the intermediated hotline. Together, these findings bring together the claim-making and policing literatures to demonstrate that police violence incentivizes citizens to report VAW to alternative channels and, in their absence, to stay silent.

title: Determinants of Inclusive Development in Africa – Machine Learning Perspective
affiliations: University of Johannesburg, University of Johannesburg, University of Johannesburg and University of Johannesburg

detail.title: Determinants of Inclusive Development in Africa – Machine Learning Perspective
detail.abstract: Across African countries, inclusive development remains limited by persistent inequalities in access to opportunities, services, and economic participation. This study examines the determinants of inclusive development using the Inequality-Adjusted Human Development Index (IHDI) for 41 countries between 2008 and 2020. Leveraging machine learning–based regularisation techniques, we systematically evaluate a broad set of 48 potential drivers, including economic structure, governance, globalization, energy, and social variables. The analysis identifies skills, governance quality, employment, health, and access to clean energy and digital technologies as the most robust predictors of inclusive development. These findings highlight the structural and institutional conditions most strongly associated with broad-based human development, offering evidence-based guidance for policies aimed at reducing exclusion and promoting equitable growth in Africa.

title: Soybean Productivity, Land Expansion, Climate, and Biotechnology in Bolivia

detail.title: Soybean Productivity, Land Expansion, Climate, and Biotechnology in Bolivia

detail.abstract: We harmonize 113 Bolivian agro-environmental sources to separate soybean yield, cultivated area, and production from 1983/84 through 2025. The 2005/06 authorization of glyphosate-resistant soybean is treated as a legal-availability boundary, not observed farm adoption. Identification is challenged with interrupted time series, ARIMA and state-space counterfactuals, panel fixed effects, event studies, synthetic and factor controls, structural-break searches, placebo dates and crops, leave-one-out tests, specification curves, wild-cluster inference, weather randomization, and causal machine learning. The data do not identify a robust positive aggregate yield discontinuity at the 2005/06 boundary. Growth accounting is clearer: most long-run production growth reflects cultivated-area expansion, while yield growth is modest and volatile. Weather effects weaken under randomization-based inference, and aggregate land-use relations remain associational at the available spatial resolution. Forecasting provides an independent test of model stability. Expanding-window comparisons span structural time-series models, ARIMA, regularized autoregression, SVR, tree ensembles, boosting, Gaussian processes, conformalized quantile regression, and guarded ensembles. Area and production are substantially more forecastable than yield. Forecasts through 2030 therefore retain wide empirical uncertainty bands and are reconciled to the exact production-area-yield identity. The evidence supports strong conclusions about the extensive margin, but much weaker causal conclusions about legalization, adoption, or environmental conversion.

title: Towards an “Environmental Competition Law”?
affiliations: University Côte d'Azur

detail.title: Towards an “Environmental Competition Law”?
detail.abstract:
Climate change has placed competition law under mounting pressure to contribute to environmental protection, yet the discipline was not originally designed with sustainability in mind. Since 2019, competition authorities across Europe and beyond have progressively integrated environmental considerations into their enforcement priorities, soft-law instruments, and decisional practice — from green exemptions and out-of-market efficiencies tests to a markedly more permissive State aid framework geared towards decarbonization. This paper asks whether these developments amount to the emergence of a genuine “environmental competition law”: a body of law with its own rules, principles, and unequivocal purpose. It argues that they do not, or not yet. What can currently be observed is, at best, an uneven and fragmented evolution — a “soft transformation” in the field of anticompetitive practices, a more far-reaching but still uncodified shift in State aid law — rather than a settled revolution, and one marked by a striking asymmetry: environmental benefits may justify distortions of competition resulting from Member State subsidies, yet no comparable justification currently exists for foreign subsidies pursuing identical climate objectives under the Foreign Subsidies Regulation.

 

The paper then turns to what such a body of law could and should become. It proposes, first, a consolidation of existing developments, including the generalization of the out-of-market efficiencies test, a legislative basis for the green exemption, and an alignment of the Foreign Subsidies Regulation with State aid law so that verifiable climate benefits are no longer treated differently depending on the geographic origin of the funding. Second, it undertakes a reconstruction of the field’s normative foundations, grounding environmental protection as a constitutional “meta-interest” within EU law rather than a mere policy preference internal to competition authorities. On this basis, it develops a three-tier typology — convergence, commensurable divergence, and incommensurable divergence — that determines when, and only when, competition law should depart from the ordinary consumer welfare standard. In the residual category of incommensurable divergence, the paper proposes a “precautionary citizen-consumer standard”, in which the precautionary principle operates as a threshold test for departing from ordinary welfare analysis, while proportionality — drawing on recent case law of the French Cour de cassation reconciling competition law with fundamental rights — provides the technique for reconciling environmental and competitive interests without granting environmental protection automatic supremacy.

title: From Climate Science to Financial Decisions: An Integrated Framework for Translating Climate Risks into Actionable Financial Information
affiliations: Tyche Investments - Climate Consulting Group

detail.title: From Climate Science to Financial Decisions: An Integrated Framework for Translating Climate Risks into Actionable Financial Information
detail.abstract: This study examines how scientific knowledge on climate change can be translated into actionable financial information for financial-sector decision-makers. It addresses the gap between the growing availability of climate information and its effective application in financial decision-making. The study adopts a qualitative, secondary-research-based approach using evidence exclusively from peer-reviewed research. The literature is systematically synthesised through thematic analysis, evidence mapping, comparative analysis and analysis of climatefinancial transmission mechanisms. The study examines physical and transition risks, exposure and vulnerability, financial impacts, financial metrics, climate scenarios and financial decision-making. The analysis shows that climate information does not automatically constitute financial information. Its financial relevance depends on exposure, vulnerability and the mechanisms through which climate risks affect economic activities, businesses and financial assets. The findings further show that financial metrics are necessary to translate climate impacts into decision-relevant information. Physical and transition risks need to be considered together, while scenario analysis provides an important forward-looking perspective under uncertainty. The study develops an integrated climate-to-finance conceptual framework connecting scientific climate knowledge with climate risks, exposure and vulnerability, economic impacts, climate-financial transmission mechanisms, financial impacts, financial metrics and financial decision-making. The framework provides a structured basis for translating climate science into decision-specific financial information.

title: What makes a Bubble Pop?
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: What makes a Bubble Pop?
detail.abstract: The 2020-2021 Pokémon card market experienced an unprecedented surge in prices, attracting investors, collectors and widespread media attention. Many economists have argued that this boom was a speculative bubble where prices were inflated to unsustainable heights because of excessive optimism and expectations of future price increases. This study investigates whether the Pokémon card boom can be classified as a speculative bubble by analyzing the price performance of vintage and modern Pokémon cards over time. Price trends are compared alongside factors such as scarcity, popularity, nostalgia, and PSA population to distinguish cards whose values were primarily supported by fundamental demand from cards driven by speculation. The findings suggest that while speculation significantly inflated many card prices, cards with stronger underlying fundamentals experienced smaller declines and recovered more successfully after the bubble burst, indicating that both speculation and intrinsic value played important roles in determining long-term market performance.

title: Adaptive Hierarchical Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Lyapunov-Driven Primal-Dual Control for Fault-Resilient Resource Management in Software-Defined Fog-Edge Infrastructures
affiliations: National University Singapore, University of Tokyo, Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) - Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST), Students and The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK)

detail.title: Adaptive Hierarchical Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Lyapunov-Driven Primal-Dual Control for Fault-Resilient Resource Management in Software-Defined Fog-Edge Infrastructures
detail.abstract: Software-defined networking (SDN) fused with fog-edge computing promises near-user intelligence at ultra-low latency, yet contemporary resource managers still collapse under scale, lack enforceable quality-of-service (QoS) bounds, and remain brittle to node crashes and traffic spikes. We present Adaptive-HiDRL, a hierarchical multi-agent deep reinforcement learning architecture that couples graph neural network (GNN) topology encoders, chance-constrained primal-dual optimization, federated Lyapunov drift control with differential privacy, and a digital-twin Transformer forecaster. The system is cast as a constrained Markov decision process (CMDP) whose tail-latency and reliability chance constraints are converted into learnable Lagrange multipliers updated by projected gradient ascent. Centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE) lets a global SDN meta-controller allocate inter-domain budgets while local agents perform millisecond-scale intra-domain offloading. Extensive discrete-event simulations on Waxman topologies of up to 5 000 nodes demonstrate that Adaptive-HiDRL cuts mean latency by 76 %, energy draw by 63 %, and 99th-percentile latency by a factor of 4.1 relative to the strongest published baselines, while sustaining a 99.4 % task completion ratio under 30 % simultaneous node failures. Ablation and statistical tests confirm that each architectural component contributes measurably to the observed gains. The framework therefore sets a new reference point for scalable, QoS-guaranteed, and failure-resilient orchestration in next-generation distributed edge systems.
