title: Who Opened Federal Reserve Accounts After the 1980 Monetary Control Act?
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago and Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago

detail.title: Who Opened Federal Reserve Accounts After the 1980 Monetary Control Act?

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of Chicago Working Paper No. 2026-15
publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Recent debates about Federal Reserve accounts have focused on interpreting the provisions of the 1980 Monetary Control Act (MCA) which expanded account access to 35,000 additional depository institutions. However, these debates have not had the benefit of an empirical foundation on historic account take-up, which we provide here. We find that opening of accounts after 1980 was gradual and concentrated among the largest institutions. These findings are consistent with the expectations of contemporaries that the MCA was not expected or intended to displace the system of correspondent banking that served smaller institutions.

title: U.S. Economic Sanctions and the Institutionalization of Iran's Parallel Resistance Economy

detail.title: U.S. Economic Sanctions and the Institutionalization of Iran's Parallel Resistance Economy
detail.abstract: Under sustained secondary sanctions, how do target states with pre-existing military-commercial networks institutionalize dual economic structures, and with what consequences for sanctions effectiveness? This paper develops a dualism pathway: such networks formalize parallel institutions that insulate strategic sectors and elite revenues while imposing efficiency and welfare costs on the formal economy; the paper argues, and traces process evidence consistent with, a decline in the marginal coercive return to sanctions intensity once these institutions are formalized. Three hypotheses are stated in falsifiable terms. Using Iran as the case and the 2025-2026 "Economic Fury" campaign as the principal source of within-case intensity variation, the paper traces the mechanism through OFAC designation text, the fourteen-point Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, and General Licenses X and X1 (17 June-7 July 2026); reports a real, sourced World Bank time series on Iran's manufacturing share of GDP for the years it is available (2020-2023) rather than the full pre/post-episode window the theory calls for; and examines co-movement between sanctions intensity and two further public proxy series-the Iranian-crude-to-Brent discount and the gap between Iran's preferential (NIMA) and open-market exchange rates. It does not estimate a synthetic control or difference-indifferences model, and no causal point estimate is reported anywhere in the paper. Claims are stated in process-traced and associational language; a candidate instrumental strategy for future causal identification is proposed but not implemented. A similarly sourced Russia comparison (manufacturing share, Urals-Brent discount) bounds external validity. The paper's contribution is to specify, in falsifiable terms, an institutional mechanism converting sanctions pressure into durable dualism, to distinguish it from Lewis's dual-economy model and from the existing resistance-economy literature, and to report what the available public record does and does not show.

title: Asset Bubbles, Uncertainty Shocks, and Endogenous Feedback
affiliations: and

detail.title: Asset Bubbles, Uncertainty Shocks, and Endogenous Feedback
detail.abstract: Asset bubbles can create the uncertainty that sustains them. We build an economy in which a gap between an assets market price and the cost of covering its dividends finances project entry, expansion, and risk taking. Those projects generate future uncertainty, which strains investors capacity to bear risk and widens the bubble. This feedback can sustain several levels of bubbles and uncertainty even when shocks do not multiply on their own. Time structure determines the outcome. With a fixed ending date, equilibrium is unique regardless of feedback strength. When projects and uncertainty repeatedly renew, the same mechanism can produce multiple equilibria. Uncertainty shocks do not merely enlarge an existing bubble: by pushing risk beyond investors capacity to bear it, they can cause one to form in the first place. The model identifies stable and unstable outcomes and remains valid in a fully closed economy.

title: Materialising Equity in Community-Centric AI Tools: The Case against Technocracy
affiliations: The University of Manchester, The University of Manchester and The University of Manchester - Global Development Institute

detail.title: Materialising Equity in Community-Centric AI Tools: The Case against Technocracy
detail.abstract: This paper responds to calls for more grounded, empirical accounts on what responsible, community-centric AI actually looks like in practice. Using the theoretical framework of advantageous digital incorporation, it examines Commons Connect, a participatory AI tool that is being used by smallholding farmers in rural India to support more equitable planning and distribution of natural resource assets at village levels. Its main message is that steering AI systems towards more equitable outcomes requires an approach that de-centres AI and its affordances, is rooted in strong problem framing, makes its focus on the wider structures of domination and oppression explicit, and demonstrates restraint in implementation.

title: The UK-Israel FTA in a Politically Dynamic Era: Economic Rationale, Moral
affiliations: Ariel University - Department of Economics and Business Administration and Ariel University

detail.title: The UK-Israel FTA in a Politically Dynamic Era: Economic Rationale, Moral

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study was approved by Ariel University's Institutional Review Board, approval number AU-SOC-DS-20240531.

detail.abstract: This paper examines post-Brexit UK-Israel trade relations through role theory, focusing on how national role conceptions (NRCs) shape trade policy. Based on official documents, media sources, and interviews, it shows strong mutual incentives to replace the 2019 continuity agreement with an upgraded free trade agreement centered on digital services, innovation, and investment. Negotiations progressed through five rounds between 2022 and 2024, aligning the UK's and Israel's strategic economic roles. However, negotiations were suspended in May 2025 under the Starmer government, reflecting a strategic shift toward an NRC that emphasizes international law. Consequently, talks remain stalled with a resumption deemed highly unlikely, notwithstanding the subsequent ceasefire achieved in late 2025.

title: When Growth Does Not Guarantee Electrification: Evidence from a developing country in SSA
affiliations: University of Zambia (UNZA) and University of Zambia (UNZA)

detail.title: When Growth Does Not Guarantee Electrification: Evidence from a developing country in SSA

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There are no competing interests to declare

declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for this study

detail.abstract: Universal electricity access remains a primary development objective in Sub-Saharan Africa. Conventional economic theory suggests that macroeconomic growth and structural transformation accelerate infrastructure expansion. This study examines whether economic growth translates into short-run electrification in Zambia using annual data from 1990 to 2024. The analysis employs an Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) bounds testing approach alongside nested short-run dynamic models with Newey-West standard errors. The results provide no evidence of a stable longrun level relationship between electricity access and standard development indicators. In the short run, gross domestic product (GDP) per capita, urbanization, and industrialization do not exhibit a statistically detectable relationship with annual changes in electricity access. Electrification exhibits negative temporal dependence, suggesting partial reversal in annual expansion rates independent of macroeconomic fluctuations. Foreign direct investment displays weak evidence of a negative association with short-run access expansion. These findings suggest that electrification in Zambia follows an independent infrastructure trajectory rather than responding mechanically to economic growth. Policymakers could consider direct, infrastructure-specific financing mechanisms rather than relying on broad economic expansion to deliver universal access.

title: When Protection Works but the Portfolio Still Lags: Long-Horizon Evidence on Downside Protection, Benchmark-Relative Drawdowns, and Persistent Equity Exposure

detail.title: When Protection Works but the Portfolio Still Lags: Long-Horizon Evidence on Downside Protection, Benchmark-Relative Drawdowns, and Persistent Equity Exposure

detail.abstract: A defensive strategy can meet its downside objective and still lag equity for years. The analysis evaluates both dimensions within the same rolling holding periods. The design is intentionally simple: U.S. equity buy-and-hold, a monthly rebalanced 50/50 equity-cash allocation, and a 12-month defensive trend rule whose position uses only information available through the previous month. The evaluation covers 5-, 10-, 15-, and 20-year periods, treating the signal horizon and blend weights as fixed design choices rather than tuning them to maximize the reported results. In the July 1927-June 2026 French-series sample, the trend rule reduces maximum drawdown in 98.2% of 20-year periods. Among those protected periods, however, 60.3% finish with lower terminal wealth than equity buy-and-hold, and the median longest benchmark-relative underwater period lasts 195 months. Fixed combinations of persistent equity exposure and tactical defense reveal a second distinction: greater persistent equity exposure is associated with substantially shallower benchmark-relative drawdowns, while underwater duration changes much less. The qualitative pattern remains under fixed trading-cost assumptions and in an independent reconstruction using Shiller and FRED data, although the magnitudes differ. The analysis considers realized downside protection together with the benchmark-relative path experienced while obtaining it. These are distinct portfolio-design dimensions and should be assessed separately.

title: The Oracle Problem in Regulated Tokenization: Institutional Facts and the Limits of Trust Minimization
affiliations: , Masaryk University, Department Finance,  Faculty of Economics and Administration and

detail.title: The Oracle Problem in Regulated Tokenization: Institutional Facts and the Limits of Trust Minimization
detail.abstract: The blockchain oracle problem states that a distributed ledger cannot verify data that originates outside it. The literature has addressed this problem predominantly through trust minimization. Decentralized oracle networks, redundant sources, staking and reputation mechanisms are treated as the canonical remedies. Reliance on a single authoritative source is treated as a design deficiency. This paper argues that the framing rests on an unexamined ontological assumption, and that the assumption fails precisely where tokenization is now moving, namely regulated securities markets. Drawing on Searle's distinction between brute facts and institutional facts, we observe that the oracle literature implicitly treats all off-chain data as brute facts. Temperatures, prices and delivery states exist independently of human agreement. They are therefore approachable through convergent observation by independent parties. Decentralization works because observation scales. Securities reference data are not of this kind. A securities identifier does not exist prior to its conferral by an entity holding recognized competence under ISO 6166 and the delegation arrangements of the Association of National Numbering Agencies. No quantity of independent observers can observe such an identifier into being. We develop the argument in two movements. A structured review of the oracle literature maps how the problem has been formulated, which application domains have been examined and why regulated capital market infrastructure has remained outside its scope. We then examine the Smart Bond Contract pilot of March 2026, in which DZ BANK issued a crypto security under the German Electronic Securities Act on a public blockchain. The architecture is instructive because it combines both fact types within a single transaction. We conclude that for institutional facts the design objective is not trust minimization but legal equivalence. The task is to establish that the on-chain representation carries the normative force of the off-chain constitutive act. We anticipate the objection that distributed consensus itself confers status functions, and we delimit the conditions under which it cannot.

title: Self-healing Machine Learning Models for Automated Fault Detection and Recovery in IT Systems

detail.title: Self-healing Machine Learning Models for Automated Fault Detection and Recovery in IT Systems

The author has no personal or financial relationships with any organizations that could have influenced this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, animals, or patient data. All data used in this research were obtained from publicly available datasets (BUSI - Breast Ultrasound Images Dataset). Therefore, no ethics approval was required.

detail.abstract: Modern information technology (IT) worlds are increasingly complex, highly interconnected, with many microservices, containers and distributed streams of data, and failure modes that are too specific and numerous for an operation team to keep track of. As a result of this so-complicated operating condition, something new has been sprung on the scene: self-healing machine learning (or ML) models. This review combines data from 55 peer-reviewed and archival papers published mainly during the period 2019-2025 and focuses on a small number of basic autonomic-computing studies, collating them to get a general picture of the current state of the art for selfhealing ML in the field of IT fault management. Based on the Monitor-Analyse-Plan-Execute over a shared Knowledge base (MAPE-K) reference model, the review covers detection algorithms, root-cause localisation techniques, recovery-action selection strategies and datasets and metrics for assessing them. It showed an obvious direction from single model based anomaly detection towards hybrid pipelines of deep sequence model and graph-based causal reasoning/reinforcement learning based closed-loop remediation. These detection metrics (self-reported precision and F1 scores) are typically above 0.85 in controlled benchmarks, while recovery actions are limited by the scarcity of data, lack of explainability for the models' decisions, and/or the risk of completely autonomous execution. A taxonomy of autonomy level in the field of selfhealing systems, and a list of outstanding challenges are introduced, including and not limited to concept drift, cross-domain generalisation, safety validation, and human/human-machine trust calibration. The findings should inform researchers and practitioners to orient them on methodological gaps which most limit the shift from supervised to autonomous self-healing IT operations.

title: Trading Scope for Credibility in Difference-in-Differences
affiliations: Ashoka University - Department of Economics and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Trading Scope for Credibility in Difference-in-Differences
detail.abstract: When parallel trends fails for some treated cohorts but not others, the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) becomes hard to recover. We propose changing the estimand rather than defending it. The credible-subpopulation local ATT (LATT) is the effect for the subpopulation of cohorts whose parallel trends is credible, and it is point-identified under parallel trends for the selected cohorts alone, a weaker requirement that can hold when the ATT's fails. It is estimated by reweighting standard group-time effects toward those cohorts, and paired with honest sensitivity bounds on the residual violation that a pre-trend screen cannot rule out. The method's advantage grows with how informative pre-trends are about post-treatment violations, as simulations confirm. In an application, a significantly positive pooled estimate of the shale boom's effect on local house prices proves to rest on cohorts already trending before onset, and the credible subpopulation reveals no effect.

title: The Price of an Arc: Rerouting and the Incidence of Shipping Pollution
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS), Department of Economics

detail.title: The Price of an Arc: Rerouting and the Incidence of Shipping Pollution

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I have no conflict of interest to declare.
declarations.ethicsApproval: N.A.
declarations.funderStatement: I have no funder information to declare.

detail.abstract: Environmental instruments price damage only when the source has a fixed address, and a ship chooses its address voyage by voyage. When the Red Sea closed in December 2023, the same goods sailed 4,133 nautical miles farther around the Cape. I solve both corridors on an ocean grid and read the diversion in satellite columns over 53 countries' coasts. A standard deviation of corridor exposure raises city nitrogen dioxide by 2-3.5 percent, arriving on the wind, and moves exposure off 81 million people on the estimation coasts onto 37 million who earn two fifths as much. A tonne of fuel on the Red Sea arc delivers 3.7 times the exposure it delivers on the Cape arc, yet every fuel-scaled instrument prices the pair at 0.7. I derive the efficient ratio of arc exposure charges, which does not depend on what exposure is worth, and carry it to twenty-eight passages. The same calculation applies to any emitter that chooses among routes.

title: Code is not Law: The Congruence Dilemma and the Limits of Legality in AI-based Public Administration
affiliations: University of Exeter

detail.title: Code is not Law: The Congruence Dilemma and the Limits of Legality in AI-based Public Administration
detail.abstract: The premise that encoding a rule in software is a way of administering it now underwrites much of the digital state. Critics mainly contest it by disputing whether algorithmic systems are accurate, fair or legitimate enough to bear it, a framing that concedes the decisive ground by treating law and code as competing technologies for one task. This article argues instead that regulation and legality are different properties, and that competence at the first entails nothing about capacity for the second. Reconstructing legality through Fuller's desiderata, we locate the distinctive failure at the eighth, congruence between declared rule and official action, and specify it as a congruence dilemma. Where an external declared norm survives, the system enacts rather than states its operative rule, so divergence must be reconstructed by investigation rather than observed by comparison; where computational implementation progressively becomes the de facto specification of a delegated standard, there is nothing left for administration to be incongruent with. Crucially, the resulting failure is not an inability to detect incongruence-Robodebt was detected repeatedly and continued anyway-but the severance of detection from correction, which automation achieves by making detected incongruence cheap to perpetuate at scale. We then show that generative AI introduces a distinct failure we call the specification illusion: a natural-language system prompt can institutionally impersonate a promulgated rule while possessing none of a promulgated rule's authoritative priority over implementation. We accept that determinism, formal runtime constraint and trajectory auditing are all technically achievable, and argue that this sharpens rather than weakens the thesis, because technical conformance is neither necessary nor sufficient for legal bindingness. We conclude by specifying contestability as a four-part institutional requirement-separation (as a binding legal envelope), record, adjudicative remedy and propagation-and assess the EU, Canadian, US and Australian instruments against it.

title: The Bankability of Power Purchase Agreements in Nigeria's Transitioning Electricity Market
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Bankability of Power Purchase Agreements in Nigeria's Transitioning Electricity Market
detail.abstract: This article assesses the bankability of Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) in Nigeria across two distinct market regimes: the Nigerian Bulk Electricity Trading Plc (NBET) single-buyer model that governed the sector from privatisation in 2013, and the bilateral trading framework inaugurated by NERC Order No NERC/2024/058 of 25 July 2024, issued pursuant to section 7(2) of the Electricity Act 2023. Bankability, as used in this article, denotes the capacity of a PPA to support project finance on commercial terms, a function of three conditions: efficient risk allocation, enforceable payment obligations against creditworthy counterparties, and credible security mechanisms that would actually pay out in a default scenario. The article applies this three-part test to the single-buyer framework and finds that while the framework was structurally coherent in design, each condition was systematically undermined in practice by institutional insolvency, accumulated payment defaults, and an enforcement gap that contract drafting alone could not cure. It then carries the analysis forward into the ongoing transition to bilateral trading and argues that the transition, while structurally necessary, relocates rather than resolves the underlying problem: the credit risk that NBET absorbed imperfectly has been redistributed to distribution companies whose existing financial positions were already precarious, and four consecutive quarters of NERC performance data since the bilateral trading Order confirm that those positions have not improved. Drawing on comparative analysis of Ghana and Kenya, the article closes by identifying the specific sequencing of fiscal, institutional, and regulatory conditions without which the bilateral model cannot deliver bankable PPAs, and assesses the realistic prospects of those conditions being achieved.

title:
Legal and Ideological Citizenship
Africans at the Crossroads of Global Trends and Tensions

detail.title:
Legal and Ideological Citizenship
Africans at the Crossroads of Global Trends and Tensions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This is a sole-authored paper. The project responded to the Call for Papers by the African Association for Rhetoric (AAR). The paper was presented at the African Association for Rhetoric (AAR) 2026 conference (July 4, 2026).

detail.abstract: Modern constitutional democracies typically vest sovereignty in "the people," as reflected in standard preambular formulations such as "We the people." A survey of 52 of Africa's 54 states confirms similar sovereign attributions, expressed through diverse constitutional and democratic configurations. Yet in many African contexts, citizens rarely assert this sovereign status in everyday interactions with political representatives and state institutions, even in states with relatively active civil societies, such as Nigeria. Persistent inequality, weak service delivery, internal displacement, and statelessness raise critical questions about the gap between constitutional and lived citizenship on the continent. This paper examines African citizenship from legal, ideological, and rhetorical perspectives and argues that the rhetorical perspective is not one lens among three but the analytical home of the other two. Its central claim is that rhetoric, not political science or information technology alone, can answer the intent-outcome accountability question, because only rhetoric possesses a formal theory of how governance commitment language generates enforceable obligations. Methodologically, the paper combines comparative constitutional analysis with rhetorical analysis of political discourse, reintroducing the Ciceronian question, Qui bono? (Who benefits?), as a computationally operationalizable diagnostic. Building on Bayart, Ellis, and Hibou's analysis of disorder as political instrumentality, and on Herbst's account of the patronage basis of African state power, it argues that the strategic maintenance of instability undermines African states' commitments to the SDGs and the African Union's Agenda 2063. Finally, it reinterprets the legal doctrines of legitimate expectation and respondeat superior as rhetorical and normative frameworks for reconstructing accountability relationships between African states and their citizens in the twenty-first century.

title: An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of the People, V: The AI Productivity Shock - Redistributing Time, not Money
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of the People, V: The AI Productivity Shock - Redistributing Time, not Money
detail.abstract:
This paper examines how redistribution of working hours, rather than excess monetary expansion, may respond to structural job displacement caused by an AI productivity shock, and compares the two paths under the directional criterion of the Wealth of the People. AI may lower some costs through supply expansion while also displacing established jobs. Excess monetary expansion may stabilize nominal expenditure, but it can raise rigid costs such as housing through asset prices and cannot itself accomplish the structural reallocation of labor. 
      The paper advances a conditional alternative: a productivity-dividend-funded reduction in working hours that broadly maintains weekly income. Shorter hours can only buffer employment pressure to a limited extent. Their more important role is to release blocks of discretionary time which, where resource and institutional conditions permit, generate a discretionary expenditure flow. That flow enters absorbing activities, supports employment across their operational, managerial, technical, professional, and frontline functions, and stimulates upstream production through demand for premises, equipment, content, and other intermediate inputs. This process may also give rise to new activity domains, industry forms, and job configurations, advancing the rebalancing of industrial structure and labor allocation. 
      The argument neither presupposes that a particular industry will expand nor establishes that a four-day workweek preserves employment. Its validity depends on whether productivity dividends can sustain income, whether absorbing activities have sufficient employment-absorption capacity, whether labor can enter and exit those activities, whether pricing and voluntary exchange function effectively, and whether additional demand becomes employment rather than primarily higher prices. Working-hours redistribution is therefore a conditional policy choice: an improvement in the Wealth of the People can be established only when employment, costs, free time, and the remaining welfarecost components do not move adversely. The paper conducts an internal-consistency check of this mechanism, not an empirical validation.

title: Innovation, Competition and Debt Funding Shock
affiliations: , University of Bristol - Department of Finance and Accounting, University of Bristol and University of Bristol

detail.title: Innovation, Competition and Debt Funding Shock
detail.abstract: We study how debt financing costs shape the link between product-market competition and corporate innovation. Using the European Central Bank's Corporate Sector Purchase Programme as a funding-cost shock, we compare firms whose eligible bonds were purchased with firms whose bonds were eligible but not purchased. Treated firms face lower bond financing costs, increase bond debt, and raise R&D, while non-R&D investment does not respond. The average response is close to estimates from eligibleversus-ineligible designs, but the average conceals the result of interest: the innovation effect is confined to highly competitive industries and is driven by firms with low product-market shares. Cheaper debt raises the value of innovation for laggards when competitive pressure makes closing technological gaps strategically valuable. The real effects of monetary interventions therefore depend on product-market structure and on firm position within the industry. Cheaper finance and competition act as complements in stimulating innovation.

title: Formulation and Optimization of Directional Overcurrent Relay Coordination Using SESNO Optimization Algorithm
affiliations: University of Jos, University of Jos, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Jubail Industrial College

detail.title: Formulation and Optimization of Directional Overcurrent Relay Coordination Using SESNO Optimization Algorithm

keywords.keywords: Directional overcurrent relay coordinationSENSOIEC Standard Inverse characteristicIEEE test systemspower system protection.

detail.abstract: Renewable energy integration into modern distribution networks introduces bidirectional fault currents and variable fault levels that compromise conventional directional overcurrent relay (DOCR) coordination. To achieve optimal DOCR coordination, it requires minimizing total relay operating time while satisfying coordination time interval (CTI) constraints, nonlinear, non-convex optimization problem that becomes more challenging with increasing network size. This study proposes the Smart Enhanced and Self-adaptive Olfactory (SENSO) optimizer, an enhanced Smell Agent Optimization (SAO) algorithm integrating tent-chaotic initialization, Fitness Distance Balance (FDB) guide selection, adaptive DE/best/1 mutation, Gaussian barebone exploitation, and boundary reflection. Evaluated on the IEEE 6-bus, 14-bus, and 33-bus systems over 30 independent runs, SENSO achieved the lowest mean total operating times (6.9033 s, 30.0040 s, and 56.9250 s), outperforming the closest competitor by up to 17.59\%, while satisfying all CTI constraints and maintaining computation times below 0.13 s per run.

title: Empirically Grounded LLM Agents for Simulating Human Behavioral Adaptation During Urban Heatwaves: A Philadelphia Case Study
affiliations: Pennsylvania State University and Northeastern University

detail.title: Empirically Grounded LLM Agents for Simulating Human Behavioral Adaptation During Urban Heatwaves: A Philadelphia Case Study
detail.abstract: Urban heatwaves increasingly disrupt daily routines, activity timing, and access to critical resources, yet cities often lack tools for simulating how heterogeneous residents adjust behavior under extreme heat. Existing mobility and survey data can describe observed responses during past events, while conventional agent-based models often rely on fixed behavioral rules that may not capture context-sensitive adaptation. This study develops an empirically grounded large language model agent framework for simulating routine-constrained human behavioral adaptation during urban heatwaves. The framework integrates American Community Survey demographic profiles, American Time Use Survey daily routines, OpenStreetMap and SafeGraph spatial context, and LLM-based decision reasoning within an urban simulation environment. Using Philadelphia as a case study, we simulate routine summer conditions and a documented July 2024 heatwave and validate model outputs against ATUS-derived normal activity profiles and an independent heatwave household survey. Results show that empirical grounding substantially improves the reproduction of normal daily routines, increasing mean correlation with empirical activity profiles from 0.528 to 0.912 and reducing mean squared error from 0.066 to 0.008. Under heatwave conditions, the grounded model also better reproduces observed activity profiles, increasing mean correlation from 0.349 to 0.836 and reducing mean squared error from 0.098 to 0.012. These findings demonstrate that empirical demographic and time-use grounding can improve LLM-agent simulations of heatwave adaptation and provide a flexible tool for evaluating urban resilience strategies under realistic behavioral constraints.

title: Energy Transition in Niger to the 2050 Horizon: A MAED-MESSAGE Modeling Framework for Sahel Countries
affiliations: Abdou Moumouni University of Niamey and Abdou Moumouni University of Niamey

detail.title: Energy Transition in Niger to the 2050 Horizon: A MAED-MESSAGE Modeling Framework for Sahel Countries
detail.abstract: This study presents the first integrated MAED-MESSAGE modeling for Niger to the 2050 horizon, under three contrasted energy scenarios: trend-based (S1-BAU), national sovereignty (S2-SNAE+), and climate commitment (S3-NDC+). MAED disaggregates final electricity demand from 3,334 GWh in 2021 to 24,918, 33,497, and 43,152 GWh in 2050 depending on the scenario, which constitutes the central constraint transmitted to MESSAGE for electricity mix optimization. Results reveal that renewable energy sources (solar PV, Tarka wind, Kandadji hydropower) reach an installed capacity of 731 MW by 2035, representing 43.6% of the non-nuclear capacity. Assessed against non-nuclear production, RES cover approximately 70.6% (S1-BAU), 49.8% (S2-SNAE+), and 32.1% (S3-NDC+) by 2035, the latter figure aligning with the SNAE target of 30% RES. Electricity sovereignty is achieved by 2030–2035 in all three scenarios (national production ≥ 97%), ending historical dependence on Nigerian imports (71% in 2022). CO2 emissions from the electricity sector drop to 0.122 Mt in S1-BAU by 2035 (−92% vs. 2030), reflecting the massive decarbonization driven by RES and mix diversification. However, the NDC target of 60% RES in the electricity mix by 2050 reveals a critical gap: a second post-2035 investment phase of +14,485 MW of solar is required for the NDC+ scenario. The fully reproducible MAED-MESSAGE methodology constitutes a reference framework for assessing energy policies and climate commitments in AES and Sahel countries.

reference: FRB of Chicago Working Paper No. 2026-16
title: Crypto Is Coming of Age: The Case of Bitcoin's Rising Beta
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, Ulm University - Department of Mathematics and Economics and UC Berkeley

detail.title: Crypto Is Coming of Age: The Case of Bitcoin's Rising Beta

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of Chicago Working Paper No. 2026-16
publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper shows that Bitcoin has transitioned from a largely idiosyncratic crypto asset into a risk-on asset with returns resembling that of the broad U.S. stock market. We estimate time-varying Bitcoin betas with respect to a tech-heavy stock index (NASDAQ), a broader economy equity index (Dow Jones), and the 10-year Treasury bond returns. Across all beta specifications, multi-factor regressions, and structural break tests, we find that Bitcoin’s equity exposure rises substantially over time, turning statistically larger than zero around 2020. In contrast, the betas for the Treasury bond returns are not distinguishable from zero. Surprisingly, after controlling for the exposure to the Dow Jones Index, the exposure to NASDAQ is small and statistically insignificant throughout our sample period. This last finding is at odds with the common wisdom that Bitcoin behaves like a decentralized tech asset and points towards Bitcoin being mostly driven by broad stock-market sentiment.

title: Disruptive Learning in the Artificial Intelligence Era: A Metacognitive Creative Destruction Model for Educational Innovation
affiliations: and International Hellenic University (IHU)

detail.title: Disruptive Learning in the Artificial Intelligence Era: A Metacognitive Creative Destruction Model for Educational Innovation
detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Metacognitive Creative Destruction (MCD) Model to explain how educational disruptive innovation can emerge through cognitive deconstruction and reconstruction processes in Artificial Intelligence (AI) enhanced environments. While prior research explores metacognition, unlearning, and educational change separately, an integrated model explaining how individuals intentionally dismantle outdated knowledge structures to foster adaptive and innovative learning has not emerged, yet. Grounded on Schumpeter's theory of "Creative Destruction", the MCD model conceptualizes "Destruction" at the cognitive level, where AI acts as a metacognitive spark for reflective disruption and epistemic revision. The model, which was developed to monitor the educational transition towards disruptive innovation, includes thirteen (13) empirically tested variables grouped into core adaptive capacities, contextual enablers / inhibitors, and learning outcomes. To validate the concept, quantitative primary research took place and data from 1,498 current and alumni students-educators of the "Administration and Management of Education Units" postgraduate program of the International Hellenic University in Greece were analyzed using structural equation modeling (SEM). Results confirmed the model's robustness and predictive validity towards disruptive educational innovation. The findings suggest that fostering in a recursive learning cycle, metacognitive flexibility, unlearning propensity, epistemic humility, the incorporation of AI as cognitive and reflective partner and psychological readiness for revision may significantly enhance knowledge reconstruction and disruptive innovation in education systems. In a sentence, the study aims to share with academia, both a validated measurement model and a theoretical lens for understanding transformational learning towards disruptive innovation, in the AI era.

title:
Legal and Ideological Citizenship:
Africans at the Crossroads of Global Trends and Tensions

detail.title:
Legal and Ideological Citizenship:
Africans at the Crossroads of Global Trends and Tensions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This paper was solely authored by me. I presented the paper at the African Association for Rhetoric (AAR) 2026 conference on July 4, 2026.

detail.abstract: Modern constitutional democracies typically vest sovereignty in "the people," as reflected in standard preambular formulations such as "We the people." A survey of 52 of Africa's 54 states confirms similar sovereign attributions, expressed through diverse constitutional and democratic configurations. Yet in many African contexts, citizens rarely assert this sovereign status in everyday interactions with political representatives and state institutions, even in states with relatively active civil societies, such as Nigeria. Persistent inequality, weak service delivery, internal displacement, and statelessness raise critical questions about the gap between constitutional and lived citizenship on the continent. This paper examines African citizenship from legal, ideological, and rhetorical perspectives and argues that the rhetorical perspective is not one lens among three but the analytical home of the other two. Its central claim is that rhetoric, not political science or information technology alone, can answer the intent-outcome accountability question, because only rhetoric possesses a formal theory of how governance commitment language generates enforceable obligations. Methodologically, the paper combines comparative constitutional analysis with rhetorical analysis of political discourse, reintroducing the Ciceronian question, Qui bono? (Who benefits?), as a computationally operationalizable diagnostic. Building on Bayart, Ellis, and Hibou's analysis of disorder as political instrumentality, and on Herbst's account of the patronage basis of African state power, it argues that the strategic maintenance of instability undermines African states' commitments to the SDGs and the African Union's Agenda 2063. Finally, it reinterprets the legal doctrines of legitimate expectation and respondeat superior as rhetorical and normative frameworks for reconstructing accountability relationships between African states and their citizens in the twenty-first century.

title: The Axioms and Apparatus of Keybernomics

detail.title: The Axioms and Apparatus of Keybernomics

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts to declare
declarations.funderStatement: self funded

detail.abstract:
As a whole, this work is an attempt to describe money and the economy in information theoretical terms, from the work of Claude Shannon in his Mathematical Theory of Communication (1948). Shannon described information as the resolution of uncertainty. This is the same mathematical relationship described by Keynes in his Treatise on Probability (1921).
The theory proposed here can be compressed to one line:
                                                        V(money) = a/h
The name “Keybernomics” is based on a combination of Keynes, cybernetics, and economics. Cybernetics
was the word coined by Norbert Weiner to describe information in its use in complex, self-regulating,
adaptive and autonomous systems: as a code, command, and feedback. The origin of the word, Kubernetes,
from the ancient Greek for “steersman” which is also the root of the word “government.”
This document states, in a single place and in plain language, the complete Keybernomics apparatus: the
four axioms on which the framework rests, and the thirty-three numbered results that derive from them,
together with their corollaries.

title: Intermediary Removal and Legacy Persistence: Evidence from Stablecoin Migration
affiliations: Hanyang University and Hanyang University

detail.title: Intermediary Removal and Legacy Persistence: Evidence from Stablecoin Migration
detail.abstract: Removing an intermediary does not ensure that its legacy claim disappears. We study seven blockchain launches in which Circle introduced issuer-native USDC beside an existing bridged version. Using 5,822 historical contract-state observations, we find that native USDC reaches an equal-weight supply share of 53.6% after roughly six months, while bridged supply falls 56.1%. Transition speed varies sharply: a native majority becomes durable after 47 to 299 days on five chains and remains unreached in the observed tails of two. A simple switching-cost model explains persistent coexistence and predicts that parallel contracts can increase fragmentation during transition. Native issuance also need not equal bridged contraction because local demand changes at the same time. The evidence identifies gradual intermediary exit as a distinct economic margin of digital-asset adoption.

title: The Two Faces of Risk in the Tragedy of the Commons: Risk Aversion, Price Uncertainty, and Strategic Resource Exploitation
affiliations: University of Glasgow, Umeå University and

detail.title: The Two Faces of Risk in the Tragedy of the Commons: Risk Aversion, Price Uncertainty, and Strategic Resource Exploitation
detail.abstract: We study how risk aversion and uncertainty shape the strategic exploitation of a common-property resource. We develop a continuous-time stochastic differential game in which heterogeneous agents extract a renewable resource non-cooperatively while facing two correlated sources of uncertainty, shocks to the resource stock and fluctuations in the output price. We implement the model in a fishery setting, with logistic biomass growth, stochastic recruitment, and a geometric Brownian output price, providing a concrete environment for mechanisms that extend more broadly to competitively exploited renewable resources. The resulting coupled Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equations are solved numerically using finite differences and policy iteration, with the solution method validated against an analytically tractable linear-quadratic benchmark. Our results reveal two opposing faces of risk in the tragedy of the commons. Greater risk aversion reduces equilibrium extraction and thereby mitigates over-exploitation, acting as a partial substitute for cooperation. Although it does not eliminate the strategic externality, risk aversion reduces aggregate extraction by up to roughly forty percent in our experiments, while welfare measured in a common monetary metric increases. By contrast, greater price uncertainty increases extraction once agents are risk-averse, as agents accelerate the conversion of uncertain future resource revenues into current returns. This volatility channel is essentially absent under risk neutrality. These opposing effects distinguish greater aversion to risk from greater exposure to risk and help reconcile conflicting findings in the literature on uncertainty and commonproperty resource exploitation. We further show how the two channels interact with heterogeneity in extraction costs, with implications for the management of strategically exploited renewable resources.

title: Digital Bank Run Dynamics: A Mean Field Hawkes Process Model with Network Contagion and Optimal Intervention under a Stochastic M0 Ceiling

detail.title: Digital Bank Run Dynamics: A Mean Field Hawkes Process Model with Network Contagion and Optimal Intervention under a Stochastic M0 Ceiling
detail.abstract:
This paper develops a unified mathematical framework for digital bank run dynamics, extending the static coordination model of Vijay Kundan Kadali's "Banking Stability as a Coordination Problem: Government Intervention, Confidence, and Moral Hazard" (2026) to a stochastic, network-aware, and strategically rigorous treatment. Withdrawal dynamics are modelled as a Hawkes self-exciting point process with intensity

Λ(t) = µ + αe−β(t−ti)ti<t

where the branching ratio ρ = α/β determines whether the system is subcritical or supercritical. The physical currency constraint is formalised as a stochastic boundary Mt, creating a race condition between cumulative withdrawals Wt and the RBI’s intervention capacity. Network contagion is modelled via a graph-Laplacian PDE whose algebraic connectivity λ2 determines systemic fragility. Government intervention is derived as the solution to a three-population Mean Field Game.

Three theorems are proved:
1. Supercriticality implies finite-time blow-up of withdrawal intensity
2. A systemic crisis occurs if and only if λ2 < λ∗ 2
3. The optimal intervention policy is bang-bang.

Monte Carlo simulation over 105 paths calibrated to Indian monetary data confirms a crisis probability of 1.000 within 2.70 hours in the supercritical regime, with an effective intervention window of approximately five minutes. Policy implications address pre-commitment rules, network minimum-exposure requirements, and CBDC as logistical infrastructure that increases the maximum intervention rate ¯u.

title: Climate-Resilient Fiscal Policy: Integrating Climate Shocks into Sovereign Budgeting, Debt Sustainability, and Public Investment Planning

detail.title: Climate-Resilient Fiscal Policy: Integrating Climate Shocks into Sovereign Budgeting, Debt Sustainability, and Public Investment Planning
detail.abstract:
Climate change has become a core fiscal risk, not an external environmental issue. As the report states, “Climate change is now a fiscal event, not an environmental one.” Acute disasters and chronic climate trends simultaneously erode revenue, raise expenditure, and push sovereign debt paths upward, especially for small and vulnerable states. Standard fiscal institutions—budgets, debt‑sustainability frameworks, and public‑investment systems—remain built for a stationary climate, creating a widening gap between assumed and actual sovereign exposure.

The report maps climate risk through three transmission channels—physical, transition, and macro‑fiscal spillovers—and shows how they interact to amplify losses. It demonstrates that recurrent climate shocks shift debt trajectories upward and widen their tails, making conventional debt‑sustainability analysis systematically understate risk. It further shows that resilient public investment, when appraised with climate‑informed methods, yields high avoided‑loss returns and is essential to reducing long‑run fiscal exposure.

A practical three‑stage policy sequence is proposed:

  1. Resilient budgeting (climate budget tagging, contingency reserves, disaster escape clauses).

  2. Climate‑sensitive debt and investment systems (fan‑chart DSA, resilience clauses, C‑PIMA appraisal).

  3. Layered risk‑finance instruments (parametric insurance, contingent credit, catastrophe bonds).

The report concludes that climate‑resilient fiscal policy is not a menu but a sequence: each stage enables the next, and skipping ahead produces instruments without durability. As summarized in the text, “A country that cannot see and absorb its first shock cannot credibly plan its fiftieth.”

title: The Global Clean Cooking Transition: Economic Pathways to Universal Access - How Affordability, Infrastructure Reliability, and Digital Payment Systems Shape Adoption across Low-income Regions

detail.title: The Global Clean Cooking Transition: Economic Pathways to Universal Access - How Affordability, Infrastructure Reliability, and Digital Payment Systems Shape Adoption across Low-income Regions
detail.abstract: Two billion people still cook primarily with wood, charcoal, dung, or kerosene. That number has fallen from 3.1 billion in 2000, but the geography of the remaining deficit has shifted in a way the stove-distribution programmes of the last two decades did not anticipate. Using World Bank household-energy, electrification, income, and Global Findex series for 189 countries through 2023, this paper shows that national clean cooking access is, first, an affordability outcome and, second, an infrastructure outcome. Among low-and middle-income countries, log income per capita alone accounts for 68 percent of the cross-sectional variation in 2023 access rates. Electricity access adds a further four points of explained variance. Account ownership-the standard proxy for digital payment systems-adds nothing once income and electricity are controlled, and the coefficient on accounts turns negative. Kenya, with 90 percent adult account ownership and 32 percent clean cooking access, is the existence proof: mobile money can re-denomination a fuel bill; it cannot create a household energy budget or a last-mile cylinder network. The same pattern appears in Uganda, Ghana, and Zambia, where digital finance and electrification have run ahead of cooking. The countries that did close the gap-Indonesia, Viet Nam, India, China, Peruclosed it by making modern fuel cheap enough, and logistically available enough, that households switched. Digital payments are a delivery technology for that affordability constraint, not a third independent driver of national access. Sub-Saharan Africa is the residual. Its access rate rose from 12 to 23 percent between 2010 and 2023, but population growth added 14 million people a year to the deficit. Universal access by 2030 would require reducing the global headcount 4.1 times faster than the 2010-2023 pace. That is not a hardware problem.

keywords: Welfare Mismeasurement JEL Classification: R11 -Regional Economic Activity: Growth
and Other Normative Criteria and Measurement

detail.abstract: Traditional macroeconomic accounting frameworks, such as Gross Domestic Product (GDP), increasingly fail to capture spatial friction and the systemic erosion of individual temporal autonomy in modern urban agglomerations. This paper introduces the conceptual and theoretical framework of Spatial Sovereign Utility (SSU), operationalizing it as an environmental conversion factor within Amartya Sen's Capability Approach. By synthesizing Gary Becker's time-allocation model with a Samuelsonian Social Welfare Function, we establish a micro-founded dynamic framework that maps spatial transportation constraints directly into aggregate welfare outcomes. To correct the systemic mismeasurement of urban well-being, we propose the Net Spatial-Temporal Welfare (NSTW) index as a supplementary national accounting metric and extend the model to evaluate spatial distribution dynamics in the emerging era of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) and autonomous mobility systems.

title: Innovationology and Brazil's Geoeconomic Transformation: From Resource Power to a Bio-Digital and Green Innovation Economy
affiliations: African Research Network (ARN)

detail.title: Innovationology and Brazil's Geoeconomic Transformation: From Resource Power to a Bio-Digital and Green Innovation Economy
detail.abstract: Brazil is entering a new phase of geoeconomic competition in which natural resources, scientific knowledge, technological capabilities, digital infrastructures, and productive transformation increasingly interact. This article develops the concept of Innovationological Geoeconomic Power to explain how Brazil can transform its resource endowments and innovation capabilities into sustained economic influence and strategic autonomy. Building on Innovationology, innovation systems theory, evolutionary economics, productive transformation, and geoeconomics, the study examines Brazil's trajectory between 2020 and 2025 across five interconnected domains: knowledge and innovation, digital and technological transformation, industrial upgrading, bioeconomy and green transition, and strategic autonomy. Evidence from the World Intellectual Property Organization, OECD, International Energy Agency, and Brazilian public institutions indicates that Brazil possesses significant innovation assets but continues to face institutional, financing, productivity, and commercialization constraints. Brazil ranked 52nd among 139 economies in the 2025 Global Innovation Index, with an output rank of 50th compared with an input rank of 63rd, indicating relatively strong innovation outputs despite weaker enabling conditions. At the same time, industrial policy, artificial intelligence, bioeconomy, and energy-transition initiatives increasingly connect innovation with national development objectives. The article argues that Brazil's emerging geoeconomic trajectory is best understood not as a departure from resourcebased power but as its innovation-mediated transformation. Brazil's distinctive opportunity lies in converting agricultural, biological, energy, mineral, and market assets into higher-value capabilities through science, technology, digitalization, industrial upgrading, and sustainable production. The article proposes Innovationological Geoeconomic Power as a framework for understanding this transition.

title: Correcting Ricardo's Production Possibility Curve

detail.title: Correcting Ricardo's Production Possibility Curve
detail.abstract: David Ricardo developed the production possibility curve (PPC) to formulate his comparative advantage theory and explain international trade. However, when his production is subject to diminishing returns, his theory collapses. The initially lower relative price associated with specialization suddenly becomes higher, while the newly chosen trade option is again more expensive. This paper corrects his PPC to strengthen his comparative advantage, to promote division of labor, and to replace gains from trade with gains from specialization.

title: Independent Reconciliation in the Producer-Level Methane Intensity Methodology

detail.title: Independent Reconciliation in the Producer-Level Methane Intensity Methodology
detail.abstract:
The import provisions of Regulation (EU) 2024/1787 take effect from 1 January 2027. A majority of 17 of the 27 Member States, together with the United States, Qatar and other exporting governments, called for those obligations to be postponed, but the Commission declined to reopen the Regulation. Instead, on 20 July 2026 it adopted two non-binding recommendations, one on compliance solutions and optional model clauses and one on the application of penalties. These measures clarify implementation but do not define the methodology required under Article 29 for calculating producer-level methane intensity. The question is therefore no longer whether the Regulation proceeds, but how its verification framework is established.

The central technical challenge concerns verification. Opponents of the Regulation have argued that producer-level methane (CH4)  intensity cannot be determined reliably, because methane molecules cannot be traced through commingled international supply chains and because no recognised methodology exists for reconciling different sources of evidence. The Commission has now confirmed that physical tracing of individual molecules is not required. What remains is the harder half of the objection. There is still no agreed way to reconcile independent atmospheric observations, operator reporting and other relevant evidence into a single producer-level figure that a competent authority or a court can rely on.

The scientific foundations needed to address this already exist. Advances in atmospheric measurement, remote sensing, metrology and measurement-based operator reporting provide an extensive evidence base, and the Commission's recent recommendations establish governance principles for recognised compliance solutions. What is still missing is the reconciliation framework that turns these sources into one producer-level figure with traceable uncertainty. This paper sets out the technical problems that the framework must solve, the measurement and metrology foundations already available, and recommendations for the year ahead. It argues that the methodology should treat cross-source reconciliation as a distinct component, carry an end-to-end uncertainty in traceable terms, account explicitly for what observing systems do not see, and sit under governance that is independent of the parties being measured and free of industry financing.

title: Digital Public Infrastructure & Economic Convergence: DPI as a Growth Engine for Emerging Markets

detail.title: Digital Public Infrastructure & Economic Convergence: DPI as a Growth Engine for Emerging Markets
detail.abstract:
Digital public infrastructure (DPI) is emerging as the most powerful convergence technology available to low‑ and middle‑income economies. The report argues that income convergence—long predicted by growth theory but achieved by only a subset of countries—is fundamentally constrained by the cost of participation in formal economic life. High transaction costs, weak identity systems, and fragmented information flows prevent firms and households from accessing accounts, credit, contracts, and markets. DPI directly attacks these barriers through three shared, population‑scale digital rails: digital identity, instant payments, and consent‑based data exchange. As the report states, “DPI is not an IT program; it is a productivity and participation technology.”

Evidence from India, Brazil, and Estonia shows rapid, measurable gains. India raised account ownership from 35% to 80% in six years and now processes ~20 billion UPI transactions monthly; Brazil moved 93% of adults onto Pix and cut cash usage from 43% to 6% in four years; Estonia digitized 99% of public services and saves ~2% of GDP annually. These rails convert previously invisible economic activity into verifiable data, expanding credit access—districts with higher UPI adoption saw lending to new‑to‑credit borrowers rise 4% and subprime borrowers 8%.

The economics are striking: instant‑payment systems cost under US$7 million to build, while modeled benefits from full digital identity reach 3–13% of GDP by 2030. DPI’s network effects—lower participation costs, greater formalization, richer data, and rising total factor productivity—create a self‑reinforcing convergence mechanism.

Risks such as exclusion, surveillance, and vendor lock‑in are real but manageable through privacy law, interoperability mandates, open standards, cybersecurity investment, and non‑digital fallbacks. As the report notes, “The choice is not between DPI and no DPI; it is between governed and ungoverned DPI.”

The core conclusion: DPI should be understood as a convergence technology. Countries that build inclusive, interoperable digital rails will lower participation costs, accelerate productivity growth, and converge faster—while those that do not will remain constrained by the frictions that have historically stalled development.

title: Green Industrial Policy in the Digital Age: Clean Manufacturing, Automation, Supply-Chain Traceability, and Circular-Economy Incentives

detail.title: Green Industrial Policy in the Digital Age: Clean Manufacturing, Automation, Supply-Chain Traceability, and Circular-Economy Incentives
detail.abstract:
Green industrial policy has re‑emerged at global scale, but the report argues its true bottleneck is no longer capital — it is information. Digitization has transformed decarbonization from a spending challenge into a measurement challenge. Clean‑manufacturing subsidies, carbon‑border rules, and circular‑economy incentives only work when emissions and material flows can be verified, not merely claimed.

The report advances a four‑pillar framework:

  • Clean manufacturing as the physical frontier, where steel, cement, chemicals, and aluminium require deep technological shifts such as hydrogen‑based reduction, electrification, and carbon capture.

  • Automation as the efficiency and measurement engine, with robots, digital twins, and AI improving precision while generating the data needed for carbon accounting.

  • Supply‑chain traceability as the infrastructure that makes embedded carbon auditable through instruments like the EU’s CBAM and Digital Product Passports.

  • Circular‑economy incentives as the mechanism that rewards keeping materials in circulation, enabled by product‑level data and verified recycled content.

Across case studies — from Stegra’s €6.5B green‑steel financing to the IRA’s data‑conditioned hydrogen credits — the same pattern holds: projects scale when their environmental performance is legible. Measurement capacity determines bankability, enforceability, and competitiveness.

The report concludes that the countries able to instrument their economies — through metering, digital twins, traceability systems, and passport infrastructure — will capture the greatest share of clean‑manufacturing value. The decisive resource of the transition is not subsidy dollars but verified data.

title:
Beyond Aid: Social Enterprise, the Blue-Green-Orange Economy, and the Path to Youth Employment in Ghana 1 

Prepared by Social Innovation Africa for the SPARK Change-makers Project (Social Enterprise Awareness & Sensitization Publications Programme)

detail.title:
Beyond Aid: Social Enterprise, the Blue-Green-Orange Economy, and the Path to Youth Employment in Ghana 1 

Prepared by Social Innovation Africa for the SPARK Change-makers Project (Social Enterprise Awareness & Sensitization Publications Programme)
detail.abstract: The era of African development depending on what he called "free money" has come to an end, and the continent must move from aid dependency to self-driven investment and economic discipline.7What this essay wants to resist is treating "beyond aid" as a government slogan that either succeeded or failed on its own terms. The more useful question is where self-reliance is actually, demonstrably happening in Ghana right now, not proclaimed from a podium, but built stall by stall and enterprise by enterprise, by people with no mandate to declare a national agenda and no particular need to wait for one.

title: AI: Blessing or Curse?
affiliations: Mastercard and Getulio Vargas Foundation (FGV) - Sao Paulo School of Economics

detail.title: AI: Blessing or Curse?
detail.abstract: The macroeconomic literature on artificial intelligence reaches sharply different conclusions. Task-based models emphasize productivity gains, labor displacement, and bottlenecks. Idea-based growth models emphasize the possibility that AI raises the productivity of research and accelerates innovation. A third strand studies catastrophic and existential risk. This paper provides a didactic survey of these approaches and organizes their main implications in a simple welfare framework. The framework shows that the welfare effect of additional AI capability can be understood through four policy-relevant margins: productivity in goods and services, productivity in innovation, uncompensated adjustment losses, and catastrophic risk. This decomposition explains why reasonable models can support opposite conclusions and clarifies the appropriate assignment of policy instruments. Safety policy should target risk directly; research policy should reflect knowledge spillovers; transfers and labor-market policies should address distribution and adjustment; and diffusion and competition policies should be used when capability fails to translate into broad productivity gains.

title: Design-Induced Bottlenecks in Platform Markets: Data Siloing, Buyer Homing, and Seller Fees *
affiliations: Astana IT University

detail.title: Design-Induced Bottlenecks in Platform Markets: Data Siloing, Buyer Homing, and Seller Fees *
detail.abstract: Many digital platforms give buyers free access and earn revenue from developers, merchants, or advertisers. Their ability to charge sellers depends on buyers' homing choices. With multi-homing, competing platforms sell access to a common buyer base; with single-homing, each controls an exclusive buyer segment. I study how personalisation systems that rely on locally generated activity influence this choice and thereby soften seller-side competition. In a two-platform model, buyers choose one or two memberships and divide a fixed amount of activity when they multi-home. Platforms choose how effectively activity transferred from the other membership contributes to personalisation before setting seller fees. Greater dependence on local activity reduces personalisation quality when buyers divide their activity while leaving the quality received by single-homers unchanged. Symmetric platform choices produce a unique homing cutoff. Complete buyer overlap makes access through the platforms perfectly substitutable and drives seller fees to zero; single-homing creates competitive bottlenecks and sustains positive fees. With indifferent buyers choosing one membership and design costs strictly increasing, one pure-strategy equilibrium has both platforms use transferred information fully and induces multi-homing. Additional single-homing equilibria arise when each platform chooses the lowest degree of local-data dependence that preserves its exclusive buyer segment, given the rival's architecture, and the resulting seller-fee revenue covers its design cost. Platforms weakly prefer the single-homing equilibria, whereas total welfare is strictly higher under full use of transferred information. A sufficiently demanding requirement for the effective use of transferred information leaves only multi-homing equilibria.

title: Capital Relief Reversal and the Limits of Private Credit Contagion
affiliations: and

detail.title: Capital Relief Reversal and the Limits of Private Credit Contagion
detail.abstract:
Regulators have mapped the exposure network between banks and private credit funds using confidential data that no outside researcher can access, replicate or audit. We rebuild it from public filings alone, combining a Call Report disclosure that first took effect in December 2024 with the borrowings notes of business development company annual reports. The bank panel reproduces the FDIC's published aggregate to within 0.006 percent, and we code the lender on 107 named facilities, recovering counterparties that FR Y-14 obligor matching misses because these funds borrow through special purpose vehicles. The coding is model assisted and validated by hand at 90.0 percent agreement.

What that bounds is 11 US chartered banks against 13 funds and 36.8 billion dollars of borrowing, about a fifth of the fund universe by value. Cells the filings leave unobserved are bounded between a maximum entropy and a minimum density reconstruction, and anchoring on observed lenders narrows the concentration gap between them by 88 percent.

Direct credit contagion is zero at every rung of a ladder calibrated to eight years of observed fund losses, under both bounds. At the statutory leverage cap a fund absorbs a 33.5 percent portfolio loss before any bank loses a dollar, against a 95th percentile of 10.2 percent. The channel that moves bank capital needs no default at all: relief from a significant risk transfer is conditional on the protection being recognised rather than on the seller performing, and a complete failure to roll expiring protection restores 252 billion dollars of risk weighted assets across these eleven banks, consuming between 6 and 9 percent of their regulatory headroom. That is a scenario on observed balance sheets rather than a transmission traced through observed edges, because no public source names which funds sell protection to which banks. Two limitations are findings in themselves. Eight of the nineteen lenders we identify, including the most frequent one, lend outside the Call Report perimeter and cannot be bounded at all, and rule based extraction of the counterparty is wrong on 11.1 percent of the facilities it answers.

title:
Diffusion Under Constraint 
How Infrastructure Gaps, Trust Deficits, And Informality Shape Technology Adoption Paths -A Crosssector Analysis of Mobile Money, Rooftop Solar, and E-Government In Frontier Markets

detail.title:
Diffusion Under Constraint 
How Infrastructure Gaps, Trust Deficits, And Informality Shape Technology Adoption Paths -A Crosssector Analysis of Mobile Money, Rooftop Solar, and E-Government In Frontier Markets
detail.abstract: Frontier-market technology adoption is routinely read as a single diffusion curve: once hardware cheapens and mobile coverage arrives, the S-curve follows. The cross-section of low-and middle-income countries rejects that reading. Using World Bank, Global Findex, IRENA, Worldwide Governance Indicators, and UN E-Government Development Index series for 131 low-and middle-income countries, this paper shows that three widely promoted technologies-mobile money, solar electricity, and digital public services-load on different constraints and therefore produce different national paths. Account ownership in Sub-Saharan Africa sits 20 percentage points above the level predicted by income, infrastructure, trust, and informality. Kenya's 90 percent account rate is 39 points above the income-accounts line. Uganda reaches 73 percent account ownership on 9 percent internet use. The same region holds 10 watts of solar capacity per capita against 506 in high-income countries, despite a 9.5-fold collapse in module prices since 2010. In the LMIC solar regression, a World Bank governance composite outpredicts both income and electricity access. E-government is a third pattern. The UN Online Service Index tracks government effectiveness (r = 0.65). The composite E-Government Development Index correlates-0.64 with selfemployment. Rwanda's online-service score of 0.82 on a telecom-infrastructure score of 0.37 is the existence proof that states can build services ahead of pipes-and the reminder that pipes still cap the composite. The policy error is to treat a mobile-money success as a digital-readiness credential. It is a statement about which constraint the technology was able to ignore.

title: Yet Another ‘Redundant’1 ‘Mash-Up’2 Index of Development: AAA Rating of Countries
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Yet Another ‘Redundant’1 ‘Mash-Up’2 Index of Development: AAA Rating of Countries

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declare that they have no personal or financial relationships with any individuals or organizations that could have influenced, or could be perceived to have influenced, this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the AAA (Availability-Affordability-Accessibility) Index, a new Composite Index (CI) designed to measure households’ Standard of Living (SoL) across countries. Traditional metrics like GDP are inadequate due to their "distributional blindness" and existing CIs are unable to capture the lived experiences of the "common man". Grounded in the Basic Needs Approach (BNA) and Cost of Living (COL), this study utilizes a hierarchy of needs inspired by Maslow to define various concepts like SoL, Quality of Life (QoL), Well-being, dignity, Life satisfaction, Economic Development, Human development and Social progress. This study treats SoL as the foundational layer of Economic Development. The AAA framework evaluates six core dimensions—food, water, electricity, housing, health, and education—across parameters of supply (Availability), distributive capacity (Affordability), and consumption (Accessibility). Focusing on median-income household, the multidimensional dashboard is consolidated into a single “vulgar”3 number to facilitate comparative rankings of countries. The AAA score is extended to be combined with unemployment rate and hours-of-work indicators into a final score reflecting both need fulfillment and labor market security. The AAA dashboard can also function as a diagnostic tool for statecraft, systematically evaluating the impact of public policy on household economic security and the fulfillment of subsistence rights.

title:
The Digitalization of Development Finance: 
How Real-time Payments, Mobile Money, and Data Infrastructure Reshape Capital access in Emerging Markets
affiliations: H Heuristics

detail.title:
The Digitalization of Development Finance: 
How Real-time Payments, Mobile Money, and Data Infrastructure Reshape Capital access in Emerging Markets
detail.abstract:
Digitalization is restructuring development finance by replacing high‑cost, relationship‑based intermediation with a three‑rail infrastructure stack: payments, money and identity, and data. Across the report, the evidence shows that exclusion in emerging markets has never been driven by weak demand for capital, but by the cost of serving small, dispersed, information‑poor borrowers. Digital rails collapse those costs. Mobile money converts the phone into a transaction and savings account, enabling consumption smoothing and lifting households—“Access to M‑Pesa lifted an estimated 194,000 Kenyan households… out of extreme poverty”—through real, causal welfare gains. Real‑time payment systems such as India’s UPI and Brazil’s Pix make transfers instant and nearly free, formalizing cash flows and generating the records needed for future lending. Digital identity systems remove the verification bottleneck that once prevented account ownership, while alternative‑data underwriting and machine‑learning models substitute for missing collateral and credit histories.

Together, these rails shift the binding constraint on capital access from geography to data. They enable relationship‑light SME lending, expand financial inclusion at unprecedented scale, and create public‑good spillovers that private markets alone will under‑provide. Yet they also introduce risks—digital divides, over‑indebtedness, platform concentration, and fragile governance—that require early regulatory guardrails. The report concludes that development finance institutions must treat payments and data infrastructure as core development infrastructure, not retail conveniences, because capital access in emerging markets now clears through digital rails.

title: Deepfakes, Synthetic Media and the Future of Evidence Law

detail.title: Deepfakes, Synthetic Media and the Future of Evidence Law
detail.abstract: Synthetic media generation has advanced from a laboratory curiosity to a courtroom problem. Evidentiary systems built around the presumption that audio, video, and photographic records are causally traceable to a real event now confront a generation of artifacts that are visually and acoustically indistinguishable from authentic recordings yet contain no photographic truth at all. This article examines the doctrinal crisis this creates for evidence law and argues that the dominant judicial response-treating synthetic media as a subset of the existing authentication problem under rules such as Federal Rule of Evidence 901-misdiagnoses the harm. The genuine threat is not only that fabricated media will be admitted as real; it is that the mere possibility of fabrication allows litigants to contest authentic, damaging evidence at negligible cost, a dynamic the literature calls the "liar's dividend." Drawing on a comparative analysis of the United States, the European Union, the United Kingdom, China, South Korea, Denmark, and Brazil, and on the jurisprudential legacy of Daubert and Frye, the article shows that no jurisdiction has yet built an evidentiary architecture equipped for bidirectional epistemic risk-the simultaneous danger of false admission and false denial. It develops the Synthetic Provenance and Evidentiary Integrity Standard (SPEIS), a tiered admissibility framework that shifts the evidentiary inquiry from ex post forensic detection toward ex ante provenance verification, differentiated burdens of production keyed to a media artifact's institutional origin, and a codified judicial response to bad-faith authenticity challenges. The article's original contribution is threefold: it reconceptualizes authentication doctrine around provenance rather than detection, it supplies a replicable comparative taxonomy of regulatory responses to synthetic evidence, and it proposes an institutionally feasible standard tested against realistic adjudicative scenarios in criminal, civil, and electoral proceedings.

title: Expedited Arbitration and Procedural Fairness: Can International Commercial Arbitration Deliver Speed Without Sacrificing Due Process?
affiliations: Senior Judicial Magistrate at Bangladesh Judicial Service

detail.title: Expedited Arbitration and Procedural Fairness: Can International Commercial Arbitration Deliver Speed Without Sacrificing Due Process?
detail.abstract: Expedited arbitration responds to a persistent criticism of international commercial arbitration: a process chosen for efficiency can itself become lengthy, costly and procedurally elaborate. Leading institutions now offer procedures that compress tribunal constitution, restrict written submissions and document production, favour sole arbitrators, encourage documents-only determination and impose short periods for rendering awards. The 2026 ICC Arbitration Rules have expanded ordinary expedited arbitration to qualifying disputes up to US$4 million and, for parties who expressly opt in, introduced a Highly Expedited Arbitration Procedure designed around a threemonth award timetable. The 2025 SIAC Rules combine an expedited procedure with a new streamlined track, while the UNCITRAL Expedited Arbitration Rules provide an opt-in model for ad hoc and administered proceedings. Speed, however, is not self-validating. An accelerated procedure remains constrained by equality of treatment, the right to present one's case, the parties' procedural agreement and the requirements of enforceability under the UNCITRAL Model Law and the New York Convention.
