This article argues that the apparent tension between expedition and due process is best resolved through contextual proportionality. Due process does not guarantee unlimited time, unrestricted document production, an oral hearing in every case or every procedural accommodation requested by a party. It guarantees a fair and reasonable opportunity to present and answer the material case. Recent Singapore appellate jurisprudence, particularly China Machine New Energy Corp v Jaguar Energy Guatemala LLC and Wan Sern Metal Industries Pte Ltd v Hua Tian Engineering Pte Ltd, demonstrates both sides of the balance: courts should defer to reasonable case management, but accelerated procedure cannot excuse a tribunal's failure to identify and cure material procedural ambiguity. The article proposes a seven-part framework for enforceable expedition based on informed consent, early issue definition, proportionate procedure, reasoned case-management decisions, procedural flexibility, preservation of a meaningful right to be heard and disciplined judicial review.

title: The Influence of Smoking and Behaviour on Health: A Pooled Analysis of 32 Countries from the European Social Survey 2014 and 2023

detail.title: The Influence of Smoking and Behaviour on Health: A Pooled Analysis of 32 Countries from the European Social Survey 2014 and 2023
detail.abstract: Smoking is a known cause of many diseases and, as such, hampers many in achieving a healthy life. In this study, the self-perceived health status is related to variables covering the lifestyle, social, physical, psychological, and demographic dimensions. Data from the European Social Survey (ESS) of 2014 and 2023 is used to run ordered logistic and stereotype logistic estimators. This study illustrates that smokers value healthy food differently than non-smokers. Moreover, the latter appear to have a greater health gain from helping others as well as from doing sports. Overall, the study confirms the relevance of earlier documented health determinants. It suggests that smoking is neither a healthy nor a social affair.

title: Creation vs. Extraction A Framework for Evaluating Pro-Social and Anti-Social Wealth Generation

detail.title: Creation vs. Extraction A Framework for Evaluating Pro-Social and Anti-Social Wealth Generation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No competing financial or personal interests to declare.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This paper is a theoretical and analytical work drawing on published secondary sources and public disclosures; it does not involve new data collection from human participants.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding or financial support.

detail.abstract: Traditional economic analysis measures wealth accumulation without adequately distinguishing between value creation and value extraction. This paper introduces a framework for evaluating whether economic actors are fundamentally pro-social-building systems that distribute value-or antisocial capturing existing value while transferring costs to others. Drawing on established research in subjective well-being, democratic theory, and institutional economics, the framework argues that the distinction between creation and extraction is not semantic. It is structural, measurable, and consequential for both democratic governance and national well-being. The paper examines how extraction operates at three scales: individual wealth accumulation, corporate market behavior, and the capture of regulatory and information infrastructure. It concludes by proposing evaluation frameworks that move beyond wealth taxation toward structural accountability for systemic harm.

title: Exploring the Short- and Long-term Impacts of Market-based Carbon Policies on Carbon Emissions: A Cross-country Panel Data Analysis
affiliations: Turkish Military Academy, National Defence University and Baskent University

detail.title: Exploring the Short- and Long-term Impacts of Market-based Carbon Policies on Carbon Emissions: A Cross-country Panel Data Analysis
detail.abstract: Market-based carbon pricing mechanisms have emerged as innovative financial mechanisms for reducing carbon emissions, but there is still a lack of comprehensive studies that explore the effects of these mechanisms on carbon emissions from both short/long-term perspectives. The main objective of the study is to fill the gap by analyzing the effectiveness of these mechanisms [carbon taxes (TAX) and Emissions Trading Systems (ETS)] on carbon emissions in the short/long-term. Using data from 31 countries between 2000 and 2023, we conducted a panel ARDL model to estimate the separate and joint effects of these policies on carbon emissions. The findings reveal that TAX and the combination of both instruments are more effective than ETS in reducing emissions in the long-run. However, both policies (alone or concurrently) appear to cause temporary increases in carbon emissions in the short-run, because of implementation costs, structural adjustment costs, market adaptation, and transitional production behaviors, etc. In different lag levels, the findings indicate that the carbon policies decrease per capita carbon emissions gradually and distinctly over time.  Overall, the study highlights that carbon tax policies and the combined use of both instruments (ETS and TAX) are effective long-term tools, and these tools offer valuable insights for policymakers.

title: From Physiological Allostasis to Artificial Risk Regulation: A Multi-Timescale Biomimetic Proof of Concept Using Three Decades of XCMG Prices, Drawdowns, and Recovery Dynamics: Biomimetic Allostatic Regulation in Nonstationary Markets

detail.title: From Physiological Allostasis to Artificial Risk Regulation: A Multi-Timescale Biomimetic Proof of Concept Using Three Decades of XCMG Prices, Drawdowns, and Recovery Dynamics: Biomimetic Allostatic Regulation in Nonstationary Markets
detail.abstract: Financial forecasting systems commonly prioritize directional classification or point-forecast accuracy, yet capital processes operating in nonstationary markets must also withstand breaches of risk boundaries and recover from recurrent shocks. Physiological allostasis offers a different design logic: anticipatory regulation, coordination across fast and slow timescales, accumulation of regulatory load, and path-dependent recovery. This study translates these functions into a Biomimetic Allostatic Risk and Viability Controller (BARVC). It conducts a longitudinal, single-security proof of concept using 7,109 daily observations for XCMG Machinery from August 28, 1996, through August 12, 2026. The sample contains 91 distinct drawdown cycles, including a historical maximum drawdown of 89.66%, and 124 major upward-move events. Model development used 1996-2018 for training, 2019-2021 for calibration, and locked 2022-2026 data for evaluation, with a 20-trading-day purge window separating calibration from testing. In the locked test period, the full-state model achieved 72.02% coverage for the P10-P90 interval, with an absolute coverage error of 7.98 percentage points; the corresponding non-allostatic model achieved 75.35% coverage and a 4.65-point error. Relative to buy-and-hold, BARVC reduced maximum drawdown from 36.08% to 21.77% and the daily severe-breach rate from 16.16% to 0.83%. However, a constant 45% risk exposure produced a lower maximum drawdown of 17.41% and no severe breaches. The empirical results supported none of the five prespecified mechanistic advantage hypotheses. The study therefore establishes the computational feasibility and falsifiability of allostatic functional translation but does not establish superior investment performance. Cross-security validation and a larger sample of independent stress events are required to determine whether the observed findings generalize beyond the focal security.

title: Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC), Bank Deposits, and Digital Payments: First Evidence from a Live Retail CBDC
affiliations: Imperial College Business School, Indian Institute of Management (IIMB), Bangalore, State Bank of India, Washington University in Saint Louis, John M. Olin Business School and

detail.title: Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC), Bank Deposits, and Digital Payments: First Evidence from a Live Retail CBDC
detail.abstract: We provide the first evidence on how a live retail CBDC affects bank funding, lending, and payments, using India’s digital rupee rollout. The RBI’s staggered bank authorization and coordinated marketing campaigns show that CBDC eligibility lowers retail deposits by 2.7%, driven by liquid savings accounts; term deposits are unaffected. Credit declines briefly before recovering. CBDC use displaces deposit-backed digital payments, not cash, and adoption is concentrated among wealthier, uninsured, and more educated depositors. A sufficient-statistics framework implies short-run welfare losses but long-run gains, as household convenience and safety benefits outweigh lost deposit franchise value, temporary credit contraction, and higher funding costs.

title: Lock-In by Design: How a Notched Transfer Tax Freezes an Asset Market
affiliations: Chapman University - The George L. Argyros College of Business and Economics and

detail.title: Lock-In by Design: How a Notched Transfer Tax Freezes an Asset Market

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No potential conflict of interest was reported by the author(s).
declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by the Faculty Research Project Development Initiative (FRDPI) grant from California State University Northridge (CSUN).

detail.abstract: Governments increasingly tax asset transfers at a notch, a tax that applies to the entire sale price once the price crosses a threshold, rather than only to the amount above it. We ask what such a tax does to a market for large, illiquid assets, using Los Angeles’s Measure ULA, which imposed a transfer tax of 4% on real property sales above $5 million and 5.5% on sales above $10 million, starting in 2023. In a difference-in-differences design that compares taxed sales with otherwise similar sales just below the threshold and in neighboring cities, volume in the taxed tier fell by roughly a third and stayed down, while volume just below the threshold was unchanged. The decline is not mechanical repricing. Sellers rushed to trade before the tax took effect, bunched just under the threshold, and pushed deals across the city border. Most tellingly, the count of distinct sellers fell as much as the count of deals: genuine lock-in, not the same owners simply trading less often. Notched transfer taxes can substantially freeze the markets they touch.

title: Dynamic corporate investment and risk management with digital transformation risk​
affiliations: Hunan University - School of Finance and Statistics and Hunan University - School of Finance and Statistics

detail.title: Dynamic corporate investment and risk management with digital transformation risk​
detail.abstract: We incorporate risky digital transformation into a dynamic q-theoretic model with financing constraints. Firms face stochastic digital technology shocks and can undertake cash-financed digital investment that is difficult to pledge as collateral. Successful implementation raises future productivity, whereas failure lowers it; the productivity spread between the two outcomes captures digital transformation risk. We characterize the joint policies for capital investment, digital investment, cash retention, and payout. Financing constraints reduce firm value and generate underinvestment in digital technologies, especially when internal liquidity is low. They also distort the composition of investment: higher transformation risk shifts scarce liquidity away from physical capital toward digital implementation. Payout policies respond nonlinearly, with the endogenous payout boundary mildly non-monotonic in transformation risk and U-shaped in the arrival rate of technology shocks. In an extension with index-futures hedging, margin requirements tie hedging capacity to liquidity. Higher transformation risk and more frequent technology shocks strengthen the firm's pre-transformation “hedge-to-survive” motive, leading to more aggressive hedging.

title: MACHINE LEARNING REGRESSION ANALYSIS FOR PERSONALIZED PET/CT IMAGING DOSIMETRY PREDICTION
affiliations: Universiti Putra Malaysia, Universiti Putra Malaysia, Universiti Putra Malaysia, Hasanuddin University, , Universiti Putra Malaysia, Universiti Putra Malaysia, Universiti Putra Malaysia and Universiti Putra Malaysia

detail.title: MACHINE LEARNING REGRESSION ANALYSIS FOR PERSONALIZED PET/CT IMAGING DOSIMETRY PREDICTION
detail.abstract: Conventional weight-based methods in Positron Emission Tomography-Computed Tomography (PET/CT) frequently overlook individual variations and changes in body habitus. Consequently, these oversights lead to suboptimal image quality and excessive radiation exposure for the patient. This study assesses machine learning (ML) regression models designed to deliver individualized recommendations for given 18F-FDG activity and computed tomography dose index volume (CTDIvol) utilizing standard demographic and anthropometric data provided. Retrospective analysis was performed on the clinical dataset of 1,000 whole-body 18F-FDG PET/CT scans, which were preprocessed using z-score normalization for feature scaling, Principal Component Analysis (PCA) for correlated variables transformation, lasso regularization for increasing model robustness, and Bayesian Optimization (BO) hyperparameter tuning for supervised regression algorithms. This study shows that Ensemble (ENS) model provides the most precise prediction for administered activity (R2 > 0.90; test RMSE: 0.43 MBq/kg), while Gaussian process regression (GPR + BO) is superior for CT dosimetry (R2 > 80; RMSE [[EQUATION]] 1.3 mGy) due to its stability across BMI ranges. Given gender-dependent performance, gender-aware optimization is vital for clinical precision. Integrating these ML models into PET/CT clinical workflow enables rapid, individualized dose that enhanced radiation safety and improved diagnostic imaging quality.

title: Will-o'-the-MISP: How Institutional Context Shapes the EU's Market Integration and Supervision Package
affiliations: London School of Economics - Law School

detail.title: Will-o'-the-MISP: How Institutional Context Shapes the EU's Market Integration and Supervision Package
detail.abstract: The European Union has long aspired to build a deep and integrated capital market. The most recent vehicle for that ambition, the Savings and Investments Union ('SIU'), has renewed the focus on the obstacles standing in its way. This has led to the identification of fragmentation in post-trade infrastructure itself and in its supervision as a key concern. In December 2025, the European Commission accordingly proposed the Market Integration and Supervision Package, or 'MISP', a set of legislative measures to harmonise EU capital markets, improve their efficiency, and reduce the cost of cross-border trades. This paper surveys the MISP, setting out its main features and showing how the package arose from prior EU capital markets policy, current goals, and the institutional architecture of EU policy-making. It suggests that some of the aspects left unaddressed in the MISP are a result of prior EU policy, the EU's interinstitutional framework and Treaty constraints, and the avoidance of the 'red lines' drawn by key stakeholder groups. Thus, the MISP tackles some of the barriers to the SIU but leaves others untouched or ineffectively contended with.

title: The Hidden Liabilities of AI Startup Acquisitions

detail.title: The Hidden Liabilities of AI Startup Acquisitions
detail.abstract:
The Core Thesis

Navigating the policy intricacies of AI startups reveals hidden, continuous liabilities for Mergers & Acquisitions; any hidden compliance risks or outstanding litigation directly transfer to the purchasing company. 

Key Successor Liabilities

  • Copyright infringement is one of the major legal and public issues surrounding AI, as its methods of training frequently utilize intellectual property without compensation or permission from the holder. To prevent a statutory breach, Big Tech AI corporations simply sign checks to be granted access to data training. Since startups don't possess the capital to afford this, they continue operating in a regulatory gray area with high exposure to copyright lawsuits. 

  • Other AI safety liabilities include addiction from sycophancy, falsified information (hallucinations), data leaking, and the unpredictable behavior of autonomous AI agents. 

Methodology & Key Findings

Throughout a three-month period, the author built and ran a custom-coded Python script that flagged any changes in Perplexity, Cohere, and Jasper's privacy policies, and the terminal would subsequently output a warning with a generated diff-report. The biggest finding occurred on July 2, 2026, in which Perplexity deleted the statement "Except as otherwise prescribed by applicable law, in the event of any inconsistency between the English language version and local language version of this Privacy Policy, the English language version will prevail." Removing the "English prevails" clause poses a significant legal liability to Perplexity; any mistranslations are now legally binding in that country. 

The Market Response

Due to the aforementioned liabilities of AI startups and increased antitrust scrutiny under the Hart-Scott-Rodino (HSR) Act, Big Tech is moving away from traditional procurement and instead hiring key employees and licensing technology from startups. This pseudo-acquisition allows companies to obtain the core aspects of a startup while avoiding regulatory oversight.

title: Education in the Ruins of Statehood: Gendered Agency, the 4Rs, and Everyday Peacebuilding in Yemen's Protracted Conflict
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Education in the Ruins of Statehood: Gendered Agency, the 4Rs, and Everyday Peacebuilding in Yemen's Protracted Conflict

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: This article examines how community-based educational practices in Yemen's fragmented state contribute to everyday peacebuilding, and identifies the structural conditions that determine whether these practices scale into sustainable peace or dissipate into isolated resilience. Drawing on 45 semi-structured interviews with educators, community leaders, and local authorities across five governorates (Aden, Taiz, Hadramawt, Marib, and Sana'a), triangulated with humanitarian data and comparative case analysis, the study develops an Adaptive Peacebuilding-Education Nexus Framework that connects the 4Rs of sustainable peacebuilding (Redistribution, Recognition, Representation, Reconciliation) with scenariobased foresight planning. The analysis identifies four mechanisms through which education fosters everyday peacebuilding: (1) spatial desegregation through mixed community-based schools; (2) curriculum mediation that replaces divisive narratives with local histories of coexistence; (3) governance experimentation through community education committees; and (4) crosscommunity dialogue facilitated by shared educational spaces. However, these mechanisms operate within severe structural constraints that limit their scalability without political settlement and redistributive justice. The article advances three contributions. First, it reconceptualizes the 4Rs framework for state fragmentation contexts. Second, it develops a participatory scenario model projecting three plausible trajectories linked to observable early warning indicators. Third, it provides empirically-grounded evidence that grassroots educational peacebuilding represents 'pockets of potential' requiring supportive policies to scale, challenging humanitarian narratives that celebrate local resilience without addressing structural drivers of conflict.

title: From Reserve Disclosure to Executable Control: A Blockchain-Native Reference Architecture for Treasury-Backed Stablecoins

detail.title: From Reserve Disclosure to Executable Control: A Blockchain-Native Reference Architecture for Treasury-Backed Stablecoins

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest relevant to the design and results reported in this manuscript.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study does not involve human participants, human-subject data, clinical research, or animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract:
Stablecoin regulation increasingly specifies eligible reserve assets, one-to-one backing, custody, disclosure, redemption, and insolvency treatment. Those requirements do not, by themselves, establish whether each reserve position is settled, unencumbered, legally controlled, operationally accessible, freshly valued, correctly allocated, and convertible into settlement money within the horizon in which redemption is demanded. This paper develops an executable reference architecture for the canonical Core Programmable Treasury Reserve Layer (PTRL) of Project ATLAS. Core PTRL uses existing eligible reserve instruments; it does not create a stablecoin, a central bank digital currency, a new sovereign security, a Treasury-auction replacement, or a public guarantee.

The paper contributes a modular EVM implementation in which a Treasury Reserve Certificate (TRC) is a non-transferable reserve-position state object rather than a tokenized government claim. Ten Core PTRL contracts connect permissioned institutional roles, protected reserve control, multi-source valuation and circuit breaking, counterparty-adjusted repo capacity, one-, seven-, and thirty-day liquidity, reserve-first minting, bank-confirmed redemption, and explicit normal, stress, resolution, and pause states. The executable mint cap equals the smallest headroom implied by risk-adjusted coverage, horizon-specific stressed redemption support, and an operational supply ceiling.

Eight end-to-end EVM tests and an integer-exact Python mirror validate the initial invariants. A four-arm dynamic experiment then separates the scenario-defined operational value of lot information, executable control, and maturity allocation under common random paths. Across 100,000 thirty-day paths and three issuers sharing dealer capacity, mean forced sales decline from 6.811% of initial reserves under aggregate information to 6.549% with current lot observation, 6.001% with executable control, and 5.034% with an equality-constrained maturity ladder. Mean liquidation losses decline from 11.473 to 9.766, 8.588, and 6.268 basis points. The allocation comparison holds total reserves, cash, weighted-average maturity, a linear yield proxy, an operating-cost proxy, and position count constant. Paired Monte Carlo intervals exclude zero for the sequential forced-sale and loss reductions, but quantify simulation error conditional on transparent scenario inputs rather than uncertainty about real-world parameters.

The results show how nominal backing can be translated into testable state-dependent constraints. They do not establish legal validity, production security, issuer behavior, market capacity, or an optimal liquidity threshold. The architecture therefore defines both an executable control layer and its boundary: code can condition action on verified evidence, but cannot itself create legal title, bankruptcy priority, confidentiality, or institutional performance.

title: Beyond Volatility: The 52-Week High and the Conditional Betting-Against-Beta Puzzle
affiliations: Old Dominion University

detail.title: Beyond Volatility: The 52-Week High and the Conditional Betting-Against-Beta Puzzle

keywords: Conditional factor timing JEL classification: D53

detail.abstract: We document a two-level relation between price-to-52-week-high (PTH) and betting against beta (BAB). Cross-sectionally, PTH-conditioned hedged BAB spreads are largest among stocks far below their own highs. The component of PTH orthogonal to momentum continues to condition the hedged BAB spread, whereas momentum orthogonal to PTH does not generate a comparable pattern; PTH also survives direct horse races with realized stock volatility and lottery-related controls. In the time series, the marketwide hedged BAB factor is strongest when the CRSP value-weighted market index is near its recent high. On a fixed common sample, market-index PTH predicts the hedged BAB factor beyond realized BAB volatility, investor sentiment, the Treasury-Eurodollar (TED) spread, and Fama-French six-factor controls. The component of market PTH orthogonal to the three state variables remains informative, especially for the volatility-managed BAB factor. A real-time PTH-managed BAB factor earns significant spanning alpha.

title: Do I Matter? Deadlines, Pivotality, and Public Good Provision
affiliations: and

detail.title: Do I Matter? Deadlines, Pivotality, and Public Good Provision
detail.abstract: While crowdfunding is typically examined through signaling, few studies approach it through behavioral motives. To examine backers' motivations, we scrape over 9,000 Kickstarter campaigns, which succeed only if pledges reach a posted goal by a deadline. Near the deadline, projects just below their goal attract 1.2 percentage points more new backers per day than those just above it, which is 43 percent of baseline flows, while average pledge size does not move. Neither private returns nor warm glow, the fixed utility of giving itself, explains this pattern. One possible explanation is altruism of caring about the impact of the project multiplied by the increase in probability of project success from an additional pledge. We call this pivotal altruism and derive it from the stochastic arrival of other backers. Fitting the model to the discontinuity moments by simulated method of moments, we find that pivotal altruism reproduces the drop and its concentration near the deadline. The largest drops occur at mid-sized goals, which separates pivotal altruism from preference of being pivotal, where only the effect on success matters and the project's scale does not.

title: Children in Bonded Labour in Pakistan

detail.title: Children in Bonded Labour in Pakistan
detail.abstract: This policy brief thoroughly analyses the socioeconomic issues relevant to children in bonded labour in Pakistan, enabling targeted intervention. Not only does it investigate the economic issues such as poverty, lack of enforcement agencies, and scarce resources within the country, but it also critiques the pre-established frameworks. Pakistan, being a developing country, continues to encounter challenges such as weak enforcement of laws and a lack of government intervention in correcting intergenerational debt transfer. While the issue is widespread across the country, children in debt bondage are particularly prevalent in agriculture, brick-making, carpet-weaving, mining, and handicraft production (mainly in Punjab, Sindh, and KPK). While the document evaluates the current attempts at correcting this socioeconomic problem, it also builds upon the foundations of possible policy initiatives. As for Pakistan, it scrutinizes the existing policy attempts, the reason for the lack of success, and a possible way to strengthen the system.

title: Biodiversity Risk and the Dynamics of Sectoral Systemic Risk
affiliations: University of Glasgow, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Biodiversity Risk and the Dynamics of Sectoral Systemic Risk
detail.abstract: Biodiversity risk is increasingly recognized as an emerging source of systemic financial risk, yet empirical evidence on whether it contains distinct financial information beyond conventional climate-related risks remains limited. This study investigates how biodiversity-related risk propagates through sectoral systemic risk in China and benchmarks its transmission dynamics against physical climate risk and climate policy uncertainty. To measure a high-frequency biodiversity risk, we construct a China Biodiversity Risk Index (BRI) from large-scale news text using large language model (LLM)-assisted annotation and deep learning classification. We then employ a Quasi-Bayesian local likelihood (QBLL) time-varying parameter VAR connectedness framework to characterize the dynamic propagation of environmental risks across sectors. The results show that biodiversity risk constitutes a distinct and economically meaningful source of systemic financial risk beyond conventional climate-related risks. While all environmental risks generate significant but predominantly short-lived spillover effects, their transmission mechanisms differ substantially across sectors. Biodiversity risk primarily propagates through ecological constraints, biodiversity-related policy developments, and supply-chain disruptions, exerting stronger effects on resource-intensive and ecosystem-dependent industries. Climate policy uncertainty mainly affects policysensitive sectors through regulatory and expectation channels, whereas physical climate risk generates more immediate disturbances in climate-exposed production systems. Dynamic network analysis further reveals a highly interconnected spillover structure, with biodiversity, climate, and policy risks reinforcing each other through evolving transmission networks. These findings provide new evidence that biodiversity risk represents an independent dimension of systemic financial risk and highlight the importance of incorporating biodiversity-related information into macro-financial risk monitoring and environmental risk governance.

title: How Far May Courts and Tribunals Extend an Arbitration Agreement to Non-Signatories Without Transforming Consent from a Jurisdictional Foundation into a Legal Fiction?
affiliations: Senior Judicial Magistrate at Bangladesh Judicial Service

detail.title: How Far May Courts and Tribunals Extend an Arbitration Agreement to Non-Signatories Without Transforming Consent from a Jurisdictional Foundation into a Legal Fiction?
detail.abstract: International commercial arbitration is founded on consent, yet contemporary transactions routinely involve corporate groups, assignees, guarantors, insurers, subcontractors, affiliates and other actors that do not formally sign the arbitration clause. Courts and tribunals have therefore developed doctrines through which non-signatories may sometimes invoke, or be bound by, arbitration agreements. The difficulty is not whether signature is indispensable; ordinary private law has always recognised agency, assignment, assumption, succession, estoppel and veil-piercing. The harder question is whether adjudicators remain faithful to consent when they treat commercial integration, group structure or transactional efficiency as substitutes for a legally attributable agreement. This article argues that non-signatory arbitration is legitimate only where the decision-maker identifies an established legal basis that connects the non-signatory to the arbitration agreement. Comparative analysis of the United States, England, France and India shows divergent methods but a common legitimacy problem. GE Energy preserves ordinary domestic doctrines; Dallah and Kabab-Ji emphasise governing law and judicial control; French law applies an autonomous rule centred on common intention; and Cox and Kings, reinforced by ASF Buildtech in 2025, retains the group-of-companies doctrine while demanding mutual intention and substantial participation. The article proposes a seven-stage Consent Integrity Test. Its central claim is that arbitration may extend beyond formal signature, but not beyond legally attributable consent, derivative entitlement or another independently recognised legal basis for being bound.

title: The Geography of Consumption in Segregated Cities: When Is It Malleable?
affiliations: Bocconi University, Harvard University - Business School (HBS) and University of Illinois Urbana Champaign

detail.title: The Geography of Consumption in Segregated Cities: When Is It Malleable?
detail.abstract: Urban consumption is highly segregated, limiting consumers' opportunities and firms' reach beyond local markets. We study its malleability in a randomized experiment with 341 Tulsa residents, followed weekly for four weeks using transaction-level spending data. Guided neighborhood exposure increases spending in targeted neighborhoods among recent migrants by 10.7 percentage points, more than twice the sample mean. Responses are largest among Black and Hispanic participants and extend beyond businesses featured in the intervention. Reallocated spending is concentrated at highly rated establishments. Consumption geography is most malleable when consumers have greater scope to learn and greater perceived social fit.

title: How Do Sectoral Shocks Shape Future GDP?
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of New York and Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond

detail.title: How Do Sectoral Shocks Shape Future GDP?

publicationDetails.detailsText: Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond Working Papers, volume 26, issue 11, 2026[10.21144/wp26-11]

publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: A production sector's size, as measured by its Domar weight, captures the contemporaneous aggregate effect of its productivity shocks. However, the presence of investment means that these aggregate effects can persist over time. We derive a dynamic generalization of Hulten's theorem in an environment that features sectoral linkages in both intermediate-inputs and investment. This generalization follows from production efficiency alone, and decomposes each sector's Domar weight into an impact and a propagation component. The relative size of these components then determines how persistent the aggregate effects of sectoral shocks are, but cannot be known absent information on the economy's production structure. We show in a tractable structural model that future GDP responses to sectoral shocks can alternatively be described as weighted sums of all sectors' Domar weights, with weights primarily dictated by the network positions and capital shares of downstream sectors. Quantifying the model with U.S. production data, we find that i) Domar weights become progressively less informative about the aggregate effects of sectoral shocks as the horizon lengthens and ii) over a three-year horizon, goods-producing sectors have larger cumulative aggregate effects than service-producing sectors, despite goods only accounting for less than one-third of GDP. Model-free local projections of U.S. GDP growth on sectoral TFP growth confirm these findings.

title: Economic Sanctions and International Commercial Arbitration: Access to Justice, Arbitrability, Procedural Fairness and Enforcement of Awards
affiliations: Senior Judicial Magistrate at Bangladesh Judicial Service

detail.title: Economic Sanctions and International Commercial Arbitration: Access to Justice, Arbitrability, Procedural Fairness and Enforcement of Awards
detail.abstract: Economic sanctions now form part of the operating environment of international commercial arbitration rather than an exceptional external complication. Asset freezes, prohibitions on making funds or economic resources available, sectoral restrictions, legal-services controls, banking de-risking and licensing requirements may affect an arbitration at almost every stage: commencement, payment of institutional and tribunal costs, appointment of counsel and experts, evidentiary exchange, interim relief, settlement, payment of an award and execution against assets. Yet sanctions do not produce one uniform legal consequence. A prohibition on payment is not necessarily a prohibition on adjudication; a designated party is not thereby deprived of the arbitration agreement; and an award rendered in favour of or against a sanctioned person is not automatically unenforceable. The legal problem is therefore one of classification. This article argues that courts and tribunals should distinguish four questions that sanctions debates frequently conflate: access to the arbitral forum, arbitrability and substantive legality, procedural equality during the arbitration, and recognition or execution of the resulting award. 2 Drawing on the New York Convention, the UNCITRAL Model Law, the ICC's 2026 compliance framework, UK and United States licensing practice, recent European Union measures, and English decisions including UniCredit Bank GmbH v RusChemAlliance LLC, UniCredit Bank GmbH v Constitution Aircraft Leasing/Celestial Aviation Services and OWH SE i.L. v RTI Ltd, the article develops a seven-stage Sanctions Compatibility Framework. Its central thesis is that sanctions should normally operate as mandatory legal constraints on transactions and remedies, not as a general jurisdictional veto on arbitration. Access to justice should be preserved through licensing and proportionate case management; public-policy review should remain tied to concrete illegality; and courts should distinguish recognition of an award from the separate question whether payment or execution against particular assets is presently lawful.

title: Climate Change, ESG and Human Rights in International Commercial Arbitration: Reconciling Party Autonomy with the Emerging Public-Interest Dimension of Arbitration
affiliations: Senior Judicial Magistrate at Bangladesh Judicial Service

detail.title: Climate Change, ESG and Human Rights in International Commercial Arbitration: Reconciling Party Autonomy with the Emerging Public-Interest Dimension of Arbitration
detail.abstract: International commercial arbitration has traditionally been understood as a private mechanism for resolving disputes generated by private bargains. That description is becoming incomplete. Climate transition, responsible-business standards and human-rights due diligence increasingly shape the performance, financing, valuation and termination of cross-border contracts. Renewable-energy projects, carbon markets, infrastructure, supply chains, sustainability-linked finance, mergers and acquisitions, insurance and long-term procurement can therefore generate disputes in which the immediate legal questions remain contractual while the factual and regulatory setting implicates interests extending beyond the parties. The 2025 Queen Mary University of London-White & Case International Arbitration Survey confirms that publicinterest issues are already encountered in commercial arbitration and that respondents expect environmental and human-rights issues to become more prominent. This article asks how arbitration can respond without abandoning its jurisdictional foundation in consent. It argues that public-interest sensitivity should alter arbitral procedure more readily than it alters arbitral jurisdiction. Tribunals should not transform the Paris Agreement, the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights or OECD responsible-business standards into freestanding private obligations unless the applicable law or the parties' contract gives them legal effect. Yet where climate, ESG or human-rights commitments form part of the contractual or mandatory-law matrix, tribunals should address them with appropriate expertise, evidential discipline, calibrated transparency and remedies that respect third-party rights. Drawing on the New York Convention, UNCITRAL Model Law, ICC climate-disputes report, Hague Rules on Business and Human Rights Arbitration, OECD standards and contemporary survey evidence, the article proposes a seven-stage Public-Interest Compatibility Framework. The framework preserves party autonomy while recognising that legitimacy, enforceability and procedural fairness may require arbitration to become more outward-looking when the dispute has consequences that are not purely private.

title: Faster Is Not Calmer: Agentic AI, Reaction-Time Compression, and the Term Structure of Volatility

detail.title: Faster Is Not Calmer: Agentic AI, Reaction-Time Compression, and the Term Structure of Volatility
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence can make markets faster without making them uniformly calmer. This paper develops a market-microstructure theory of reaction-time compression: after a public signal, AI-assisted investors may submit a fixed amount of information-driven demand over fewer intervals, even when their portfolio rules, private signals, and final positions remain heterogeneous. The separation between trade targets and response delays is a maintained identification assumption, not an equilibrium result. In the model, order flow moves the permanent component of price, while finite market depth and gradual liquidity recovery create a temporary displacement. Four results follow. First, compressing a fixed price adjustment raises short-horizon realized variation because the squared-return contribution of the common order is governed by the concentration of its arrival weights. Second, capacity exceedance is Schur-convex: a more concentrated arrival schedule places weakly more flow beyond a fixed replenishment capacity. Third, the long-run fundamental price change is unchanged in expectation once temporary displacement decays. Fourth, a relative-clock index-the market's liquidity-recovery half-life divided by the order-arrival half-life-organizes the zero-threshold linear special case; in the nonlinear threshold model it remains informative but is not a sufficient statistic. Numerical illustrations show that moving from human-paced to agentic arrival profiles shifts both information incorporation and realized variance toward the announcement, increases temporary price dislocation, and reduces the effective number of independent arrival intervals. The theory yields eventtime predictions that distinguish temporal synchronization from conventional herding, model monoculture, and generic high-frequency trading.

title: Arbitrator Independence and Disclosure in International Commercial Arbitration: Conflicts of Interest, Repeat Appointments and the Limits of Mandatory Transparency
affiliations: Senior Judicial Magistrate at Bangladesh Judicial Service

detail.title: Arbitrator Independence and Disclosure in International Commercial Arbitration: Conflicts of Interest, Repeat Appointments and the Limits of Mandatory Transparency
detail.abstract:
The legitimacy of international commercial arbitration depends substantially on confidence that the decision-maker is impartial and independent. Yet the modern arbitral market makes that assurance increasingly complex. Arbitrators often practise in specialised professional communities, sit repeatedly with the same co-arbitrators, receive recurring appointments from particular parties or law firms, work within firms that have extensive global client relationships, and encounter third-party funders, experts and affiliates that may not be apparent from the case caption. Disclosure has therefore become the principal procedural mechanism through which parties test potential conflicts before they mature into challenges to the tribunal or the award. The 2026 ICC Arbitration Rules significantly strengthen that architecture: doubts are expressly resolved in favour of disclosure; disclosure itself is stated not to establish lack of independence or impartiality; parties must supply lists of persons and entities relevant to conflict checking; funding relationships must be identified; and the duty remains continuous throughout the arbitration. The 2024 IBA Guidelines likewise reinforce a distinction that is central to this article: the threshold for disclosure is deliberately broader than the objective threshold for disqualification.

This article argues that mandatory transparency is essential but not unlimited. Over-disclosure can generate strategic challenges, information overload, privacy problems and an erroneous inference that every disclosed relationship is disqualifying. Repeat appointments illustrate the difficulty. The 2024 IBA Guidelines classify two or more appointments by the same party within three years, and more than three appointments by the same counsel or law firm, as Orange List circumstances requiring disclosure, while recognising that specialised sectors may justify a different contextual assessment. In Halliburton Company v Chubb Bermuda Insurance Ltd, the UK Supreme Court similarly held that overlapping appointments may generate a legal duty of disclosure, but that failure to disclose does not automatically establish apparent bias.

The article proposes a seven-part Proportionate Transparency Framework. It separates disclosure from disqualification, requires reasonable conflict investigation, distinguishes repeat appointments from repeat dependence, treats party-provided entity lists as aids rather than substitutes for arbitrator inquiry, protects confidentiality through minimum-necessary disclosure, disciplines waiver and challenge timing, and directs courts and institutions to assess nondisclosure contextually rather than mechanically. The central claim is that transparency strengthens arbitration only when it reveals information necessary to evaluate impartiality without converting disclosure into a presumption of conflict.

title: Optimal Decision Under Partial Observability and Distributional Uncertainty: A Unified Stochastic Control Framework with Sharp Detection Delay Bounds

detail.title: Optimal Decision Under Partial Observability and Distributional Uncertainty: A Unified Stochastic Control Framework with Sharp Detection Delay Bounds
detail.abstract: We present a unified mathematical framework for sequential decision-making under the simultaneous presence of partial observability and distributional uncertainty. Our contribution is fourfold. First, we establish the piecewise-linear and convex (PWLC) structure of the value function for distributionally robust partially observable Markov decision processes (DR-POMDPs) under Wasserstein ambiguity sets, extending the classical Sondik-Pineau theory to adversarial environments. Second, we derive sharp minimax lower bounds on detection delay in quickest change detection problems with distributional uncertainty, generalizing Lorden's classical bound and quantifying the fundamental cost of ambiguity. Third, we prove strong duality for the resulting infinite-dimensional minimax optimization, establishing tractable reformulations via Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality. Fourth, we develop a distributionally robust point-based value iteration (DR-PBVI) algorithm with explicit convergence rates that decompose into approximation error and irreducible ambiguity cost. The framework is grounded in Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) viscosity solution theory, with rigorous well-posedness results for the associated fully nonlinear integro-differential equations. Our analysis reveals fundamental trade-offs between robustness, observability, and detection latency that are intrinsic to any decision system operating under adversarial uncertainty.

title: Authorship Integrity and Cognitive Discretion: An Ordinal Fracture Model of Decision Systems: A Formal Model of Narrative, Agency, Boundary, and Self-Recognized Authorship Under Influence

detail.title: Authorship Integrity and Cognitive Discretion: An Ordinal Fracture Model of Decision Systems: A Formal Model of Narrative, Agency, Boundary, and Self-Recognized Authorship Under Influence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This work is a purely theoretical and conceptual paper that does not involve human participants, clinical trials, or patient data. Consequently, formal institutional ethics committee review or IRB approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant or financial support from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The work was conducted entirely independently by the author.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a descriptive theoretical model of authorship integrity within bounded decision episodes. The Cognitive Discretion Layers System (CDLS) represents the external-facing Surfacing boundary, the concurrent internal structures of restriction, influence, and reasoning at L1-L3, and the L0 authorship state constituted by Narrative, Agency, and Boundary (NAB). It addresses a gap in decision theory: existing accounts explain valuation, constraint, and selection but generally leave unresolved whether a resulting action remains recognizable to the deciding system as its own. The model distinguishes an intact reference configuration from seven qualitatively ordered fracture modes that represent how recognized authorship may be preserved or disrupted. It separates influence and constraint from the terminal locus of decision selection through a terminal-selection invariant and represents a spillover dynamic through which sustained influence pressure may generate authorship strain without displacing selection authority. Four falsifiable hypotheses concern temporal sequencing, authority reconfiguration, cross-layer contradiction, and strain propagation. The paper further specifies an empirical coding and validation program for testing the model's classifications and predictions. CDLS is not an applied framework, decision methodology, or practical toolkit; its contribution is a formal, non-clinical representation that makes recognized authorship independently analyzable and testable rather than leaving it implicit in accounts of decision selection.

title: Evolving Landscape of Performance Measurement Research: A Bibliometric Analysis
affiliations: Thammasat University - Thammasat Business School, , Faculty of Business Administration, Kasetsart University, Thailand and University of Tokyo

detail.title: Evolving Landscape of Performance Measurement Research: A Bibliometric Analysis
detail.abstract:
Purpose: This study aims to identify clusters in and future avenues of research on performance measurements through a review of the published literature. Design/methodology/approach: A bibliometric analysis was used to review papers published on performance measurement research. 

Findings: The results showed that there are eight main clusters of research in this field: strategic performance measurement, implementation of performance measurement, design of performance measurement, and performance measurement in the supply chain, the public sector, maintenance, hospitality, and humanitarianism. 

Originality: This study applies a bibliometric literature review method using a combination of cocitation network analysis and text mining techniques, which is rarely used in the literature review in the field of performance measurement. The results obtained from this study are also different from those of previous studies. 

Practical implications: Practitioners can better understand the different facets of performance measurement, providing deeper insights into how organisations may exploit this bibliometric analysis to their advantages.

title: A Comparative Analysis of GAAP (USA) and IFRS (Europe): Evaluating the Need Global Accounting Standards (GAS)

detail.title: A Comparative Analysis of GAAP (USA) and IFRS (Europe): Evaluating the Need Global Accounting Standards (GAS)
detail.abstract: This study presents a comprehensive comparative analysis of Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) used in the United States and International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) predominantly applied across Europe. Using secondary data from 2020-2024, the research evaluates both frameworks across multiple dimensions including economic performance, financial transparency, audit quality, fair value measurement, ESG disclosure, taxation transparency, cyber security reporting, and digital transformation. The findings reveal that while GAAP demonstrates strong regulatory enforcement and audit control, IFRS offers superior global comparability, flexibility and ESG integration. Based on identified strengths and weaknesses, the study proposes the development of a hybrid Global Accounting Standard (GAS) that integrates the rule-based rigor of GAAP with the principlebased adaptability of IFRS. Such a framework could enhance international financial transparency, investor confidence and regulatory consistency.

title: Multiparty and Multicontract Arbitration: Joinder, Consolidation, Consent and Procedural Fairness in Complex International Commercial Disputes
affiliations: Senior Judicial Magistrate at Bangladesh Judicial Service

detail.title: Multiparty and Multicontract Arbitration: Joinder, Consolidation, Consent and Procedural Fairness in Complex International Commercial Disputes
detail.abstract:
International commerce is increasingly organised through contractual networks rather than bilateral bargains. Construction projects, energy ventures, syndicated finance, mergers and acquisitions, supply chains, joint ventures and infrastructure concessions commonly involve several contracts and multiple corporate actors whose rights and obligations are factually interdependent but legally distinct. Arbitration, however, remains founded on consent. This creates a structural tension: resolving connected disputes separately may duplicate evidence, increase cost and generate inconsistent awards, while combining them may bind parties to a procedure, tribunal or procedural configuration they did not agree to.

This article examines four principal mechanisms used by contemporary arbitral institutions to manage that tension: joinder, consolidation, a single arbitration under multiple contracts, and coordinated proceedings. It compares the ICC Arbitration Rules 2026, the SIAC Rules 2025 and the HKIAC Administered Arbitration Rules 2024, and places those mechanisms within the wider due-process framework of the UNCITRAL Model Law and the New York Convention. Particular attention is paid to tribunal constitution and the continuing significance of BKMI and Siemens v Dutco, which established equality in the appointment of arbitrators as a matter of international arbitral legitimacy.  

The article argues that multiparty efficiency should be governed by a principle of consentsensitive proportionality. The more a procedural mechanism alters party identity, tribunal constitution or the legal separateness of proceedings, the stronger the consent justification required. It proposes a seven-stage Complex Arbitration Compatibility Test that asks whether the relevant parties are bound by compatible arbitration agreements, whether the disputes arise from a sufficiently connected legal or transactional relationship, whether procedural integration threatens equal participation or appointment rights, whether coordination could achieve the same efficiency with less jurisdictional intrusion, and whether the resulting award will remain enforceable. Institutional innovation can legitimately overcome fragmentation, but only where efficiency remains anchored to consent and procedural equality.

title: The Sacralization of Power: Exploring Religious Manipulation within the Electoral Process

detail.title: The Sacralization of Power: Exploring Religious Manipulation within the Electoral Process
detail.abstract: This paper explores the “sacralization of power,” a phenomenon where political actors exploit religious devotion to obscure systemic socio-economic failures and secure electoral dominance. Recognizing that faith is fundamentally a public and potent phenomenon in developing democracies, the commentary examines how the political elite weaponize religious identity to entrench divisions, mask their consolidation of the political economy, and shield themselves from civic accountability. Driven by severe economic deprivation and structural inequality, vulnerable populations frequently turn to spiritual institutions for the security that secular governments fail to provide. Opportunistic politicians capitalize on this reliance by employing three primary mechanisms of manipulation: stoking identity polarization to frame political elections as existential spiritual battles, co-opting sacred spaces through transactional financial patronage in exchange for clerical endorsements, and moralizing policy debates to reframe legitimate political critique as a rebellion against divine order. Consequently, this calculated fusion of sacred imagery with political ambition threatens to replace democratic compromise with devastating, zero-sum conflict. To dismantle this architecture of manipulation, the paper proposes a coordinated tripartite framework of resistance. First, religious institutions must reclaim their autonomy by enforcing strict, internal bans on political campaigning from the pulpit. Second, state agencies must exercise rigorous financial oversight to track campaign financing and revoke privileges for non-compliant religious bodies. Finally, a vigilant civil society must engage in robust civic education, empowering citizens to identify emotional manipulation at the ballot box and ensuring that faith remains a catalyst for social healing rather than an instrument of political subjugation

title: Parallel Proceedings and International Commercial Arbitration: Lis Pendens, Anti-Suit Injunctions, Res Judicata and the Risk of Inconsistent Decisions
affiliations: Senior Judicial Magistrate at Bangladesh Judicial Service

detail.title: Parallel Proceedings and International Commercial Arbitration: Lis Pendens, Anti-Suit Injunctions, Res Judicata and the Risk of Inconsistent Decisions
detail.abstract: Parallel proceedings are a recurring structural problem in international commercial arbitration. The same commercial controversy may generate litigation in one State, arbitration at the chosen seat, related proceedings involving affiliates or guarantors, and later enforcement disputes elsewhere. Classical lis pendens rules seek to prevent duplication by privileging the court first seised, but chronology is an unstable organizing principle where the parties have already allocated adjudicative authority by arbitration agreement. This article argues that international arbitration requires a consent-and-finality model of coordination rather than a transposition of court-to-court lis pendens. The New York Convention and the UNCITRAL Model Law generally require courts to respect the arbitration agreement; anti-suit injunctions can enforce that bargain, but must be disciplined by comity, promptness and proportionality. Where overlap is partial, case-management stays may coordinate court and arbitral proceedings more effectively than categorical injunctions. Parallel arbitrations call instead for consolidation, concurrent conduct and careful sequencing under institutional rules. Once a final award exists, res judicata becomes the principal back-end mechanism for controlling re-litigation, although disagreement remains over its governing law and 2 scope. Drawing on English, French, European Union and Singaporean authorities, as well as recent IBA work on arbitral res judicata, the article proposes a six-stage Coordination Framework designed to preserve consent, reduce inconsistent decisions and maintain enforceable finality without creating an inflexible global first-seised rule.

title: The Law Governing International Arbitration Agreements after the Arbitration Act 2025: Party Autonomy, Separability and the Shift from Enka to the Law of the Seat
affiliations: Senior Judicial Magistrate at Bangladesh Judicial Service

detail.title: The Law Governing International Arbitration Agreements after the Arbitration Act 2025: Party Autonomy, Separability and the Shift from Enka to the Law of the Seat
detail.abstract:
The law governing an arbitration agreement determines questions that can decide whether arbitration occurs at all: the agreement's validity, scope, interpretation, extension to particular disputes or persons, and the legal consequences of separability. English conflict-of-laws doctrine became especially prominent after Enka Insaat ve Sanayi AS v OOO Insurance Company Chubb, where the Supreme Court held that a choice of law for the matrix contract will generally extend to an arbitration clause contained in that contract, while the law of the seat ordinarily supplies the default where no choice has been made. Kabab-Ji SAL v Kout Food Group applied that approach at the enforcement stage, and UniCredit Bank GmbH v RusChemAlliance LLC reaffirmed it shortly before legislative reform.

The Arbitration Act 2025 now changes the architecture. New section 6A of the Arbitration Act 1996 provides that the arbitration agreement is governed by the law expressly chosen for that agreement; absent such express choice, the law of the seat applies. A governing-law clause for the matrix contract does not, by itself, constitute an express choice for the arbitration agreement. This article examines the statutory shift and argues that section 6A is best understood not as a rejection of separability or party autonomy, but as a reordering of both. It privileges an express, arbitration-specific choice over inferred contractual intention and converts the seat from a residual connecting factor into the primary statutory default. The reform improves predictability and aligns the applicable law with the juridical home of the arbitration, but it also creates new drafting and interpretative questions, particularly concerning express choice, foreign-seated arbitrations, transitional cases, investor-State exclusions, and the interaction with Article V(1)(a) of the New York Convention. The article proposes a six-stage method for courts, tribunals and practitioners applying section 6A.

reference: The Journal of Transport History, volume 22, issue 1, 2001[10.7227/TJTH.22.1.2]
title: The Channel Tunnel (1955-1975) : When the Sleeping Beauty woke again

detail.title: The Channel Tunnel (1955-1975) : When the Sleeping Beauty woke again

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: unrelevant
declarations.funderStatement: Journal of Transport History

publicationDetails.detailsText: The Journal of Transport History, volume 22, issue 1, 2001[10.7227/TJTH.22.1.2]

detail.abstract:
The aftermath of the Second World War could have brushed aside for years the greatest engineering project of the century: a railway tunnel under the Channel. In 1875 two companies had been granted a concession in France and special powers in England for this purpose. After a failed attempt in 1883 both had slowly lost influence. The London office had been bombed during the blitz. Air and road transport were in competition with rail. The Channel tunnel was the Sleeping Beauty of its main shareholders, the State-owned French Railways and the Southern Railway Company in Britain, both of which had other priorities.

As early as December 1945 a question was asked of the Minister of Transport, with little success. Lobby groups in both parliaments were divided. Notwithstanding, interest remained high. The lack of a Channel tunnel had been cruelly felt during the retreat from Dunkirk and the project could prove useful for the economy and strategy of the emerging Western Europe.

This article focuses on the postwar period up to 1975, which covers the design, promotion and first failure of the twin bored tunnel for car shuttles and through trains. A substantial part of today's Channel tunnel engineering, management and finance originated during these two decades. Colonial crisis, European construction freezes and oil embargoes were reflected in the stops and goes of this great transport infrastructure project. The scope of the article is limited to corporate history, with the necessary insights into government relations. Several books on the Channel fixed links discuss the geological and technical arguments for the competing schemes. A full history of the various Channel projects still has to be written from the numerous consultants' reports produced in the last seventy years.

This article will reassess the role of the Channel Tunnel Study Group in the light of new material. Official contacts between both Channel tunnel companies were resumed in January 1947, and parliamentary groups were formed soon afterwards. Railway nationalisation encouraged closer cooperation between the British Railways Board and the SNCF. The British Transport Commission (BTC) at that time owned 26.3 per cent of the capital of the Channel Tunnel Company Ltd, and customarily nominated a director on its board. The new chairman, Leo F. A. d'Erlanger, was a francophile Catholic and europhile Tory.

detail.title: Targeting Interventions Under Resource Constraints: A Risk Assessment Case Study of Mothers of Children with Disabilities in Rural India

Clinton Fellow for Service in India (funded by the American India Foundation) in partnership with Satya Special School, which collected the primary data. detail.abstract: Non-profit organizations operating in resource-constrained environments face a targeting challenge when it comes to service delivery: how can high-risk populations in need of interventions be efficiently identified? Maternal mental health interventions for mothers of children with disabilities in rural India face this very problem. Disability services in India are organized almost entirely around the child's diagnosis (Government of India, 2016), and caregiver psychiatric morbidity is typically addressed only as a byproduct of child-focused programming, leaving no clear mechanism to identify mothers in most need of direct support. This paper uses case-study data from 416 households of children with disabilities in Puducherry and rural Tamil Nadu, yielding key findings that can directly inform prioritization in this region. Peripartum anxiety risk correlates more closely with employment instability than with income alone. Five specific factors—maternal trauma history, paternal intoxication, consanguineous marriage, peripartum infections, and lack of genetic counseling awareness—predict maternal distress within this population. The analysis compresses these variables into a practical, point-based risk scorecard for frontline use with reliable discriminative accuracy (AUC 0.73). Presented as a demonstrative framework specific to the case-study, this paper proposes piloting the scorecard framework at established antenatal and early-postnatal contact points to validate its operational utility and accuracy.

title: Climate-Tech Diffusion and Inclusive Growth: How Adaptation-Tech Adoption Affects Productivity, Inequality, and Long-Run Development Trajectories

detail.title: Climate-Tech Diffusion and Inclusive Growth: How Adaptation-Tech Adoption Affects Productivity, Inequality, and Long-Run Development Trajectories
detail.abstract:
Adaptation technology is emerging as one of the most powerful yet under‑utilized levers for inclusive growth in a warming world. Climate damages are nonlinear, regressive, and concentrated in low‑latitude, low‑income regions, where a one‑degree hotter year reduces growth by ~1.3 percentage points and repeated shocks permanently bend development trajectories downward. Adaptation technologies—stress‑tolerant seed, irrigation, cooling, early‑warning systems, and resilient infrastructure—directly avert these losses, delivering exceptionally high and progressive returns. As the report notes, “the technology that averts those damages delivers its largest returns exactly where incomes are lowest” .

Despite this potential, diffusion remains weakest where need is greatest. Adoption is rationed by credit constraints, information gaps, insecure land tenure, gender disparities, and risk aversion, producing an adaptation deficit in which fewer than 10% of households in the hottest regions own cooling, only ~50% of countries have adequate early‑warning systems, and adaptation finance covers under 5% of estimated annual needs. As the report states, “the binding constraint on inclusive growth under climate change is not the availability of adaptation technology but the governance of its diffusion” .

The report introduces the Adaptation Diffusion Funnel, a five‑stage model—availability, affordability, adoption, complementary investment, and inclusive outcome—that explains why high‑return technologies fail to reach the exposed poor. Leakage is greatest at the middle stages, where households lack the complements (insurance, energy, fertilizer, tenure security) that turn adoption into resilience. Case studies from Sub‑Saharan Africa, India, Bangladesh, and Ahmedabad show that pro‑poor diffusion channels—local seed firms, community volunteers, municipal heat‑action systems—unlock large, durable gains, while centralized or market‑led channels stall.

The report concludes that adaptation is not a defensive cost but a development strategy, and that inclusive growth under climate change is fundamentally a diffusion‑governance problem. The binding term: “Treat every adaptation‑technology adoption as a distributional intervention before it is a productivity intervention.”
