title: When the Going Gets Tough, Do the Incentivized Get Going? A Field Experiment on Uniform Incentives and Reward Attainability in Multitasking Service
affiliations: and Southern Methodist University (SMU) - Information Technology and Operations Management Department (ITOM)

detail.title: When the Going Gets Tough, Do the Incentivized Get Going? A Field Experiment on Uniform Incentives and Reward Attainability in Multitasking Service

publicationDetails.detailsText: SMU Cox School of Business Research Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: SMU Cox School of Business Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Financial incentives are a common tool for improving service-worker performance, especially on difficult tasks. However, firms often apply uniform incentives to broad operational categories whose tasks differ substantially in reward attainability. In multitasking environments, workers may respond to such coarse incentives according to each task's perceived reward attainability rather than the firm's category labels, creating distortions within the incentivized category itself. We examine this possibility using a six-week field experiment in the live-chat customer service operation of a Fortune Global 100 firm. The firm introduced a salient bonus opportunity for resolving difficult customer cases while agents concurrently handled multiple randomly assigned cases of varying difficulty. We find that the bonus improves average performance on incentivized, firm-defined "difficult" cases, increasing customer satisfaction by 5.8% relative to the control-group mean and reducing future recontact for the same issue by 3%. This average effect, however, masks a sharp threshold pattern. Among the most difficult bonus-eligible cases, where reward attainability is lowest, customer satisfaction declines by 24.3% and future recontact increases by 1.1%. In contrast, performance improves for less difficult incentivized cases and spills over to unincentivized, "easy" cases, where customer satisfaction increases by 8.5% and future recontact decreases by 6.7%. These patterns are consistent with workers prioritizing tasks by perceived bonus attainability: the bonus helps difficult-but-attainable cases but induces neglect once attainability falls below a threshold. Higher ability and heavier workloads sharpen this prioritization. The findings suggest that incentive design should account for task attainability, worker ability, and workload.

title: Should the Rules Be Different When Prediction Markets Play Sportsbook?
affiliations: Marquette University

detail.title: Should the Rules Be Different When Prediction Markets Play Sportsbook?
detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of U.S. prediction market platforms has triggered a complex legal debate over whether event contracts functioning as sports wagers should be regulated under federal derivatives law or state gambling frameworks. While information-driven markets aggregate valuable macroeconomic data and facilitate financial hedging, sports contracts on platforms like Kalshi largely serve as mass-market recreational wagering. The author advocates for a functional regulatory approach that distinguishes contracts based on their actual economic purpose rather than their shared technological mechanics.

title: The Limited Structural Impact of Rural Electrification: Village-Level Evidence from Cambodia
affiliations: and Keio University

detail.title: The Limited Structural Impact of Rural Electrification: Village-Level Evidence from Cambodia
detail.abstract: A stable and accessible power supply is pivotal for economic growth and development. We study the impact of nationwide residential electrification in Cambodia on sectoral employment. Leveraging annual village-level administrative data from 2013 to 2021, we estimate the employment effects of electrification using a novel difference-indifferences estimator designed to accommodate staggered adoption and treatment-effect heterogeneity across groups and over time. In our preferred specification, electrification reduced agricultural employment by around 2.4 percentage points in the long run but raised service employment by only 1.5 percentage points; the agriculture-to-services transition was also more pronounced among working-age women. The magnitude of these estimates is substantially smaller than those reported in earlier studies, consistent with a pattern of premature deindustrialisation in which electrification induces only limited structural transformation. The modest inter-sectoral shift in labour appears to operate through a mix of channels, including agricultural productivity, labour demand, investment in human capital, and migration, although the contribution of each channel, considered in isolation, is minor. Our findings highlight that agrarian workers who detach from the labour market may not necessarily re-enter it when complementary markets and demand are absent. We further underscore the importance of comparing model estimates across alternative constructions of the treatment variable, as the novel estimator we employ permits continuous, discrete, or binary treatments.

title: From Label to Construct: Building Cumulative Strategy Research on Artificial Intelligence
affiliations: , NHH Norwegian School of Economics and NHH Norwegian School of Economics

detail.title: From Label to Construct: Building Cumulative Strategy Research on Artificial Intelligence
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly become a central object of strategy research, yet the field risks building a literature in which findings accumulate without cumulating. AI often serves as a broad label for markedly different technical systems, epistemological roles, organizational configurations, and strategic tasks. Drawing on construct-clarity theory, we argue that AI risks functioning in strategy research as a pseudo-multidimensional construct, an umbrella term that groups related phenomena without the specification required for construct-level inference. We develop three tools for moving the field from label to construct. First, a typology that distinguishes AI systems by technical system, the system in use, and role in the study. Second, an anatomy of the compound-treatment problem, showing how observed outcomes in AI strategy studies are jointly produced by eight stacked layers, from the knowledge substrate to the evaluation standard, several of them hidden in proprietary systems. Third, a durability hierarchy distinguishing architecture-derived claims, human-AI interaction claims, and model-context-specific claims, explaining why some AI-strategy findings travel across systems and time, whereas others are situated snapshots. The three tools yield design principles and reporting conventions intended to help strategy scholars produce cumulative knowledge about AI while preserving relevance to rapidly evolving technologies.

title: The Economics of Sustainability: Reconciling Economic Growth, Resource Constraints, and Environmental Stability

detail.title: The Economics of Sustainability: Reconciling Economic Growth, Resource Constraints, and Environmental Stability
detail.abstract: The growth-versus-environment debate is still fought as if the relevant quantity were a single ratio. It is not. Between 1990 and 2022, world GDP in the Maddison Project series more than tripled while the carbon intensity of that output fell 45 percent. Fossil-and-cement CO₂ still rose 70 percent through 2024, to 38.6 gigatonnes. That pattern is relative decoupling, and it is now the global default. Absolute decoupling-GDP up, emissions downis a different fact. In a 2005-2019 window chosen to avoid the pandemic, 39 of 163 countries with complete series reduced territorial CO₂ while growing. Thirty of those 39 are high-income. On consumption-based accounting the count falls to 27. On domestic material consumption it falls to 24, and the global material footprint rose from 58 to 99 billion tonnes between 2000 and 2022. The Global Carbon Budget 2024 remaining budget for 1.5 °C at 50 percent likelihood is 200 GtCO₂ from 1 January 2025: five years of 2024 emissions. Solar photovoltaic levelized cost fell 90 percent from 2010 to 2024, to 43 dollars per megawatt-hour, and still fossil fuels supplied 81 percent of primary energy. The reconciliation is not a choice between "green growth" and "degrowth" as identities. It is a measurement rule. A falling CO₂/GDP ratio is an efficiency result. An absolute decline in territorial emissions is a production result. A consumption result that still overshoots the remaining carbon budget is not a sustainability result.

title: Weak Institutions and the Enduring Culture of Corruption in Ghana: Hidden Constraints on Economic Development, Social Inclusion, Inequality Reduction, Entrepreneurship, Innovation, Industrialization, and Youth-Led Economic Growth

detail.title: Weak Institutions and the Enduring Culture of Corruption in Ghana: Hidden Constraints on Economic Development, Social Inclusion, Inequality Reduction, Entrepreneurship, Innovation, Industrialization, and Youth-Led Economic Growth
detail.abstract: Ghana is widely regarded as one of Sub-Saharan Africa's most stable multiparty democracies, yet a decade of political continuity has coincided with stagnant institutional quality, a sovereign default, and a widening gap between macroeconomic stabilisation and structural transformation. This article asks why technically sound policies, anti-corruption agencies, industrial promotion schemes, and fiscal adjustment programmes have repeatedly failed to convert into durable development outcomes. Drawing on new institutional economics and the political-economy literature on democracy capture and combining a longitudinal analysis of governance and economic indicators (2015-2026) with structured case studies of two critical episodes, the campaign against illegal small-scale gold mining ("galamsey") and the One District, One Factory (1D1F) industrial policy, the article argues that Ghana's binding constraint on development is not policy design but the selective, politically contingent enforcement of rules. Triangulating data from Transparency International, the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund, the Ghana Statistical Service, and Afrobarometer against peer-reviewed political-economy scholarship, the analysis shows that successive governments have stabilised the macroeconomy twice in fifteen years without addressing the underlying capacity of powerful actors to evade accountability. The article contributes to debates on institutions and development by demonstrating through a single-country longitudinal case how electoral competitiveness can entrench rather than discipline rent-seeking and concludes with implications for industrial policy design and anti-corruption institutional reform in comparable competitive-clientelist settings.

title: Differential Farming Systems, Farm Productivity, and Resource Use Efficiency: Evidence from Wheat Production in Afghanistan
affiliations: University of Tsukuba, BRAC and University of Tsukuba

detail.title: Differential Farming Systems, Farm Productivity, and Resource Use Efficiency: Evidence from Wheat Production in Afghanistan
detail.abstract: Afghanistan faces persistent challenges in achieving food security in wheat production, its principal staple crop, accounting for 70 percent of cereal consumption. This study investigates wheat productivity and technical efficiency across irrigated and rainfed farming systems using household-level data from the Afghanistan Living Conditions Survey (ALCS) 2016-17, covering 6,351 wheat-producing households. To address the potential endogeneity of production inputs, the study employs the endogenous stochastic frontier model of Karakaplan and Kutlu (2017), treating working capital, hired labor cost, and cultivated land as jointly endogenous and identified using instruments for market access, household labor availability, and wealth. A robustness check combines working capital and hired labor cost into a composite measure, yielding an overidentified specification with formal tests of instrument validity. Accounting for endogeneity matters: exogenous and endogeneity corrected models yield systematically different estimates of input elasticities, returns to scale, and efficiency. Working capital and cultivated land are robust determinants of output, while hired labor cost is less stable, reflecting its zero-inflated distribution. Returns to scale are decreasing under the exogenous model but approach constant returns for irrigated farming once endogeneity is corrected for, while rainfed and aggregate farming remain under decreasing returns. Irrigated farming operates closer to the frontier with higher, more concentrated efficiency than rainfed farming, and pooling the two systems obscures input effects and instrument validity apparent only when analyzed separately. These findings contribute to the productivity literature by applying an endogenous stochastic frontier approach to Afghan agriculture, with implications for irrigation development and food security policy.

title: Chile under Pinochet: A Multidimensional Counterfactual Audit

detail.title: Chile under Pinochet: A Multidimensional Counterfactual Audit

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known financial or personal relationships, competing interests, or other circumstances that could have influenced, or could reasonably be perceived to have influenced, the research reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, patient data, clinical interventions, or the collection of personally identifiable information. The research relies exclusively on secondary, publicly available and/or aggregated data. Accordingly, institutional ethics approval and informed consent were not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant or financial support from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The study was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: This paper conducts an adversarial, multidimensional counterfactual audit of Chile around the 1973 military coup and the Pinochet regime. The estimand is deliberately narrower than a claim about one person or one reform: it is the country-level trajectory associated with the 1973 regime-onset bundle, with the 1982-84 crisis, the late-1980s recovery, the 1988 plebiscite, and the 1990 democratic transition treated as distinct phases or separate designs. A 93-column country-year panel combines 89 quantitative fields with identifiers, drawing on Maddison, Penn World Table 11.0, the Global Macro Database, World Development Indicators, World Bank commodity prices, V-Dem v16, Economic Freedom of the World, and legacy complexity and Heritage data. The revised audit adds sex-specific mortality and longevity, adolescent fertility, manufacturing and agricultural performance, consumption composition, labor productivity, output per hour, capital per worker, fiscal and trade balances, and demographic growth outcomes. Identification is triangulated using exact and regularized synthetic control, augmented SCM, factor and matrix-completion methods, matched difference-in-differences/event-study diagnostics, time-ordered validation ensembles, structural time-series sensitivity models, predictive machine-learning falsification models, and experimental robust counterfactual estimators. Adversarial checks include 112 legacy GDP specifications, moving pretreatment windows, leave-one-pre-year-out designs, treatment-date jitter, anticipation cuts, regime-stability donor restrictions, complete-case designs, targeted and random donor deletion up to 40%, in-time and in-space placebos, residual pretrend tests, omitted-trend tipping points, multiple-testing-adjusted placebo diagnostics across 19 outcomes, and a joint V-Dem rights placebo statistic. The main GDP finding is not a single invariant number: credible counterfactual models generally imply a negative 1973-1988 income gap, while magnitude varies materially by estimator and source. Random donor-deletion experiments preserve the negative sign in every replication, but spatial placebo inference for GDP remains non-decisive. Institutional results are larger and more coherent: democracy, expression, association, rule of law, human rights, and physical-integrity indices fall sharply relative to counterfactual paths. Health and demographic outcomes are heterogeneous and cannot be interpreted as a single welfare index. The paper introduces DR-SCM, CASES, MORSE, SACR, TB-SCM and a deliberately severe cross-source shared-weight stress test; simulation and empirical validation show that none is universally dominant. The strongest defensible conclusion is therefore asymmetric: market opening and export expansion coexist with a large institutional-rights collapse and substantial evidence of foregone income/productivity relative to plausible untreated trajectories, while causal attribution to any single policy mechanism remains limited by the bundled nature of the historical treatment.

title: The Metaphysics of Power: Indigenous Survival and Lani Cosmology: Why Some Life Goes Extinct While Other Life Survives

detail.title: The Metaphysics of Power: Indigenous Survival and Lani Cosmology: Why Some Life Goes Extinct While Other Life Survives

detail.abstract: This paper argues that the deepest determinant of civilisational survival is neither military force nor economic wealth, but trust-based concentrated power rooted in ontological foundations. Drawing from the Psycho-Cosmocide framework and the cosmological vocabulary of the Lani people of West Papua, the paper develops a comprehensive theory of metaphysical power that distinguishes between coercive, symbolic, epistemic, and ontological dimensions of power, while demonstrating how trust integrates these dimensions into the most durable form of collective force across civilisational history. The paper grounds this argument in Lani ontological architecture—AP, Ap-ap, Oʼgur, Muʼnggar, Aʼnggena, and Kugi—and traces the operation of the Civilisational Psycho-Cosmocide Virus (CPCV) as a mechanism through which colonial power systematically destroys the internal conditions necessary for trust formation, converting the cosmologically intact Ap into Ap-ap: an ontological counterfeit that unknowingly performs the colonial order. The argument is situated in comparative engagement with the work of Michel Foucault, Frantz Fanon, Sylvia Wynter, Walter Mignolo, Ibn Khaldūn, Enrique Dussel, Achille Mbembe, Martin Heidegger, Vine Deloria Jr., and Ubuntu philosophy. It argues that the Lani ontological framework both converges with and exceeds existing decolonial theory by providing a positive ontological architecture grounded in a living Indigenous tradition. The paper concludes that the Papuan experience of ontological dispossession reveals a wider civilisational crisis, and that the reconstruction of trust-based cosmobian life (a term coined within this framework and defined in the Key Conceptual Definitions section below) constitutes both a specifically Papuan liberation project and a contribution to the broader survival of civilisation itself.

title: The Einstein Moment
affiliations: The Digital Economist and The Digital Economist

detail.title: The Einstein Moment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported and published by The Digital Economist.

detail.abstract: The Einstein Moment: What Leaders Must Do Now to Stay Relevant in the Age of Agentic AI explores one of the defining leadership challenges of our time. As agentic AI transforms industries at unprecedented speed, organizations are investing heavily in technology, yet many executive teams remain unprepared for the deeper transformation required to lead effectively.The challenge is rarely technological; it is psychological. Much of the way leaders perceive risk, make decisions, and shape organizational culture is driven by mental models formed for a world that no longer exists. These hidden patterns can quietly limit an organization's ability to adapt, innovate, and realize AI's full potential.Drawing on neuroscience, behavioral science, and leadership case studies, including Satya Nadella's cultural transformation at Microsoft, this paper introduces the Mindset of Possibilities System, a practical framework designed to help leaders recognize hidden assumptions, develop new ways of thinking, and translate personal transformation into organizational change through three disciplined practices: Explore, Step Up, and Level Up.Ultimately, The Einstein Moment argues that leadership readiness in the Age of Agentic AI is not defined by technical expertise alone, but by the capacity for conscious self-transformation. The leaders who cultivate that capacity today will be best positioned to shape the next generation of organizations.‍

title: Need, Alignment, or Commerce? Recovering the Revealed Priorities of Foreign Aid Donors through Inverse Optimization
affiliations: University of Massachusetts Dartmouth

detail.title: Need, Alignment, or Commerce? Recovering the Revealed Priorities of Foreign Aid Donors through Inverse Optimization
detail.abstract: Foreign aid allocation is classically understood as a contest among competing donor motives—recipient need, diplomatic alignment, and commercial interest—yet the empirical literature has characterized these motives almost entirely through regression coefficients rather than through the optimization framework the allocation problem naturally invites. We recast each donor-year as a constrained resource-allocation problem over three objectives and use a KL-divergence-based inverse-optimization estimator—a revealed-preference method, conceptually motivated by classical inverse optimization—to recover, from observed allocations, the weight each donor places on need, diplomatic alignment, and commerce, together with a goodness-of-fit diagnostic and bootstrap confidence intervals. Applying the framework to 24 donors—the near-complete universe of providers reporting comparable official development assistance to the OECD, spanning traditional DAC members and Gulf/non-Western donors—across 142 recipients over 2010–2022, we find that donor allocation is organized far more by a need–commerce axis than by diplomatic alignment. A need-and-alignment model explains essentially none of the allocation structure—its mean fit is ρ ≈ 0.013, and it fits no better than a uniform split for a large share of donor-years—whereas admitting commerce as a third objective raises mean fit to ρ ≈ 0.27. The improvement concentrates precisely among the donors long described as commercially motivated: France, Japan, and Germany, whose allocations are fit worse than uniform by need and alignment alone (ρ < 0) yet well explained once commerce enters. The recovered weights place Belgium, the Netherlands, and the Nordics at the need pole; Japan, France, and Germany at the commerce pole; and identify diplomatic alignment as a materially weighted motive almost exclusively for Gulf donors (Western–Gulf need-weight gap significant at p < 0.01). Temporal decomposition reveals a marked post-2018 commercial drift in the United Kingdom, deepening commercialization in Japan and France, and a small but significant economy-wide dip in need-weighting during the COVID-19 years. Donor-level regressions show that Western status is the dominant structural predictor of need-weighting (p < 0.05), while colonial history and portfolio concentration predict lower alignment-weighting; the decomposition is invariant to the diminishing-returns parameter (rank correlation ρ ≈ 0.98 across α) and to the need measure. The results quantify, mechanism by mechanism, the “altruistic versus egoistic” donor typology previously established only through reduced-form estimation.

title: When Quality Mandates Backfire: Environmental Spillovers of Mandatory GMP Regulation
affiliations: East China Normal University (ECNU),  and  Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)

detail.title: When Quality Mandates Backfire: Environmental Spillovers of Mandatory GMP Regulation
detail.abstract: Mandatory quality regulations are a central tool for ensuring product safety, yet little is known about their environmental consequences. We examine the impact of China's 2010 Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) regulation in the pharmaceutical industry, a reform that sharply raised production and compliance requirements. Using firm-level data and a continuous difference-indifferences design based on pre-regulation exposure intensity, we find that more exposed firms increased COD emission intensity after the policy took effect. The adverse effect was stronger among non-state-owned firms, firms located in areas with weaker environmental enforcement, and traditional Chinese medicine producers. Mechanism analysis suggests that the cost and cash-flow pressures induced by GMP compliance led firms to strategically reduce pollution abatement efforts along both the process-level and end-ofpipe margins. Our findings shed light on the conditions under which unintended consequences of mandatory quality standards may arise: firms' capacity to absorb compliance costs and the stringency of local environmental oversight jointly shape whether product quality regulation crowds out pollution control and worsens environmental outcomes.

title: Satellite-Derived Bathymetry Using Multi-Sensor Remote Sensing: Principles, Sensors, Physics-Based Models, Artificial Intelligence, ICESat-2 Integration, and Future Perspectives
affiliations: Tribhuvan University and Florida International University

detail.title: Satellite-Derived Bathymetry Using Multi-Sensor Remote Sensing: Principles, Sensors, Physics-Based Models, Artificial Intelligence, ICESat-2 Integration, and Future Perspectives

declarations.declarationOfInterest: yes
declarations.ethicsApproval: yes
declarations.funderStatement: no funder

detail.abstract: Satellite-derived bathymetry (SDB) has evolved from locally calibrated multispectral regressions into a broader family of optical, lidar-assisted, physics-based, machine-learning, and multi-sensor approaches for mapping shallow aquatic topography where conventional hydrographic surveys are sparse, expensive, or difficult to repeat. This review synthesizes the physical basis of SDB, sensor capabilities, preprocessing requirements, empirical and radiative-transfer inversion methods, artificial intelligence, ICESat-2 photon-counting bathymetry, multi-sensor fusion, validation, uncertainty, applications, operational implementation, and future research. The evidence shows that no universally optimal sensor-model combination exists. Empirical log-ratio and log-linear methods remain valuable when water is optically simple and representative calibration depths are available; semianalytical and physics-based inversion can reduce site-specific dependence but impose stronger optical assumptions and computational demands; and machine learning can exploit nonlinear spectral, spatial, and environmental relationships while remaining vulnerable to domain shift and spatially non-independent validation. Deep learning is mature for selected image-to-depth and bathymetric lidar tasks but remains datalimited for globally transferable SDB, whereas foundation models, graph architectures, diffusion models, and physics-informed networks are largely emerging or prospective in this specific domain. ICESat-2 fundamentally changes the calibration problem by providing sparse, globally distributed, refraction-correctable depth observations that can seed optical models over data-poor coasts, and the operational ATL24 product strengthens this role. Across methods, atmospheric correction, tide and vertical-datum harmonization, bottom-type variability, turbidity, reference-data quality, and uncertainty reporting remain central constraints. The review therefore advocates environment-specific sensor selection, physically constrained and uncertainty-aware AI, spatial cross-validation, standardized cross-site benchmark regions, FAIR provenance, cloud-native processing, and repeatable quality-control workflows. These priorities are essential for moving SDB from successful local demonstrations toward defensible regional products, hydrographic decision support, coastal digital twins, and eventually operational global shallow-water mapping.

detail.abstract: The rapid proliferation of digital technologies, including the pervasive influence of social media, has fundamentally reshaped human society, offering unprecedented connectivity, efficiency, and innovation. However, this digital transformation is not without significant environmental consequences, ranging from substantial energy consumption and e-waste generation to the carbon footprint of advanced computational processes like Artificial Intelligence (AI) and blockchain. This article explores the critical nexus between digital ethics, social media, and environmental sustainability, arguing that a robust ethical framework is imperative to mitigate the adverse ecological impacts of the digital age. It examines the multifaceted environmental challenges posed by digital technologies, delves into the ethical dilemmas arising from their intersection with environmental concerns, and proposes a pathway towards more sustainable and ethically sound digital practices. By integrating principles of environmental justice, resource efficiency, and responsible innovation, this paper advocates for a proactive approach to ensure that technological progress contributes to, rather than detracts from, a healthy planet.

detail.abstract: The expected-utility group-decision model of Bueno de Mesquita — deployed by the CIA as Policon and long credited with striking forecasting accuracy — has never had a complete open implementation or a fair public evaluation. We provide both. Our replication, built from the Scholz–Calbert–Smith reconstruction with every interpretive choice logged, reproduces the published reference case. Evaluated on 351 expert-coded EU legislative controversies with sourced actor capabilities and reference points, the model fails a pre-registered accuracy gate against a far simpler benchmark: the capability-and-salience-weighted mean of actor positions. A pre-registered successor search — its data split committed to version control before any fitting — produces two structurally-motivated candidate models; a tournament of four further solution concepts drawn from the field's other traditions extends the comparison to eight in all, counting the weighted mean and the challenge model, and none separates from the mean on held-out data. A flexible cross-validated oracle then shows the weighted mean sits at the extractable-signal ceiling for this domain and input set. We conclude that the lineage's documented successes, including its models outperforming the very analysts who supplied their inputs, are attributable to structured elicitation rather than to solution dynamics: structure, not magic. The model's home-turf claim — superiority in coercive settings — remains open, pending an ex-ante coded case library we introduce alongside a live, cryptographically sealed forecast ledger, which has now recorded its first graded cycle. All results regenerate by one command from repository artifacts, given the one third-party dataset the paper documents.

title: The Impact of Workplace Flexibility on Gender Equality in the Labor Market
affiliations: INSEAD and

detail.title: The Impact of Workplace Flexibility on Gender Equality in the Labor Market
detail.abstract: Flexible work is often understood as a way to narrow gender labor market inequality, though causal evidence remains limited. We exploit the UK's 2014 extension of the Right to Request Flexible Working, which broadened eligibility from parents and carers to all sufficiently tenured employees. We find that the reform widened the gender earnings gap by 4.6 percent for eligible workers. This is driven by reductions in women's labor supply, with no change in the price of an hour of work. Our results suggest that equal access to flexibility may widen earnings inequality if gendered norms around labor supply remain unaddressed.

title: The Condolence Gap: Retraction Watch, Jason Arday and the Duty of Editorial Reconciliation
affiliations: Independent Scholar

detail.title: The Condolence Gap: Retraction Watch, Jason Arday and the Duty of Editorial Reconciliation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial or commercial competing interests relevant to this article.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This commentary analyses publicly accessible documents and does not report research involving human participants or animals.

detail.abstract:
Background: Retraction Watch, a journalism website, published a detailed report on allegations concerning Jason Arday on 27 July 2026, promoted the report in later round-ups, hosted an extensive comment thread, updated the report after Cambridge announced an investigation and Arday resigned, and expressed shock and sorrow after his death. The coexistence of accusatory coverage and later condolence is not, by itself, hypocrisy. It does, however, expose a distinct governance question: whether a publisher that reports human consequences will also re-examine the archive through which it helped give allegations public force.
Method: This commentary analyses the publicly visible Retraction Watch report, its updates, related weekend round-ups, the death notice, the website's funding and comments policy, the public correction record, Arday's resignation statement, and contemporaneous reporting available by 15 August 2026. It examines published material only and does not infer unpublished editorial deliberations, determine plagiarism, identify the cause of death, or attribute legal or moral causation to any person or organisation.
Analysis: The reviewed record combines document-specific material with categorical source judgments, biographical expansion, racialised context and a comment section containing personal allegations and motive speculation that appear difficult to reconcile with the website's published moderation policy. After Arday publicly described profound personal and family distress, later coverage continued to circulate the allegation narrative. The death notice expressed sorrow and supplied crisis-support information, but the original report, its comment environment and its person-level inferences were not visibly reconciled with the changed circumstances when reviewed.
Conclusion: The record does not justify treating Retraction Watch's Arday coverage as an adjudicative finding of plagiarism, intent, personal dishonesty, professional unfitness or responsibility for death. It may be consulted as journalism and as a source of leads, but any institution relying on it must independently obtain, verify and assess the underlying evidence. In that role-specific sense, the archive is disqualified from functioning as a substitute integrity verdict unless it is supported by a transparent evidentiary record and an accountable process of editorial reconciliation.

title: The Construction of Content Creators' Ethics in Digital Space: A Bugis-Makassar Local Wisdom Perspective

detail.title: The Construction of Content Creators' Ethics in Digital Space: A Bugis-Makassar Local Wisdom Perspective

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Penelitian ini bersifat independen untuk pengembangan ilmu komunikasi dibiayai secara mandiri
declarations.ethicsApproval: Penelitian ini telah mendapat persetujuan etik dari Fakultas Ilmu Sosial dan Ilmu Politik Universitas Hasanuddin, Makassar, Indonesia

detail.abstract: Digital transformation has fundamentally altered the global media landscape by empowering audiences to become active content creators who shape narratives. This study examines how Bugis-Makassar creators from South Sulawesi, Indonesia, embed local wisdom into digital ethics via four pillars: Siri' na Pacce (collective shame and empathy), Sipakatau (humanizing each other), Sipakainge (reminding the community), and Sipakalebbi (mutual respect). Utilizing digital ethnography, content analysis of 25 YouTube videos, and in-depth interviews, the research reveals that Siri' na Pacce functions as a non-verbal mechanism for emotional control, while Sipakainge facilitates social correction through feedback and humor. The merging of local values with global ethical norms fosters a decolonial-local model that emphasizes collective accountability and balances commercial gains with cultural preservation. The study advocates for digital content moderation policies that are inclusive, culturally sensitive, and adaptive to evolving global digital dynamics.

title: Strategic Leadership Framework for Successful Ecosystem Orchestration: A Systematic Literature Review

detail.title: Strategic Leadership Framework for Successful Ecosystem Orchestration: A Systematic Literature Review
detail.abstract:
Background: Ecosystem strategy has become a dominant lens in management research, and with it comes growing interest in how firms successfully orchestrate ecosystems. However, the literature on ecosystem orchestration and strategic leadership has developed largely separately, leaving an integrative framework lacking. This systematic literature review (SLR) addresses three interrelated questions: (RQ1) what factors determine successful ecosystem orchestration; (RQ2) how integration capabilities influence ecosystem orchestration; and (RQ3) what role strategic leadership plays in successful ecosystem orchestration. 

Methods: We followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines and searched Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar for peer-reviewed articles published in Scopus Q1/Q2 journals between January 2015 and May 2026. Of the 259 records identified, we removed 79 duplicates, screened 180 records, and assessed 35 full texts for eligibility; 29 studies met all inclusion criteria. Each included article then underwent a Verification and Validation stage using the CrossRef API to ensure DOI validity and metadata accuracy. We assessed risk of bias using an adaptation of CASP appropriate for management research, and then synthesized the findings narratively through thematic analysis.

Results: The 29 studies spanned 2017-2026 and included conceptual papers (n = 7), case studies (n = 15), systematic reviews and meta-analyses (n = 3), formal models (n = 2), and one sequence analysis. We assessed the risk of bias as Low for all 29 studies. Three findings stand out. First, ecosystem orchestration succeeds through a configuration of multiple factors, not a single one: alignment structure, complementarity management, dynamic feedback control, orchestration practices, design contingencies, the balance between value creation and capture, and multi-level coordination. Second, integration capabilities operate as a three-layer mechanism (technical, relational, and strategic) connecting orchestrators with their partners. Third, strategic leadership in ecosystems is multidimensional, operating simultaneously as a dynamic capability, a cognitive microfoundation, a distributed practice, and a stakeholder engagement strategy. 

Conclusion: We propose a Strategic Leadership Framework for Ecosystem Orchestration with three pillars: Vision Shaping (sensing), Capability Integration (seizing), and Distributed Orchestration (reconfiguring), supported by the enabler Attention-and Trust-based Governance. This framework draws on converging evidence from empirical and conceptual studies. This framework provides practical guidance for orchestrators in both private-sector ecosystems and state-led mega-infrastructure programs, including state-owned enterprise-driven coordination platforms in Indonesia.

title: Due Process Paranoia in International Arbitration: Procedural Fairness, Robust Case Management and the Enforceability of Arbitral Awards
affiliations: Senior Judicial Magistrate at Bangladesh Judicial Service

detail.title: Due Process Paranoia in International Arbitration: Procedural Fairness, Robust Case Management and the Enforceability of Arbitral Awards
detail.abstract: International arbitration depends simultaneously on procedural fairness and procedural discipline. Yet tribunals are often said to suffer from 'due process paranoia': a reluctance to reject extensions, late evidence, repetitive submissions or weak procedural applications because an adverse party may later seek annulment or resist enforcement. This article argues that such defensive case management rests on a doctrinal mistake. The transnational minimum of due process is not an entitlement to every requested procedural step, but a contextual entitlement to equality, notice and a genuine opportunity to present and answer the material case. Drawing on the UNCITRAL Model Law, the New York Convention, English, French and Singaporean law, and contemporary institutional rules, the article shows that leading legal systems ordinarily preserve a substantial zone of tribunal discretion and increasingly combine fairness obligations with express powers of procedural acceleration. The analysis is sharpened by the Singapore Court of Appeal's decisions in China Machine and Wan Sern: the former rejects unlimited procedural entitlement and requires deference to reasonable tribunal choices, while the latter demonstrates that genuinely prejudicial failures remain reviewable. Against that background, the article proposes a five-part Proportionate Procedural Judgment Framework: notice and foreseeability; genuine opportunity; functional equality; materiality and prejudice; and reasoned proportionality. Properly applied, the framework permits robust case management without weakening due process and provides a more accurate method for assessing enforceability risk than defensive procedural indulgence.

title: Equal Output Sharing in Teams with Heterogeneous Agents
affiliations: INSEAD - Technology and Operations Management, The University of Sydney - School of Economics, INSEAD and University of Sydney

detail.title: Equal Output Sharing in Teams with Heterogeneous Agents
detail.abstract: Why do many teams share output equally, despite differences in their members' productivity and contributions? We identify conditions on the production technology under which equal sharing is optimal despite heterogeneous costs and productivity. These conditions are satisfied by separable logarithmic-affine technologies and, for two-worker groups, by transformed bilinear technologies under specific cross-effect and curvature conditions. In organizations where output is separable into different groups' contributions, equal sharing within each group is optimal when these conditions hold at the level of the group. Otherwise, equal sharing is typically not optimal. Our results are consistent with the high prevalence of equal sharing in partnership settings (e.g., law or medical partnerships) and in small teams (e.g., two-partner joint ventures), and with its lower prevalence in large teams that may involve non-separable production technologies (e.g., large manufacturing or innovation teams). In sum, equal sharing is often optimal in team production.

title: Sanctions and International Commercial Arbitration: Arbitrability, Payment Restrictions, Due Process and the Enforcement of Awards
affiliations: Senior Judicial Magistrate at Bangladesh Judicial Service

detail.title: Sanctions and International Commercial Arbitration: Arbitrability, Payment Restrictions, Due Process and the Enforcement of Awards
detail.abstract: Economic sanctions increasingly affect international commercial arbitration at every stage of the process, but their legal consequences are frequently misclassified. Asset freezes, payment prohibitions, services restrictions, licensing requirements and no-claims provisions may impede the financing of an arbitration, alter substantive contractual obligations, constrain settlement or payment, and complicate recognition and execution of an award. They do not, however, necessarily extinguish the arbitration agreement or render the dispute non-arbitrable. This article argues for a stage-specific approach that separates four questions: arbitral jurisdiction and arbitrability; lawful access to the arbitral process; the substantive effect of sanctions on liability and payment; and recognition, enforcement and execution of awards. Drawing on the New York Convention, the UNCITRAL Model Law, ICC compliance practice, UK and US licensing regimes, the developing EU framework, and recent decisions including UniCredit Bank GmbH v RusChemAlliance LLC, UniCredit Bank GmbH v Constitution Aircraft Leasing/Celestial Aviation Services and OWH SE i.L. v RTI Ltd, the article develops a seven-stage Sanctions Compatibility Framework. It also examines the 2026 Advocate General Opinion in Reibel, which sharpens the distinction between arbitrability and the prohibition on satisfying a sanctions-affected claim. The central thesis is that sanctions should ordinarily operate as mandatory legal constraints within arbitration, not as a general jurisdictional veto. Due process requires proportionate accommodation of genuine regulatory obstacles, while enforcement courts should distinguish the legal validity of an award from the separate lawfulness of payment or execution against particular assets.

title: A Social-Spatial Network Choice Model with Application to Pop-up Store Operations
affiliations: , The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) - CUHK Business School and The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) - CUHK Business School

detail.title: A Social-Spatial Network Choice Model with Application to Pop-up Store Operations
detail.abstract: Social interactions are increasingly shaping consumers' movements and visits to physical venues. Visits are also spatially linked, as consumers frequent nearby locations and demand spills over across adjacent sites. So, visit decisions may depend jointly on (i) social relationships among individuals and (ii) spatial relationships among locations. Modeling and estimating dual-network dependence is challenging because utilities spill over through both networks, inducing high-dimensional dependence across a choice space that grows with the product of the number of individuals and locations. We develop an integrated framework for modeling and estimating individual-location choices under social and spatial dependence and use it for operational decisions. The framework begins with a social-spatial network choice model in which both dependence channels jointly propagate through individual-location utilities. For scalability, we exploit the dual-network structure and construct a copula surrogate that preserves model-implied first-and secondorder information, yielding a pairwise likelihood estimator and closed-form visit probabilities for downstream optimization. We apply the framework to pop-up store operations, where a firm jointly selects a temporary location and seed users for promotion. We develop an exact reformulation and a scalable approximation method for this joint decision problem. Synthetic experiments show our estimator accurately estimates parameters across multiple data generating processes. Using real-world location-based social network data, we document positive, statistically significant social and spatial dependence in users' recorded check-in behavior. In this application, coordinating both decisions substantially improves expected demand over location-only optimization, and the optimal seed set balances broad social reach against promotional effectiveness at the selected site.

title: Early Determination in International Commercial Arbitration: Efficiency, Due Process and the Risk of Premature Disposal of Claims
affiliations: Senior Judicial Magistrate at Bangladesh Judicial Service

detail.title: Early Determination in International Commercial Arbitration: Efficiency, Due Process and the Risk of Premature Disposal of Claims
detail.abstract: Early determination has become an increasingly important case-management device in international commercial arbitration. It enables tribunals to dispose, at an early stage, of claims or defences that are plainly untenable, thereby avoiding the cost and delay of full pleadings, disclosure, witness evidence and hearings on issues that cannot realistically succeed. The 2026 ICC Arbitration Rules mark a significant development by moving early determination from institutional guidance into Article 30 of the Rules themselves. The new provision permits applications where claims or defences are manifestly without merit or manifestly outside the tribunal's jurisdiction. Comparable mechanisms now appear in the SIAC 2025 Rules, the HKIAC 2024 Rules, the LCIA 2020 Rules and the SCC Rules, while the Arbitration Act 1996, as amended by the Arbitration Act 2025, now expressly empowers tribunals seated in England, Wales and Northern Ireland to make awards on a summary basis where a party has no real prospect of success. This convergence strengthens arbitral efficiency but also sharpens an enduring legitimacy concern: summary disposal must not become premature disposal. This article argues that early determination is compatible with due process when treated as a disciplined exception to full merits procedure rather than a substitute for it. The Early Determination in International Commercial Arbitration 2 governing inquiry should combine a demanding merits threshold with procedural proportionality. Tribunals should distinguish issues that fail even on the applicant's opponent's assumed factual case from disputes requiring contested evidence, credibility assessments, expert evaluation or substantial legal development. Drawing on the UNCITRAL Model Law, the New York Convention, institutional rules, recent practice and Singapore appellate jurisprudence on natural justice, the article proposes a seven-safeguard framework for enforceable early determination. The objective is not simply to decide faster, but to identify cases in which less procedure is sufficient to produce a fair, reasoned and internationally enforceable award.

title: The Tribunal's Duty to Apply the Law in International Commercial Arbitration: Party Pleadings, Iura Novit Curia and the Limits of Due Process
affiliations: Senior Judicial Magistrate at Bangladesh Judicial Service

detail.title: The Tribunal's Duty to Apply the Law in International Commercial Arbitration: Party Pleadings, Iura Novit Curia and the Limits of Due Process
detail.abstract: International commercial arbitration places the tribunal in a difficult position between two propositions that are both fundamental to legitimate adjudication. The first is that the tribunal must decide the dispute according to the applicable law rather than merely choose between the parties' legal submissions. The second is that an award may not rest on a dispositive case that the parties had no fair opportunity to address. The tension is commonly expressed through the civillaw maxim iura novit curia-adapted in arbitration as iura novit arbiter-but the real problem is broader: how far may arbitrators research, identify, recharacterise and apply legal rules not pleaded by counsel without exceeding the submission to arbitration or violating due process? This article develops a comparative answer through the UNCITRAL Model Law and New York Convention, the 2026 ICC and 2020 LCIA Rules, English, Swiss, French and Singapore law, and recent judicial authority. It argues that tribunals should enjoy substantial legal autonomy but not procedural surprise. The decisive boundary is whether an unpleaded legal proposition remains within the submitted factual and remedial framework and whether it could materially alter the evidence, advocacy or relief. The article proposes a six-stage Law-Application Integrity Test that distinguishes pure questions of law from mixed questions of law and fact, uses reasonable foreseeability as the central due-process trigger, and requires targeted procedural dialogue before an award rests on a genuinely new dispositive legal basis.

reference: Journal of Applied Accounting Research, volume 27, issue 3, 2026[10.1108/JAAR-02-2025-0093]
title: Do Data Breach Notification Laws Affect Accounting Conservatism?
affiliations: Louisiana State University Shreveport, Kean University - School of Accounting and Finance and Louisiana State University, Shreveport

detail.title: Do Data Breach Notification Laws Affect Accounting Conservatism?

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Applied Accounting Research, volume 27, issue 3, 2026[10.1108/JAAR-02-2025-0093]

detail.abstract: This paper studies the effects of data breach notification law (DBN) on corporate accounting conservatism. Exploiting the staggered adoption of state-level DBN laws, we find that mandatory data breach notification laws lead to an increase in accounting conservatism. The findings remain robust in an entropy-balanced sample and adhere to the parallel trends assumption. We find similar results using alternative accounting conservatism measures. Further analysis shows that the impact is more pronounced in financial constrained firms. Our results suggest that firms reduce their risk preferences by reporting earnings more conservatively when confronted with increased risks and costs related to disclosed breaches.

title: Betting on Bets: Anytime-Valid Tests for Stochastic Dominance
affiliations: Center for Mathematics and Computer Science (CWI), , Luiss University Dipartimento di Economia e Finanza and INSEAD

detail.title: Betting on Bets: Anytime-Valid Tests for Stochastic Dominance
detail.abstract: How can we monitor, in real time, whether one uncertain prospect has any upside over another? To answer this question, we develop a novel family of sequential, anytimevalid tests for stochastic dominance (SD), a classical and popular notion for comparing entire distribution functions. The problem is distinct from that of testing mean dominance, and it is particularly useful when comparing distributions with similar means or with ordinal outcomes. We first derive powerful, nonparametric e-processes that quantify evidence against the null hypothesis that one prospect is stochastically dominated by another. For first-order SD, these e-processes are based on mixtures of growth-rate optimal e-variables, yielding a test of power one that retains validity under continuous monitoring. We then generalize the approach to sequential testing for higher-order SD and other integral stochastic orders. Empirically, we find that the tests are competitive in power with classical, non-anytime-valid SD tests. Our realworld application examines a controversial phenomenon in baseball analytics, known as the "third-time-throughthe-order (3TTO) penalty," viewed as a monitoring problem. We close by sketching the complementary problem of testing whether a prospect has a definite upside, formalizing conditions under which we can derive a powerful anytime-valid test.

title: From Operational Visibility to Tactical Decision-making: Integrating Performance Dashboards across Organizational Levels
affiliations: Swiss Management Centre University (Switzerland)

detail.title: From Operational Visibility to Tactical Decision-making: Integrating Performance Dashboards across Organizational Levels

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Not applicable
declarations.ethicsApproval: My own academic work
declarations.funderStatement: Not applicable

detail.abstract: Operational and tactical dashboards are frequently distinguished by user group, time horizon and level of detail, yet organisations often implement them as disconnected reporting products. This conceptual paper examines their differences, similarities and interdependence. Operational dashboards provide highfrequency visibility of processes, events and exceptions to support immediate control. Tactical dashboards aggregate and analyse performance over short-to medium-term horizons to support resource allocation, project oversight and functional adjustment. Both depend on governed definitions, appropriate visualisation, actionable indicators and explicit ownership. Drawing on performance-measurement and dashboard-design literature, the paper proposes a vertically integrated architecture in which operational signals are aggregated into tactical patterns, tactical decisions modify operational priorities, and both levels remain connected to strategic objectives. The model distinguishes shared data and semantic foundations from role-specific presentation. It also identifies risks including visual clutter, inconsistent definitions, alert fatigue, target gaming and the false assumption that dashboards themselves improve performance. The contribution is an integrated decision-loop framework that shifts attention from dashboard classification to organisational learning and action. Practical recommendations address audience analysis, latency, drill-down, exception design, governance and evaluation.

title: Professionalism as Stewardship
affiliations: Australian Council of Professions

detail.title: Professionalism as Stewardship

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Self-funded and self-published
declarations.funderStatement: Self

detail.abstract:
This paper completes a trilogy on the evolution and future of professionalism. Building on earlier arguments that professionalism remains relevant (Beaton, 2010) and has become more important than ever in conditions of complexity, uncertainty and declining institutional trust (Beaton, 2022), it advances a new and consequential thesis: professionalism will not survive without deliberate stewardship.

The paper argues that experienced professionals have a moral obligation not merely to practise competently and ethically, but to actively transmit the values, judgement, norms and standards of professionalism to the next generation. Professionalism is understood not as a set of rules or competencies, but as a living social compact grounded in expertise, ethics and service. Drawing on the classical sociological tradition of Parsons, Freidson and Larson, the paper contends that professional authority depends upon communities capable of reproducing their cultures of judgement and responsibility across generations.

A central claim is that professionalism is learned primarily through socialisation rather than formal instruction. Much of what distinguishes professional practice, including ethical judgement, discretion, reflection, restraint, empathy and the ability to navigate ambiguity, constitutes tacit knowledge that is acquired through observation, mentoring and guided experience. When stewardship weakens, professionalism risks being reduced to technical competence, compliance and commercial performance, undermining the social legitimacy on which professional autonomy rests.

The paper identifies five stewardship obligations for experienced professionals: making implicit judgement visible; modelling professional conduct; explaining ethical reasoning; creating psychologically safe learning environments; and fostering reflective practice. These obligations are examined through two contrasting professional contexts, legal practice and nursing, demonstrating that while the mechanisms of transmission differ, the underlying stewardship responsibility is universal across professions.

The argument acquires particular urgency in light of contemporary structural pressures. Artificial intelligence is compressing or eliminating many traditional apprenticeship pathways through which professional identity has historically been formed. Remote and hybrid work arrangements reduce opportunities for observational learning and informal mentoring. At the same time, declining trust in institutions and the earlier assumption of responsibility by younger professionals heighten the need for sound professional judgement. These developments threaten not simply the practice of professionalism but the mechanisms through which it is reproduced.

The paper concludes that stewardship must be recognised as both an individual and institutional responsibility. Professional services firms, hospitals, universities, professional associations and regulators must create conditions that deliberately cultivate professional formation. Professionalism is ultimately an inheritance rather than a credential. Its survival depends upon whether each generation of experienced professionals consciously accepts responsibility for passing it on. In an era of technological disruption and social change, stewardship is not an optional dimension of professionalism; it is essential to its continuity and legitimacy.

title: Impacts of Artificial Intelligence Integration in Corporate Environments: A Comparative Analysis of Efficacy and Overuse

detail.title: Impacts of Artificial Intelligence Integration in Corporate Environments: A Comparative Analysis of Efficacy and Overuse

declarations.declarationOfInterest: AI and Business, Education
declarations.ethicsApproval: na
declarations.funderStatement: The writer

detail.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into organizational decision-making has intensified debate regarding the balance between technological efficiency and human judgment. While prior research often portrays AI adoption as either beneficial or detrimental, less attention has been given to the conditions under which AI creates sustainable organizational value. This study addresses that gap through a systematic review of literature on human-AI collaboration, algorithmic management, governance, and AI-enabled decision-making. Building on these findings, the study proposes AI Reliance Equilibrium Theory (AIRET), which suggests that the relationship between AI reliance and organizational performance is nonlinear. Specifically, moderate levels of AI reliance enhance performance by augmenting human capabilities, whereas excessive reliance contributes to cognitive surrender, automation bias, professional deskilling, and reduced organizational resilience. The review further identifies governance quality and AI literacy as critical factors that influence whether AI adoption leads to sustainable augmentation or harmful overreliance. Findings suggest that organizations achieve the greatest benefits when AI complements rather than replaces human judgment and when governance mechanisms preserve oversight, accountability, and transparency. The study contributes a framework for balancing AI-driven innovation with human agency and long-term organizational performance.

title: A plant-wide mechanistic model quantifies EGSB and A/O treatment performance, operational costs, and carbon emissions for methomyl pesticide wastewater
affiliations: Dalian Minzu University, Dalian Minzu University, Dalian Minzu University, Dalian Minzu University, Dalian Minzu University, Dalian Minzu University, Dalian Minzu University, Dalian Minzu University and Dalian Minzu University

detail.title: A plant-wide mechanistic model quantifies EGSB and A/O treatment performance, operational costs, and carbon emissions for methomyl pesticide wastewater
detail.abstract: A full-scale mechanistic model was configured for a methomyl pesticide wastewater plant to simulate and predict treatment performance, operational cost, and carbon emissions of two configurations, with and without an expanded granular sludge bed (EGSB), under five influent chemical oxygen demand (COD) scenarios (2000-10000 mg/L). Unlike conventional recalibration, this study transfers the model by redefining influent components rather than kinetic constants, based on the premise that wastewater specificity lies in organic component distribution. This directly applies the original biopharmaceutical model to pesticide wastewater. The model was validated using independent plant data.Over one-year simulations, EGSB integration delivered 95-97% COD removal, 93-97% total nitrogen removal, and ~98% ammonia removal, improving performance by 0.66-3.19%, 1.20-44.41%, and 2.48-6.18% versus the control. At 4000 mg/L COD, EGSB reduced daily net operating cost by 22.33% and carbon emission intensity from 0.65 to 0.61 kg CO2-eq/m3. When influent COD doubled, its cost increased by only 2.58% and remained 21.60% lower than the non-EGSB system. The framework supports robust, low-carbon, and cost-effective retrofitting decisions.

title: Social Responsibility Community-Centered Governance Model for Enhancing Citizen Participation and Social Innovation in Local Government: An Integrative Research Framework for Sustainable Local Governance
affiliations: , , University of Caloocan City, , University of Caloocan City, Graduate School and University of Caloocan City

detail.title: Social Responsibility Community-Centered Governance Model for Enhancing Citizen Participation and Social Innovation in Local Government: An Integrative Research Framework for Sustainable Local Governance
detail.abstract: Local governments worldwide are increasingly confronted with multidimensional governance challenges, including declining public trust, weak citizen engagement, social inequalities, policy fragmentation, and limited innovation capacity. Contemporary governance scholarship suggests that these challenges cannot be effectively addressed through traditional bureaucratic approaches alone. Instead, social responsibility, community-centered governance, citizen participation, and social innovation have emerged as interconnected governance mechanisms capable of fostering more inclusive, democratic, and sustainable local development. The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) emphasizes that participatory and deliberative governance improves policy legitimacy, strengthens trust in public institutions, and enhances policy effectiveness. Likewise, recent studies demonstrate that social innovation ecosystems flourish when citizens actively participate in local decision-making processes. This study develops a Social Responsibility Community-Centered Governance Model (SRCCGM) through an integrative review and meta-synthesis of contemporary governance literature published between 2015 and 2025. Findings reveal that community-centered governance serves as a strategic mediator between social responsibility and social innovation by strengthening participatory governance, civic empowerment, public trust, and collaborative policy-making. The study proposes a comprehensive theoretical model for local governments seeking to institutionalize citizen participation and promote sustainable innovation-driven development.

title: From Footprint to Motive
affiliations: and Chiang Mai University

detail.title: From Footprint to Motive

declarations.declarationOfInterest: no
declarations.ethicsApproval: na
declarations.funderStatement: self

detail.abstract: Strategic actions underdetermine the intentions that produced them, and large language models now sit inside the gap. Strategic actions often underdetermine the intentions that produced them. A state restricting a technology may be reducing a genuine security vulnerability, preserving an economic advantage, building bargaining leverage, responding to a rival's prior restriction, or pursuing several of these objectives at once. International-relations theory has long treated the resulting uncertainty as a central feature of the security dilemma, and social psychology has documented the human tendency to infer dispositions and motives from observable conduct. A new actor now enters this old problem. Large language models are increasingly used to retrieve evidence, summarize contested events, compare explanations and infer why states or institutions acted as they did. This paper develops a conceptual framework for that role and applies it interpretively to three documented episodes from the period between April 2025 and August 2026: China's rare-earth export controls and their subsequent expansion and suspension, the pairing of a United States export-licensing relaxation with a Section 232 tariff on the following day, and the August 2026 drone tariff proclamation. It defines machinemediated intent attribution as the use of a large language model to infer latent motives from observed strategic conduct, and introduces an Intent Attribution Chain that separates action, stated justification, consequence, beneficiary, access or proximity, influence and intent. The chain functions as a discipline for reading rather than as a measurement instrument. Two recurring interpretive failures are described: the attribution leap, in which a motive claim travels beyond the strongest available evidence, and the caveat-conclusion gap, in which an appropriate qualification is stated and then narrated past. The paper further argues that reliance on external models for strategic interpretation constitutes a form of interpretive dependency distinct from dependencies on resources, compute infrastructure and model access, and that verification capacity rather than ownership is the governing variable. The aim is not to establish that large language models are politically biased, nor that strategic motives are unknowable, but to specify what disciplined interpretation requires and to show, on the public record, where the record actually stops.

title: The World and Freedom
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The World and Freedom
detail.abstract: “The World and Freedom” seeks to address the dire crisis in which we are all ensnared by giving freedom back its original meaning and restoring the incalculable value of philosophy and ethics. Both sciences would enable us to recognise the paradigms which constrain our vision of the world like an invisible cage. In the second part, this essay suggests a new ethics, based on a transindividual “worthiness of interest”, which can encompass new subjects: the planet and humanity. Including them would lead to significant changes in politics and law of the world. The last part discusses another facet of ethics, called the “ethics of free destiny” (“ethics of the good”), which, it is suggested, could be situated in a middle ground between the individual and society: our shared heritage.

title: Non-Participation and Default in International Commercial Arbitration: Procedural Fairness, Evidentiary Consequences and the Enforceability of Default Awards
affiliations: Senior Judicial Magistrate at Bangladesh Judicial Service

detail.title: Non-Participation and Default in International Commercial Arbitration: Procedural Fairness, Evidentiary Consequences and the Enforceability of Default Awards
detail.abstract: Non-participation is a recurring but conceptually misunderstood feature of international commercial arbitration. A respondent may ignore the notice of arbitration, decline to file a defence, refuse to attend a hearing, withdraw after an adverse procedural ruling or participate selectively while withholding evidence. These situations create an obvious practical need to permit the arbitration to continue, but they do not convert arbitral procedure into a private form of default judgment. This article argues that default changes the procedural conditions of adjudication, not the tribunal's obligation to establish jurisdiction, test the claimant's case and respect the non-participating party's continuing entitlement to proper notice and a reasonable opportunity to be heard. Drawing on the UNCITRAL Model Law and Arbitration Rules, the New York Convention, the 2026 ICC Rules, current LCIA, SIAC, HKIAC and SCC rules, the English Arbitration Act 1996 as amended in 2025, and recent Singapore jurisprudence including Sai Wan Shipping, Rakna Arakshaka Lanka, STS Seatoshore and Pacmar Shipping, the article distinguishes procedural continuation from evidentiary sanction. It proposes a seven-stage Default Award Integrity Protocol: verify jurisdiction, create a reliable notice record, classify the default, assess sufficient cause, require affirmative proof, use proportionate inferences only where justified, and reason the award for enforcement. The central claim is that enforceability depends not on whether an award was rendered in a party's absence, but on whether the record demonstrates a fair opportunity, disciplined proof and an adjudicative decision rather than victory by forfeiture.

title: Red Teams and Revealing Defences
affiliations: University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management

detail.title: Red Teams and Revealing Defences
detail.abstract: A software firm that red-teams a product chooses how a confidential finding will guide remediation, post-release defence and defence placement. Following the report seems natural, but it can be wrong. Remediation changes the composition of residual risk: a missed attack class may become more dangerous than the class that was reported and repaired. Testing, therefore, affects defence through both risk removal and risk allocation. Holding remediation fixed, greater test precision raises optimal coverage only when precision is sufficiently high and attacker reconnaissance sufficiently weak; otherwise it weakly lowers coverage. Holding precision fixed, greater remediation weakly lowers coverage. A report-contingent defence can also reveal the report to an attacker that fingerprints its location. When recognition neutralises the defence and reconnaissance is fixed, the firm either adapts placement fully or pools across reports. When the attacker chooses reconnaissance effort, partial adaptation emerges. The analysis distinguishes requirements to test, remediate, deploy, condition placement on a finding and disclose technical detail. Conditional on the other portfolio choices, requiring defence to follow the finding can protect the wrong attack surface or induce additional reconnaissance.

title: Feeding the Machine: The Security Risks of Generative AI Use by Public Sector Employees in Southeast Asia
affiliations: Saki Partners and Southern Cross University

detail.title: Feeding the Machine: The Security Risks of Generative AI Use by Public Sector Employees in Southeast Asia
detail.abstract: As public sector employees across Southeast Asia adopt generative artificial intelligence to draft correspondence, summarise reports and support policy analysis, they routinely transmit text, documents and data to servers owned by private firms headquartered outside the jurisdiction whose information is being processed. This paper examines the security risks this creates for governments, applying securitization theory and the human-factor literature on insider threat to four documented incidents: the leakage of proprietary Samsung data through ChatGPT in 2023; a platform-side vulnerability that exposed users' conversation histories and billing data; the 2025 upload of restricted government contracting documents by the acting head of the United States' national cybersecurity agency to a public chatbot; and the 2025 bans on the Chinese model DeepSeek across government networks in Australia, South Korea and Taiwan. Read together, these cases show that the risk is not confined to deliberate espionage but arises structurally from where AI infrastructure is hosted, how vendors handle retained data, and how easily an official under time pressure treats a chat window as a private notebook. The paper concludes with recommendations for sovereign hosting, tiered data-classification rules, and the explicit governance of senior-level exception pathways.

title: AI-Driven Autonomous Enterprise Architecture for SAP S/4HANA Cloud: A Next-Generation Framework for Intelligent Business Operations

detail.title: AI-Driven Autonomous Enterprise Architecture for SAP S/4HANA Cloud: A Next-Generation Framework for Intelligent Business Operations
detail.abstract: The intelligent enterprise is still changing at a breakneck speed, further driving the digitization of the business world to become more efficient, agile, and data-informed. Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) platforms have thus evolved from business transaction systems into intelligent, digital platforms that enable predictive analytics, automation, and real-time orchestration across the enterprise. Of these, SAP S/4HANA Cloud is a top-tier next-generation ERP system that enables companies to future-proof their business processes with cloud-native features and capabilities and with built-in analytics. At the same time, the era of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping ERP ecosystems into independent business environments that can adaptively make decisions and optimize continuously, such as machine learning, generative AI, intelligent process automation, and predictive analytics (Dwivedi et al., 2021; Pokala, 2024). However, despite all these technological developments, enterprise architectures are still not very well integrated within many organizations; there is not much interoperability, the governance process is not very streamlined, and operational frameworks are missing in many organizations that are based on AI (Dziembek & Turek, 2025; Devireddy, 2025). The purpose of this study is to create an autonomous enterprise architecture for SAP S/4HANA Cloud using the concepts of AI. This study aims to synthesize existing academic research and industrial knowledge to build a conceptual autonomous enterprise architecture for SAP S/4HANA Cloud using the concepts of AI. The research follows a systematic literature review, conceptual framework development, and comparative analysis of the latest studies on intelligent ERP transformation. The results show the transformative power of embedding AI services, business process automation, digital assistants, predictive intelligence, and autonomous decision engines in SAP S/4HANA Cloud to increase operational efficiency, enhance organizational resilience, and deliver enterprise intelligence. From the above results, a wide-ranging AI-based autonomous enterprise architecture is proposed to enable intelligent business operation, better decision-making, and continuous business innovation. Future studies should focus on empirical validation, approaches for implementing AI in specific industries, governance mechanisms for responsible AI, and the incorporation of new technologies like multi-agent AI systems, digital twins, and autonomous enterprise ecosystems (Pulluru, 2025).
