title: Governing Delegated Authority in Autonomous Finance: The MARQUE Framework for Institutional Accountability beyond Model Risk

detail.title: Governing Delegated Authority in Autonomous Finance: The MARQUE Framework for Institutional Accountability beyond Model Risk
detail.abstract:
Autonomous financial systems increasingly research, construct, and execute live market strategies. While the governance literature focuses heavily on system-level control and model risk validation, this paper identifies a critical antecedent gap: the formal governance of the delegation boundary itself. Because AI agents lack legal personality, an authority instrument operates not as a power of attorney to software, but as an evidentiary record of an institution's self-imposed limitations.

This paper introduces MARQUE, an eight-question reference architecture designed to govern operational capacity and close the "policy–evidence gap" in autonomous deployments. To establish this gap empirically, the author maps MARQUE against the 230 control objectives of the February 2026 Financial Services AI Risk Management Framework (FS AI RMF), revealing that while 39 objectives touch authority workflows, none requires the production of a versioned, attributable delegation grant. This structural blind spot is compounded by the April 2026 joint regulatory guidance (SR 26-2), which explicitly carved out agentic AI from standard model risk oversight.

This paper establishes MARQUE as a foundational theoretical architecture, providing a fully operationalized, machine-readable JSON schema, a twelve-dimension assessment instrument scored on evidence rather than intention, a worked execution-desk record, and five standard legal instruments to serve as a transactional diligence baseline for the next phase of autonomous financial regulation.

title: IoT-Based Predictive Maintenance in UK Hotels -Barriers and Enablers
affiliations: and

detail.title: IoT-Based Predictive Maintenance in UK Hotels -Barriers and Enablers
detail.abstract: The UK hospitality sector faces escala4ng opera4onal pressures, making facili4es and maintenance management a strategic concern. Within this context, facili4es and maintenance management has become a strategic concern, yet most UK hotels con4nue to rely on reac4ve or 4me-based maintenance approaches that generate avoidable costs, energy inefficiency, and service disrup4on. Internet of Things-enabled predic4ve maintenance (IoT-PdM) offers a data-driven alterna4ve capable of reducing unplanned down4me, improving asset performance, and suppor4ng Net Zero objec4ves. Despite its demonstrated benefits, adop4on within UK hotels remains limited. This study examines the technological, organisa4onal, and environmental factors shaping IoT-PdM adop4on in UK hotels using an integrated Technology-Organisa4on-Environment (TOE) and Diffusion of Innova4on (DoI) framework. Adop4ng a cri4cal realist stance, the research employs a cross-sec4onal quan4ta4ve survey of UK hotels with 50 or more rooms. Descrip4ve analysis benchmarks awareness and adop4on maturity, while mul4ple regression and structural equa4on modelling test hypotheses concerning adop4on inten4on and implementa4on level. By empirically ranking the rela4ve influence of key barriers and enablers, the study provides evidence-based priori4sa4on for hotel decision-makers opera4ng under resource constraints. The research contributes theore4cally by extending TOE-DoI integra4on into a UK hospitality IoT-PdM context, methodologically through hypothesis-driven quan4ta4ve tes4ng, and prac4cally by offering ac4onable guidance for hotel operators, industry bodies, and policymakers seeking to enhance opera4onal resilience and sustainability performance.

title: The Observability Shadow: Endogenous Observability and Competing Effects of Higher Exposure in Repeated Institutional Systems

detail.title: The Observability Shadow: Endogenous Observability and Competing Effects of Higher Exposure in Repeated Institutional Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human subjects, identifiable personal data, or clinical intervention. The analysis is based on conceptual and methodological development and simulation experiments; therefore, institutional review board approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract:
Public benefit systems repeatedly require individuals to complete renewals, submit documentation, respond to notices, and navigate verification procedures. These interactions can generate administrative exposure over time, but they also generate the records, responses, calls, and other traces through which institutions observe participants and determine when intervention may be warranted. This raises a distinct question: can administrative exposure remain dynamically manageable while the institution loses visibility into the states in which intervention is warranted?

We formalize this problem through endogenous observability: the informational environment through which an institution observes a governed state can itself be endogenous to that state. In the model, observation probability declines with contemporaneous latent administrative exposure, p(E) = exp(-αE), so the institution receives progressively less telemetry as exposure increases. Because governance acts on an institutional belief rather than directly on the latent state, an observability shadow occurs when pre-intervention exposure exceeds the intervention threshold while pre-intervention belief remains below it. We derive an exact one-period conditional decomposition of shadow probability and show that higher exposure creates two competing effects: it reduces observation probability while, conditional on observation, raising the signal level that can trigger intervention.

Simulation experiments evaluate shadow-event prevalence and conditional missed-intervention probability in a repeated intervention-coupled system. At baseline, endogenous observability raises shadow-event prevalence from 5.63% to 6.68% and the conditional missed-intervention rate from 45.93% to 50.17% relative to a calibrated fixed-observability comparator. Both contrasts remain positive across all 30 prospectively specified replication seeds. Grid-resolved sensitivity further identifies tested configurations that satisfy the inherited exposure-stability diagnostic while continuing to exhibit observability-shadow effects.

The results establish that state dynamics and state observability are distinct properties of repeated institutional systems. A system can maintain dynamically manageable administrative exposure while remaining unable to observe actionable states reliably enough to intervene. Exposure stability therefore does not imply governance observability. More broadly, when the information environment is endogenous to the state being governed, the capacity of an institution to know when action is warranted becomes a dynamic property of the governance system itself.

title: FLAP-X: A Dual-Leaf Attestation Protocol for Cross-Agent Regulatory Governance with Retrospective Cryptographic Verification

detail.title: FLAP-X: A Dual-Leaf Attestation Protocol for Cross-Agent Regulatory Governance with Retrospective Cryptographic Verification

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No.
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: Self-funded. No funding received.

detail.abstract: Cryptographic verification presupposes determinism: a hash either matches or it does not, and a signature either holds or it fails. Agentic AI systems violate this precondition-identical inputs may produce different outputs, so there is no fixed expected value against which behaviour can be verified, and the naive application of cryptographic audit to AI fails at the first step. This paper takes a different route: separate what can be held invariant from what cannot. Credentials, delegation chains, prompt-template versions, access profiles, and controlexecution records are invariant by construction; model output is not. FLAP-X anchors the invariant set cryptographically and governs the variable residual with a calibrated tolerance, making non-deterministic multiagent systems retrospectively auditable. The dual-leaf attestation structure follows from this separation: Leaf 1 at the decision layer captures clause discharge, controls fired, and output hash; Leaf 2 at the workflow layer captures orchestration, delegation, and template version; the leaves are cross-linked and hash-bound to a principal chain rooted in a human agent owner. A four-check verification protocol operates across both surfaces. We parameterise a 15-condition test protocol in four parts-core verification (8), adversarial (3), governance lifecycle (3), and a comparative experiment (1) demonstrating two fault classes a single-surface record cannot handle: output substitution, which the single-surface record passes as a false negative, and surface attribution, which it cannot distinguish. We report honest negatives: adjacent-agent collusion producing mutually consistent false attestations passes verification, and a stolen signing key defeats signature checks; both are stated trust-boundary limitations addressed by the lifecycle layer, not the attestation layer. Effectiveness of the lifecycle controls at production scale remains future work; the author is actively seeking an empirical validation partnership.

title: LLMs Make Robust Stochastic Optimization Easier: An Agentic Workflow
affiliations: , , Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Department of Decisions, Operations and Technology, CUHK Business School, The Chinese University of Hong Kong and School of Business and Management, The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

detail.title: LLMs Make Robust Stochastic Optimization Easier: An Agentic Workflow
detail.abstract: Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) provides a principled framework for decision-making under uncertainty, but its practical use remains challenging. Users must identify uncertain quantities, specify ambiguity sets, formulate worst-case objectives or constraints, and implement the resulting model in solver-compatible code. These barriers limit adoption by practitioners and make DRO difficult to teach and learn. Although large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities for automated optimization modeling from natural-language (NL) descriptions, existing approaches largely focus on deterministic optimization and often fail to produce reliable DRO formulations and implementations. This paper studies the automatic translation of NL descriptions of problems into mathematical formulations and executable code. We construct an NL-to-DRO dataset through a human-guided reverse-engineering pipeline. Each instance contains three components: an NL description of the DRO problem, an intermediate representation (IR) of the mathematical formulation, and executable code in Robust Stochastic Optimization Made Easy. The dataset covers diverse DRO structures and supports systematic evaluation of automated DRO modeling. We further develop an LLM-based workflow centered on the IR for formulation construction, validation, and implementation generation, supported by a knowledge library built from the dataset.  Computational experiments with both closed-source and open-source LLMs show that the proposed workflow substantially improves modeling reliability over direct code generation, achieving success rates of up to 91.1% for closed-source models and approximately 60% for fine-tuned open-source models. These results demonstrate that our IR-centered agentic workflow can lower implementation barriers for practitioners, provide reusable instructional resources for educators, and help students connect NL problem statements with rigorous DRO formulations and executable code. To facilitate access and reuse, we provide a companion website, https://zoe-wan.github.io/LLM4DRO/, where users can connect their own LLM API accounts and use the agent to formulate, validate, and implement DRO models for practical applications.

title: Interpretive Entropy: The Degradation of Reasoning Coherence in Fragmented Systems

detail.title: Interpretive Entropy: The Degradation of Reasoning Coherence in Fragmented Systems
detail.abstract: This paper introduces the concept of Interpretive Entropy: the tendency of reasoning coherence to degrade in fragmented systems over time. Interpretive Entropy is distinct from Shannon's information entropy, which measures the quantity of symbols transmitted through a channel. Shannon explicitly abstracted away from meaning to solve an engineering problem. Interpretive Entropy operates in the domain Shannon deliberately excluded-the domain of meaning, context, and the coherent relationship between information and the reasoning that generated it. The paper argues that fragmented systems do not primarily lose information. They lose the interpretive scaffolding that made information meaningful-and that this loss is structurally invisible to conventional measurement, cumulative over time, and significantly more costly than the information loss it accompanies.

title: P vs. NP: A Loop-Theoretic Approach

detail.title: P vs. NP: A Loop-Theoretic Approach
detail.abstract:
This paper develops a formalization of the versus problem inside the operator-theoretic framework of Loop Theory. Rather than importing Turing-machine intuitions into the proof, we define internal Loop-theoretic complexity classes and directly in terms of the Whole-space , the step-indexed Archive , the compression operator , the decompression operator , and the archival transition operator .

Within this framework: ● corresponds to the existence of polynomially verifiable presented archival codes. ● corresponds to the polynomial-step construction of those codes by archival transitions. ● Verification is the local action of on an already-presented code. ● Discovery is the nonlocal action of across an open archival gap . We prove that, under the internal Loop-theoretic finite-transition capacity principle, an exponentially dimensional yes-witness subspace cannot be decoded by a polynomially bounded archive. Consequently, for witness-saturated NP-complete problem families. Interpreted through explicit Loop-to-complexity bridge axioms, this yields the classical separation archival spaces: as a conservation law of step-indexed An incomplete archive cannot compress an unarchived Whole-space element into a valid code without paying the required step-count price.

title: Competition and Cooperation in Service Systems
affiliations: , City University of Hong Kong, Lingnan University and University of Science and Technology of China

detail.title: Competition and Cooperation in Service Systems
detail.abstract: This paper studies cooperation among service providers when customers choose servers strategically. Traditional models assume exogenous customer arrivals, which fails to capture the interdependence between different firms. We incorporate equilibrium customer behavior into a cooperative game framework, where the resulting game exhibits inter-coalition externalities. To address this, we formulate the problem as a partition function game and identify the rational coalition structures that emerge following deviations. This allows the game to be equivalently represented as a characteristic function game, enabling tractable analysis. Interestingly, the core may be empty even though full pooling dominates partial pooling. We further characterize conditions for the existence of the core, and provide closed-form expressions for its extreme points. When the core is empty, we derive the minimum subsidy required to sustain the grand coalition and introduce a Benefit-to-Subsidy Ratio to assess the efficiency of intervention. Moreover, we characterize the minimum penalization for stabilizing the grand coalition, and show that reducing subsidies by one unit can be equivalently achieved by increasing penalties by (n-1)/n units. We also derive an explicit expression for the Shapley value and show that it always lies within the core when the core is non-empty. Our results highlight how strategic customer behavior fundamentally affects coalition stability and payoff allocation, offering insights for the design of cooperative arrangements in service systems.

title: When Capability Becomes a Liability: Business Model Transitions, Core Rigidity, and the Structural Sustainability Gap in Investment Banking

detail.title: When Capability Becomes a Liability: Business Model Transitions, Core Rigidity, and the Structural Sustainability Gap in Investment Banking
detail.abstract: Why do firms that successfully pioneer new business models ultimately disappear as independent entities? Resource-based view predicts that superior capabilities generate sustained competitive advantage, yet the history of investment banking reveals a three-phase pattern that existing theory cannot explain: incumbent rigidity enabling new entrant dominance, followed by new entrant disappearance through acquisition or failure. Drawing on Leonard-Barton's (1992) core capability/core rigidity framework, Christensen's (1997) disruptive innovation theory, and historical case analysis of US, European, and Japanese investment banks supported by primary interview data from Goldman Sachs' New York headquarters in the 2000s, we develop a theory of Strategic Window Advantage and Structural Sustainability Gap. We argue that new entrants exploit Strategic Windows created by business model transitions, but face a Structural Sustainability Gap when windows close and competition shifts to capital depth, regulatory capacity, and global network scale. Goldman Sachs represents the singular exception—a firm that converted window advantage into structural sustainability through partnership capital accumulation, preemptive diversification, and strategically timed public offering. Three propositions specify the conditions under which new entrants survive versus are absorbed in post-transition competitive environments, with implications for incumbent response strategy, new entrant survival, and the theory of competitive dynamics under business model change.

title: The Effect of Organizational Justice on Ethical Behavior of Employees: Insights from the RMG Sector in Bangladesh
affiliations: Jahangirnagar University and Jahangirnagar University

detail.title: The Effect of Organizational Justice on Ethical Behavior of Employees: Insights from the RMG Sector in Bangladesh

declarations.funderStatement: No funding

detail.abstract: Although the relationship between organizational justice and employees' ethical behavior has been investigated in various sectors and countries, this association remains largely unexplored in the context of Bangladesh's labor-intensive ready-made garment (RMG) industry. To address this gap, this study finds out how distributive, procedural, interactional, and informational dimensions of organizational justice affect workers' moral conduct in Bangladesh's RMG sector. This study collects data from 134 RMG machine operator employees through a survey method. This research paper employed regression analysis to examine the relationships. The results show that employees' ethical behavior in Bangladesh's RMG sector is significantly improved by all four organizational justice categories (R² = .807), with distributive justice having the most influence (β = .577, p < .001). These findings show how important fairness beliefs are in shaping workers' moral conduct. The study contributes by investigating the ways in which different aspects of organizational justice impact the moral conduct of employees in Bangladesh's RMG sector.

title: The Philosophical Back-Turn: How Leadership Studies Kept Philosophy's Words and Reversed its Demands

detail.title: The Philosophical Back-Turn: How Leadership Studies Kept Philosophy's Words and Reversed its Demands

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declared no potential conflicts of interest with respect to the research, authorship, and/or publication of this article.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this article. It presents a conceptual and historical analysis and involves no human participants, human data, or human tissue. The hospital described in the opening section is an illustrative composite constructed to exhibit a type of situation; it does not report a particular organisation, individual, or set of events.
declarations.funderStatement: The author received no financial support for the research, authorship, and/or publication of this article.

detail.abstract: Leadership studies did not merely translate philosophically demanding ideas into measurable constructs. It reversed their intellectual direction. The field retained terms such as transformation, authenticity, ethics, service, responsibility, and political skill while reconstructing the phenomena those terms named around the requirements of portable form. This article names that recurrent operation the Philosophical Back-Turn and specifies its two forms. Managerial codification reorganises a demanding phenomenon as a sequenced programme of executive action. Operational admissibility reorganises it as an empirical construct. An intellectual history of transforming leadership establishes the decisive historical case: Burns's moral and political account was carried into corporate management by Tichy and Ulrich, reconstructed by Bass as measurable leader effects, and completed as a staged executive architecture by Tichy and Devanna. Five comparative stress tests then establish the wider signature of the operation, placing Aristotle, Kierkegaard, Nietzsche, Weber, and Machiavelli beside modern leadership constructs addressing related problems. In each, a constitutive difficulty that limits mastery is displaced by an observable proxy that leaders can display, develop, and be rated upon. The vocabulary survives while its philosophical demand is reversed. The result is not false knowledge. It is bounded knowledge whose boundary disappears from view, and it disappears most completely in the conditions where leading is hardest.

title: The Cost of Convenience: Dignity Debt and the Future of Human-Centered Software
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Cost of Convenience: Dignity Debt and the Future of Human-Centered Software
detail.abstract:
Modern enterprise and wellness software frequently operates on a structural flaw: it optimizes for frictionless engagement, continuous data extraction, and algorithmic prediction while largely ignoring the biological and cognitive constraints of the humans using those Apps. This creates Dignity Debt: a compounding experiential liability that users pay through eroded privacy, fractured attention, and diminished human agency.

Framed as a design manifesto, this paper introduces Experiential Software Architecture, a technical framework built to structurally discharge Dignity Debt. By synthesizing systems theory from cybernetics, occupational psychology, and the non-dualistic epistemology of Advaita Vedanta, the framework establishes six enforceable design principles. 

Central to this architecture is the shift from reliance on policy assurances to mechanical, structural guarantees. Key mechanisms include local-first AI inference, missing-data penalization to counter the false calm of statistical averaging, and a Semantic Firewall that operationally prevents AI from issuing psychometric diagnoses it lacks the standing to make.

Methodologically, this paper is not an empirical study. It offers a live, public reference implementation, Entropy of Us, a shipped iOS application designed by a single practitioner-researcher to subject the architecture to real-world friction rather than theoretical simulation. The claims here are falsifiable by anyone who downloads the app and checks, that is the evidentiary standard this paper is actually offering.

Written for CXOs, systems architects, and technology leaders who dictate the parameters of next-generation, human-centered software, this paper argues that privacy, dignity, and human observability do not have to be merely promised, they can be mechanically guaranteed.

title: Information Literacy and the Shaping of Reality
affiliations: and

detail.title: Information Literacy and the Shaping of Reality
detail.abstract: Is information literacy (IL) capable of enabling people to effectively use information in the age of AI? The advent of artificial intelligence (AI) into the mainstream has been even more disruptive than previous technological advancements, such as the World Wide Web or social media, and in some ways has fostered much disorder and uncertainty within the world of information. While new IL models and tools are being developed to address AI, they have tended to treat AI-generated information similarly to how earlier IL models provided checks and balances for considering human-created information sources and tools. Continuing to enable effective use of information, IL needs to keep pace with evolving ideas of AI-generated information and its effects on the human beings that interact with it.

reference: Research in the Sociology of Organizations, 89: 115-127
title: Web3 As Decentralization Theater? A Framework for Envisioning Decentralization Strategically

detail.title: Web3 As Decentralization Theater? A Framework for Envisioning Decentralization Strategically

publicationDetails.detailsText: Research in the Sociology of Organizations, 89: 115-127

detail.abstract: Web3's raison d'être is decentralization. Quite problematically, however, few industry analysts can articulate what "decentralization" really entails; whether it differs at all from the notion of "distribution," and how either construct can be measured with observable data to enable a meaningful analysis of the industry's core promise. Instead, Web3 is akin to a decentralization theater in which archetypical characters, who resonate with the likes of Hamlet and Godot, enact decentralization based on fictitious narratives. After critically reassessing these narratives about decentralization, this paper offers a fresh perspective to evaluate, less theatrically and hopefully more rigorously, future claims about "being decentralized." I argue that the crucial issue lurking behind the decentralization narrative is the dispersion of authority within blockchain platforms, which consists of two fundamental dimensions, namely the dispersion of information and of decision-making. The value proposition of Web3 will not be taken seriously until the industry can provide reliable indicators of authority dispersion and demonstrate that the latter affects strategic outcomes for blockchain platforms, including innovation, growth, and value creation.

title: The Asymmetric Model of Organizational Productivity A Qualitative and Functional Analysis of Human Capital Impact under Ceteris Paribus Conditions
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Asymmetric Model of Organizational Productivity A Qualitative and Functional Analysis of Human Capital Impact under Ceteris Paribus Conditions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study is a theoretical and conceptual research paper and did not involve human participants, clinical trials, or patient data requiring ethical approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
Estimating the impact of individual employee behavior on an organization's overall productivity requires isolating Human Capital variables from environmental, technological, or market dynamics. This paper presents the Asymmetric Model of Organizational Productivity, an illustrative theoretical framework under ceteris paribus conditions that maps 5 behavioral archetypes (Proactive X=0, Reactive X=25, Passive / Wait-and-See X=50, Lazy / Disengaged X=75, Unproductive Negative / Toxic X=100) divided into 4 equal 25-point intervals across a 0-100 scale. 

We conceptually position the economic-functional break-even point (Break-Even Line, Y=0) at the Passive / Wait-and-See profile (X=50), placing laziness and toxicity strictly within net negative territory (Y < 0). Integrating principles of Organizational Citizenship Behavior (OCB) and empirical findings on the Toxic Worker Effect (Housman & Minor, 2015), the curve models 4 distinct stages of systemic impact and provides a transparent scoring mechanism for HR managers. 

The model exhibits maximum reliability in organizations characterized by high task interdependence (project teams, IT services, consulting, R&D). It is equally robust in agile and creative environments where proactivity generates exponential value and hostility halts workflow. Conversely, its observational clarity is reduced in isolated, mechanical roles where individual output is constrained by machine speeds rather than interpersonal dynamics. 

Finally, to maintain operational validity, three core baseline assumptions are specified: 1) Standard leadership quality; 2) Normal team population distribution; 3) Temporal dynamics and contagion amplification.

title: Parents Want Help with Clearing Information Landmines: Information Literacy Programs for Parents of Children under Twelve
affiliations: George Washington University

detail.title: Parents Want Help with Clearing Information Landmines: Information Literacy Programs for Parents of Children under Twelve
detail.abstract: Considering the ubiquity of devices available to children and content created for them, parents of children 12 and younger should be targeted as a specific group for new information literacy programs.  A May 2025 Pew Research Center survey reported that parents of children 12 and younger allow their children to use various devices (TVs, tablets, smart phones) to access platforms (YouTube and social media), for reasons such as entertainment, learning, staying connected, and calming down. Parents of the same survey also reported that smartphones and content created for social media is more harmful that beneficial and that tech companies and law makers should do more to prevent harms. They also reported challenges about deciding what to allow and how to manage screentime for their children. Many reported they felt a need to improve their decision making related to screentime and content. Today, families are less likely to receive instruction and support from libraries to evaluate technology and content for children than in the past due to more option to access devices and information.

title: Rural Women Hold Some of Iran's Most Valuable Knowledge. Can Information Literacy Help Them Keep It?
affiliations: University of Birjand

detail.title: Rural Women Hold Some of Iran's Most Valuable Knowledge. Can Information Literacy Help Them Keep It?
detail.abstract: When people hear the term information literacy, they often think about searching online, spotting misinformation, or evaluating websites. These skills matter. Yet recent thinking in Information Literacy suggests that IL is also about understanding how knowledge is created, valued, shared, and sustained within communities. Information literacy is not only about finding information. It is also about recognizing valuable knowledge, preserving it, sharing it responsibly, and ensuring that it survives for future generations. In Iran, one of the most important priorities for the future of IL may be helping rural women preserve the indigenous knowledge they already possess and pass on to future generations.

title: College Students as Key Learners in Information Literacy Programmes for Combating Misinformation and Disinformation Sana

detail.title: College Students as Key Learners in Information Literacy Programmes for Combating Misinformation and Disinformation Sana
detail.abstract: Have you ever used strategies while searching for a specific problem? Well, most youngsters do not even bother whether they are consuming actual information on the internet or not, because they only care about synthesized information to fulfill their needs. The major issue in developing nations like Pakistan is that we, as students, face the risk of believing all the information we find on Google or social media is accurate. When it comes to information literacy, people who consume content on social media and in their daily lives don’t bother about the authentication of the news they consume. So, the question is what will happen when students get literacy instructions at college and early university life in all disciplines?

title: In Pursuit of Social Justice: Reclaiming Information Literacy as a Transformative Practice

detail.title: In Pursuit of Social Justice: Reclaiming Information Literacy as a Transformative Practice
detail.abstract: Over the last fifty years, IL has evolved from a “niche” library practice and skill into a concept connected to democracy, social justice and human rights. Yet much discussion in the field still revolves around definitions, frameworks and competences, while broader social and political realities shaping information practices receive less attention. If IL is to be socially relevant and “fit for the future”, its value cannot lie only in conceptual refinements, but in its ability to respond to the conditions affecting our lives.

title: Stability of Compute-Capital Networks: Funding-Technology Feedback and Scenario Diagnostics
affiliations: and

detail.title: Stability of Compute-Capital Networks: Funding-Technology Feedback and Scenario Diagnostics
detail.abstract: We study the local stability of funding-technology feedback after an upstream contract economy has supplied an economically executable configuration, a smooth agreement stratum, agreement-compatible dynamics, and a valid reduction. The resulting object is a directed reduced propagation graph, distinct from the typed undirected contract graph. For the deterministic reduced flow, J =-R + W and the normalized propagation index is A = ρ(R-1 W). For a nonnegative transmission matrix W , we establish local asymptotic stability when A < 1, instability when A > 1, a transcritical branch exchange under explicit nondegeneracy conditions, and the associated Perron and directed-Laplacian representations. In a two-node funding-technology motif, Λ = bd/(rxrz) is the squared motif radius. We also give an exact bistable symmetric cubic realization and delimit what follows from the general asymmetric boundary calculations. Public filings do not identify the complete normalized operator. We therefore report scenarioconditioned diagnostics rather than an empirical distance to fragility or a crisis forecast. Under the declared normalization ωi/rz,i = 1, the funding-block radius is 0.654 and the base combined index is 0.984; maintained refinements illustrate how common collateral and circular buffers can move the index. A source-dated telecom back-cast identifies several vendor-financing objects but neither a complete R-1 W nor its spectral regime. A separately labelled Lucent-Winstar motif shows the retained-share, utilization, loss, rate, and buffer assumptions required to apply the threshold. The contribution is a transparent stability diagnostic, its mathematical boundaries, and an explicit account of what public data do and do not identify.

title: The Lipstick Effect: Informal Micro-entrepreneurship as Economic Mitigation in High-inflation West Africa

detail.title: The Lipstick Effect: Informal Micro-entrepreneurship as Economic Mitigation in High-inflation West Africa

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships that could have influenced the research or its interpretation.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The study involved an anonymous exploratory survey of 20 beauty entrepreneurs. No personally identifying information was collected. The research was conducted as an independent exploratory study and did not receive formal institutional ethics review. Given the small, anonymous nature of the survey, the findings are presented as preliminary descriptive evidence rather than generalizable conclusions.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The study was independently conducted by the author.

detail.abstract: The Lipstick Effect is traditionally used to describe the tendency of consumers to continue purchasing relatively affordable luxury goods during periods of economic uncertainty (Hill et al., 2012; MacDonald & Dildar, 2020). This paper proposes a contextual adaptation of this concept within the informal economy of West Africa, with particular attention to beauty entrepreneurship in Nigeria. Rather than examining the Lipstick Effect solely as a consumer response to financial hardship, the study explores whether the beauty sector can also function as a source of income generation and economic resilience for young entrepreneurs operating in an environment characterized by inflation, limited formal employment opportunities, and expanding digital commerce. An exploratory survey of 20 beauty entrepreneurs was used to examine four dimensions of the proposed framework: economic necessity as a motivation for entrepreneurship, continued demand for affordable beauty products and services, reliance on digital platforms as business channels, and perceptions of self-directed income compared with conventional employment. The original survey summary indicated strong agreement across these dimensions, including unanimous responses on economic necessity and digital storefront use and 95% agreement regarding continued consumer demand for affordable beauty products and services. Because of the small convenience sample and the absence of a recoverable respondent-level dataset, these findings are treated as preliminary descriptive evidence rather than statistically generalizable results. The paper proposes the concept of the West African Lipstick Effect Mutation, in which beauty entrepreneurship represents not only a response to consumer demand but also a potential economic adaptation to financial insecurity. The study contributes a preliminary conceptual framework linking consumer resilience, informal entrepreneurship, and digital commerce, while identifying the need for larger and more rigorous comparative studies.

title: From Procurement Data to Procurement Intelligence: A Capability-Based Framework for Data-Driven Decision-Making
affiliations: Usmanu Danfodiyo University, Sokoto

detail.title: From Procurement Data to Procurement Intelligence: A Capability-Based Framework for Data-Driven Decision-Making
detail.abstract: Procurement generates data through every requisition, tender, contract, invoice, delivery and supplier interaction, yet greater data availability has not automatically produced better procurement outcomes. This paper develops a Procurement Data-to-Value Capability Framework, drawing on the Resource-Based View, Dynamic Capabilities Theory and the Information Processing View, to explain how procurement data becomes procurement intelligence and, ultimately, strategic value. The framework treats value creation as a capability-dependent process comprising seven stages: data generation, data foundation, data integration, analytical capability, procurement intelligence, decision execution and value realisation. Procurement data is not inherently strategic; its value depends on an organisation's ability to govern, integrate, analyse and act on it. Its empirical centre of gravity is Nigeria: the Bureau of Public Procurement, the Nigeria Open Contracting Portal (NOCOPO), the World Bank-financed SPESSE reform programme, and the forthcoming Electronic Government Procurement (e-GP) platform, and set alongside Ukraine's Prozorro ecosystem, the United Kingdom's analytical approach to competition enforcement, and OECD evidence on digital-government integration. The comparison is instructive because Nigeria does not fit the usual narrative of either failure or success: it has built genuine transparency infrastructure and reports substantial savings, yet its procurement outcomes remain constrained less by the availability of data than by weak decision execution and uneven institutional independence. The paper closes with ten testable propositions, a candidate measurement instrument, and a research agenda anchored in Nigeria's experience but relevant to comparable emerging markets.

title: Campus Emergency Notification Systems: An Examination of Factors Affecting Compliance with Alerts
affiliations: State University of New York, SUNY at Stony Brook University, College of Business, Karamanoğlu Mehmetbey University, State University of New York (SUNY) - Management Science and Systems and University of Texas at San Antonio

detail.title: Campus Emergency Notification Systems: An Examination of Factors Affecting Compliance with Alerts
detail.abstract: The increasing number of campus-related emergency incidents, in combination with the requirements imposed by the Clery Act, have prompted college campuses to develop emergency notification systems to inform community members of extreme events that may affect them. Merely deploying emergency notification systems on college campuses, however, does not guarantee that these systems will be effective; student compliance plays a very important role in establishing such effectiveness. Immediate compliance with alerts, as opposed to delayed compliance or noncompliance, is a key factor in improving student safety on campuses. This paper investigates the critical antecedents that motivate students to comply immediately with messages from campus emergency notification systems. Drawing on Etzioni's compliance theory, a model is developed. Using a scenario-based survey method, the model is tested in five types of events-snowstorm, active shooter, building fire, health-related, and robbery-and with more than 800 college students from the Northern region of the United States. The results from this study suggest that subjective norm and information quality trust are, in general, the most important factors that promote immediate compliance. This research contributes to the literature on compliance, emergency notification systems, and emergency response policies.

title: Finfluencers and the Consumification of Stock Investment
affiliations: Dresden University of Technology and Dresden University of Technology

detail.title: Finfluencers and the Consumification of Stock Investment
detail.abstract: Financial influencers (finfluencers) increasingly disseminate investment advice through short-form videos embedded in consumer and lifestyle content. We study whether their stock recommendations adopt to consumption context or merely replicate analyst advice. We develop a consumption-hedging view of finfluencer recommendations, arguing that retail investors may value shares of firms whose products they consume because equity ownership can hedge exposure to future increases in the prices of those products. Using a handcollected sample of 544 explicit and reasoned TikTok stock recommendations from 98 finfluencers between 2023 and 2025, we test the predictions of the consumption-hedging view using a triple-difference design that exploits exogenous variation in consumption. We find that periods of higher consumption increase recommendations of consumer-goods firms by a factor of 2.02, generate greater engagement with finfluencers, and do not lead to inferior longhorizon performance relative to analyst recommendations. Our findings show that finfluencer investment advice provides value beyond information about expected returns by incorporating consumption objectives of retail investors.

title: Critical Infrastructure Concentration and Systemic Financial Fragility

detail.title: Critical Infrastructure Concentration and Systemic Financial Fragility
detail.abstract: The financial sector runs on a shared digital infrastructure: a small number of cloud platforms, core banking software vendors, payment and market utilities, data and identity services, and a growing layer of artificial-intelligence model providers. As institutions outsource more of their information systems to this common layer, the concentration of the layer itself becomes a source of system-level risk. We develop an analytical model in which a continuum of financial institutions chooses provider portfolios from a market with endogenous concentration, and in which providers fail through both idiosyncratic and common-cause channels. We prove that equilibrium diversification falls strictly short of the social optimum whenever a joint-failure externality is present, with provider concentration strictly above the planner's when entry responds; we derive comparative statics on the resulting wedge, and we characterize optimal governance. Following Weitzman (1974), we compare a price on concentration with a quantity rule that requires minimum portfolio diversity. The quantity rule typically dominates under empirically plausible conditions, because the marginal social damage from concentration is steep near the concentrated region while the marginal private cost of diversification is comparatively flat. We also study how the provider market responds, which can amplify or attenuate the value of regulation, and we derive a robust-optimization characterization of optimal portfolios when the common-cause failure structure is uncertain. The paper connects the information systems literature on IT outsourcing and cloud concentration to the financial-networks, pecuniaryexternality, and operations research literatures, and it speaks directly to the critical third-party and digital operational resilience regimes now being implemented by the Financial Stability Board, the European Union, and national regulators: the United Kingdom's critical third parties regime entered live operation in July 2026 with the designation of four cloud providers, the first concrete instance of the oversight architecture the model evaluates. The model is deliberately kept simple enough that every result is available in closed form, with the general-model counterparts collected in a separate technical companion; the analysis is foundational, and we are explicit about the limits of the model for setting regulatory parameters directly.

title: Price Advantage and Passion: Social Interaction, and Cognitive and Affective Loyalty in Social Commerce
affiliations: National Taipei University, Da-Yeh University and National Taipei University

detail.title: Price Advantage and Passion: Social Interaction, and Cognitive and Affective Loyalty in Social Commerce
detail.abstract: The growth of the Internet and social media platforms has made socially oriented social commerce an emerging trend, and the interactive enthusiasm exhibited between buyers and sellers constitutes the primary distinction between social commerce and conventional e-commerce. This study adopts both qualitative and quantitative approaches. The qualitative component employs a case-study method, drawing on actual cases to illustrate social commerce sellers who compete on cost-effectiveness and sellers who compete on passion, respectively. The quantitative component employs a questionnaire survey, collecting 285 valid responses that were analyzed using structural equation modeling. The findings confirm that, in addition to cost, seller passion is an important factor influencing purchasing behavior in social commerce. In terms of loyalty, this study departs from prior research by further dividing loyalty into cognitive loyalty and affective loyalty. Accordingly, this study develops an integrated model linking cost-effectiveness, seller passion, social interaction, and cognitive and affective loyalty, which may serve as a reference for future marketing strategies among social commerce practitioners.

title: CUSTOMER SATISFACTION IN THE DIGITAL PURCHASE PROCESS: A DISCRIMINANT ANALYSIS OF INTERACTIONS WITH HUMAN SALES AGENTS AND AI-POWERED CHATBOTS
affiliations: University of Zagreb

detail.title: CUSTOMER SATISFACTION IN THE DIGITAL PURCHASE PROCESS: A DISCRIMINANT ANALYSIS OF INTERACTIONS WITH HUMAN SALES AGENTS AND AI-POWERED CHATBOTS
detail.abstract: The increasing use of AI-powered chatbots in digital commerce has transformed how customers obtain information and support during the purchase process. However, the interaction characteristics that differentiate customer experiences with chatbots and human sales agents remain insufficiently understood. This study examines the variables that distinguish customer evaluations of interactions with human sales agents and AI-powered chatbots in the digital purchase process. Data were collected from 200 respondents using a questionnaire adapted from a previously validated measurement instrument and analyzed using linear discriminant analysis. The results indicate that information quality dimensions, particularly Information Completeness, Information Accuracy, Information Relevance, and Information Believability, contributed most strongly to differentiating customer evaluations of the two types of interactions. In contrast, interaction-related variables, including Perceived Waiting Time, Pleasure Interacting, and Arousal Interacting, exhibited comparatively weaker discriminatory power. The discriminant function significantly differentiated between the two groups. The findings contribute to the literature on AI-enabled customer service by highlighting the central role of information quality in shaping customer evaluations and provide practical guidance for organizations seeking to optimize the balance between human sales agents and AI-powered chatbots in digital commerce.

title: Do People Actually Listen? A Survey on Email Security Awareness and Communication Strategies

detail.title: Do People Actually Listen? A Survey on Email Security Awareness and Communication Strategies
detail.abstract:
Phishing works because attackers know how to trick busy people. Even with modern spam filters, clever fake emails still make it into employee inboxes, and once they do, the company's defense relies on whether an employee clicks or reports. Most companies force their staff to watch a long compliance video once a year and call it a day. But does anyone actually remember that training when a realistic email shows up three months later? Almost never.

To see what really works, we surveyed 428 people across colleges, software firms, hospitals, and banks, followed four test groups for a full year with real mock phishing emails, and talked directly with 24 IT admins and office workers.

Here is what we found: Telling people "be scared, hackers are everywhere" does not change behavior. What actually works is giving people quick, practical confidence and making the reporting process as simple as one click. If reporting an email takes five complicated steps and interrupts work, people will just delete it and move on. In our 12-month experiment, switching to quick 30-second nudges inside the email app and short team challenges dropped phishing clicks from 36.8% to just 3.4%, and got people reporting suspicious emails in under 8 minutes instead of two and a half hours. We turn these findings into four simple steps any IT team can use to build real security habits without burning out their employees.

Keywords: Email Security, Usable Security, Protection Motivation Theory, Theory of Planned Behavior, Phishing Inoculation, Just-In-Time Nudges, Security Fatigue, Structural Equation Modeling, Behavioral Cybersecurity.

title: Automation at Both Ends: A Coasean Theory of Determinacy and the Adoption of Generative Systems

detail.title: Automation at Both Ends: A Coasean Theory of Determinacy and the Adoption of Generative Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial or personal relationships that could be perceived to have influenced this work. The author is a Senior Researcher at the Thailand Development Research Institute, an independent non-profit research institute. The views expressed are the author's own and do not necessarily reflect those of the Institute. This paper is theoretical and reports no empirical results, contracts, or commercial engagements.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a theoretical paper. It involves no human subjects, no patient or participant data, no interviews, and no personally identifiable information.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The author's time was supported by his position at the Thailand Development Research Institute.

detail.abstract:
Coase made the boundary of the firm turn on what it costs to transact across it; Barzel located that cost in the difficulty of measuring what changes hands. Both acquire new force with a production input that has no refusal mode. A jammed loom stops and a compiler rejects: their failures announced themselves, so the price of a boundary could be ignored. A generative system always produces, errs at a rate that does not fall to zero, and delivers an artifact that looks the same either way. Nothing downstream is told when it fails.

This paper applies Coase and Barzel one level down, to the boundary between one task and the next, and asks what a firm pays to split work between two agents. Recent work has established that job boundaries are endogenous and that the cost of splitting moves them, while treating that cost as a primitive: an occupational attribute, a hand-off time, a coordination parameter (Garicano, Li and Wu 2026; Gans 2026; Demirer et al. 2026). Here it is derived, from one property of the work: whether a fact of the matter about conformance exists. Competent assessors draw verdicts, and the share of variance they share is the axis. What a mechanical check can establish, whether a defect draws an objection, and how accurate a trained machine is on it all follow from that one property.

The consequence is that interface cost is single-peaked. It is low where the machine is well trained and its defects are mechanically findable, low again where nothing turns on conformance, and high in between, where errors have grown common while consequence has not yet decayed and a person must read work she did not produce for evidence of a process she did not see. Boundaries fall where interface cost is low, so the machine takes both ends of the axis while the interior stays whole and is augmented. No model in which the cost of splitting is exogenous can produce that pattern.

title: How Digital Transformation Shapes Unequal Employee Experiences: An Interpretive Case Study of a Chinese State-Owned Enterprise
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, The University of Manchester - Global Development Institute and The University of Manchester - Global Development Institute

detail.title: How Digital Transformation Shapes Unequal Employee Experiences: An Interpretive Case Study of a Chinese State-Owned Enterprise
detail.abstract:
Digital transformation (DT) is widely recognised as a systemic organisational change, yet research reports sharply divergent employee experiences and offers a limited explanation of how and why these differences emerge over time. This gap persists because employee experience is often treated as a static outcome or reduced to individual-level variation, leaving the contextual processes that shape experience underexamined. This study adopts the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) framework as a sensitising lens to understand how DT reshapes work conditions and employee experience as an unfolding process.

The study draws on an interpretive single-case study of a large Chinese state-owned enterprise (SOE) undergoing a six-year DT initiative. In this case, two connected processes emerged. First, DT was experienced as producing differentiated working conditions through hierarchical position and organisational roles, with demands and resources distributed unevenly at the team level. Second, employees interpret and reclassify these changed team-level conditions into individual experiences over time through iterative meaning-making shaped by positional cues, institutional norms, and contextual change.

The case suggests that DT shapes work conditions at the collective level, and channels them unevenly to individuals, and that whether these conditions function as demands or resources is produced through ongoing interpretation. It contributes to JD-R theory by reconceptualising demands and resources as context-dependent meaning categories, and illustrates how interpretive case research can help explain structural and institutional dynamics that are less visible in scale-based approaches.

title: Sequential ETA Disclosure on On-Demand Platforms: Reference Dependence and Field Evidence
affiliations: and Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Information Systems, Business Statistics and Operations Management

detail.title: Sequential ETA Disclosure on On-Demand Platforms: Reference Dependence and Field Evidence
detail.abstract: Consumers on food-delivery platforms see an estimated delivery time twice: on the listing page before choosing a restaurant, and at checkout after committing to one. We develop a reference-dependent model in which the listing-page ETA anchors the consumer's initial expectation and the checkout-page ETA revises it, generating structurally distinct effects that depend on display format. We test these predictions with two randomized field experiments on a major food-delivery platform, using randomized minute offsets as instruments for the rendered ETAs across more than 30 million sessions. A one-minute increase in the listing-page ETA reduces click-through by 0.022 percentage points and order conversion substantially once the within-session ETA gap is held fixed, consistent with the listing-page ETA anchoring the consumer's reference point. The checkout-page ETA moves conversion in opposite directions by format: a one-minute increase lowers conversion by 0.127 percentage points under exact-minute display but raises it by 0.051 percentage points under interval display. The reversal is concentrated among active users who have learned that interval promises run conservative, a pattern we term credible-slack learning. For realized orders, a higher checkout-page ETA raises actual arrival time less than one for one and leaves repurchase essentially unchanged. These results show that the listing-page ETA primarily gates demand while the checkout-page ETA operates as a credibility signal, so the two cannot be optimized by a single, format-invariant rule.

title: An Evaluation of The Use of Technology To Enhance Judicial Efficiency In Ghana’s Judicial System

detail.title: An Evaluation of The Use of Technology To Enhance Judicial Efficiency In Ghana’s Judicial System
detail.abstract: The integration of digital technology into the Ghanaian judicial system represents a critical shift towards resolving systemic inefficiencies, such as protracted case backlogs, and undue delays. This study evaluates the extent to which the introduction of various e-justice initiatives, including the Electronic Case Distribution Management System, the Criminal Justice Case Tracking System, electronic filing, and virtual court sessions, effectively enhances judicial efficiency within Ghana's judiciary. Anchored in the sociological jurisprudence framework of Law in Action, the study adopts a doctrinal research methodology to critically interrogate e-justice policies implementation within the Ghanaian legal ecosystem. By tracing the historical transition from manual processes to modern digital infrastructure, the research assesses the practical utility of these tools for litigants, lawyers, and judicial officers. The study identifies barriers impeding the sustainable implementation of these reforms, notably a deficit in technically trained personnel, a persistent institutional attachment to manual long hand recording, and infrastructural limitations such as unreliable internet connectivity. Ultimately, the study argues that while the adoption of technological tools establishes the foundation for an efficient judiciary, achieving true optimisation and equitable access to justice necessitates addressing systemic and operational challenges to bridge the gap between technological implementation and practical efficacy.

title: Neurodiverse Perceptions of Information Literacy
affiliations: University College London

detail.title: Neurodiverse Perceptions of Information Literacy
detail.abstract: In many academic and professional settings, IL is treated as something people either possess or lack. Once someone is qualified or trained, they are often assumed to be information literate by default. In contrast, we believe that becoming information literate in the workplace is a continuous, effortful, and highly contextual process, particularly for neurodivergent people, for example, for autistic librarians in the workplace.

title: Quantum-Classical Orchestration for Non-Terrestrial Edge Platforms
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Quantum-Classical Orchestration for Non-Terrestrial Edge Platforms
detail.abstract: Non-terrestrial networks (NTNs) are being asked to do far more than relay bits. Low Earth orbit constellations, high-altitude platforms, and autonomous aerial nodes now host sensing, inference, and optimization workloads that were, until recently, the exclusive business of ground segments. As small-scale quantum co-processors and quantum-inspired accelerators begin to appear in these payloads, the orchestration problem changes character: the classical host must now share a power budget, a thermal envelope, and a duty cycle with a quantum resource whose availability is dictated by physics rather than by a scheduler. This letter proposes a Non-Terrestrial Quantum-Classical Orchestrator (NT-QCO), an on-board orchestration architecture that couples an Orbital Orchestration Layer (OOL) with contact-window-aware Shadow Queues and radiation-tolerant checkpoint logic. NT-QCO treats quantum duty-cycle gaps, eclipse periods, and out-of-contact arcs as schedulable resources rather than as dead time. We formalize the resulting admission problem as a deadline-constrained scheduling problem over a time-varying resource availability function, and give a hardware-realizable approximation of its solution. In a 24-satellite LEO simulation running routing, quantum machine learning inference, and sensor-fusion workloads, NT-QCO improved effective task completion by 38%, raised payload processor utilization from 31% to 72%, and cut deadline misses from 22% to 5.8%, with no measurable loss of result fidelity and under 2.1% area overhead on the payload system-on-chip. An ablation study attributes roughly two-thirds of the deadline improvement to contact-window awareness specifically, rather than to raw throughput. The result is a deployable, high-TRL blueprint for architects designing the next generation of orbital and aerial edge platforms.

title: Objections to the Language Model as Judge: Normativity, Aristotelian Phronesis, and Arendtian Common Sense
affiliations: Thompson Rivers University - Faculty of Law

detail.title: Objections to the Language Model as Judge: Normativity, Aristotelian Phronesis, and Arendtian Common Sense
detail.abstract: Scholarship and policy on the use of artificial intelligence in legal judgment continues to be shaped by a consensus formed at an earlier stage in AI's development. AI cannot be sensitive to context, reason normatively, or be responsive to novel facts. Recent experiments challenge these assumptions by showing that language models prompted to decide a case based on party materials uploaded to the model can render a reasoned decision comparable in quality to that of a human. This new capability of AI casts in a new light philosophical reservations about algorithmic judgment based on ideas about normativity, Aristotle's concept of phronesis (practical wisdom), and Hannah Arendt's theories common sense and reflective thought. Revisiting these arguments in the context of AI's new capabilities illuminates how differences between human and algorithmic judgment are evolving and supports a pragmatic alternative basis for accepting the language model as judge in some cases.

title: Worker Voice in Workplace AI Governance: An Empirically Grounded Comparative Typology

detail.title: Worker Voice in Workplace AI Governance: An Empirically Grounded Comparative Typology

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or non-financial interests that could have influenced the research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required because the study is based exclusively on publicly available documentary sources and did not involve human participants, interventions, or the collection of personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Worker voice is increasingly invoked in AI governance, but participation labels do not show how workers or their representatives enter decisions, what authority they possess, or whether formal arrangements operate in practice. This paper uses structured comparative documentary analysis of 17 purposively selected international, European, and North American arrangements to examine how worker voice is institutionally organised. It identifies three non-hierarchical configurations: procedural information and advisory voice (six cases); negotiated monitoring and review constraints (seven); and negotiated ex ante and use-condition constraints (four).

The contribution is twofold. First, the paper develops a comparative typology based on decision point, authority, institutional basis, contestability, and expert access. Second, it separates adoption from implementation, exercised enforcement, and operational outcomes. Public follow-up evidence supports implementation in three cases and identifies one reported or perceived operational outcome, while no qualifying evidence of exercised enforcement was identified under the documented protocol. The empirical record therefore documents adopted governance architecture more consistently than operation or effects.

The findings show that worker voice is more often institutionalised through information, consultation, monitoring, review, and negotiated constraints than through co-decision or veto authority. Formal enforceability and operational authority are analytically distinct, and institutional basis alone does not determine authority level. The paper argues that stronger worker voice in AI governance depends not simply on participation, but on earlier entry into the decision process, enforceable procedural rights, credible contestability, access to independent expertise, and clearer escalation routes.

title: Who Manages the Variance? Operational Concentration and the Regulation of Financial Infrastructure

detail.title: Who Manages the Variance? Operational Concentration and the Regulation of Financial Infrastructure
detail.abstract: The financial system now runs on a shared digital infrastructure (a handful of cloud platforms, core processing vendors, payment utilities, data and identity services), and the regulation of that infrastructure has begun in earnest: in July 2026 the United Kingdom placed four cloud providers under direct supervisory oversight as its first designated critical third parties. This paper makes the economic case for what such regimes should do next, in terms a supervisor can use. The organizing idea fits in one sentence: expected systemic damage from operational failure is governed by a mean and a variance; the market already manages the mean, because every institution cares about its own uptime; nobody manages the variance, which is determined by who fails together; and concentration, cross-layer alignment, and the timing of failures are all variance, not mean. From that identity follow five recommendations: cap system-wide concentration rather than mandating firm-level diversity alone; prefer quantity instruments to price instruments; calibrate the instrument to each provider market; mandate dependency disclosure and build the system-level map; and pair any concentration instrument with reliability standards. We confront directly the strongest practical objection (that in some markets, above all core processing, no institution can realistically run two vendors) and show that the framework's answer is not to force dual sourcing but to shift the instrument: system-level share discipline, sub-dependency separation, switchability, and a deliberate program to lower the cost of diversification over time. Every quantitative statement rests on the formal model and calibration of a companion analytical paper.

title: The Chatbot Will See You Now: When Access Isn’t Enough
affiliations: Uppsala University

detail.title: The Chatbot Will See You Now: When Access Isn’t Enough
detail.abstract: Digital healthcare can increase convenience, reduce travel time, and make services available to more people, more quickly. Patients can access test results, book appointments, renew prescriptions, and, in many countries, read their medical records online. Yet as healthcare becomes increasingly digital, I find myself asking a different question: who is this system really designed for? More specifically, who is expected to understand it?

title: Beyond the Bot: Why Information Literacy Is More Critical Than Ever in the AI Age
affiliations: Rajarata University of Sri Lanka

detail.title: Beyond the Bot: Why Information Literacy Is More Critical Than Ever in the AI Age
detail.abstract: In an age where generative AI tools like ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, and Claude can produce essays, summarize research, generate code, create lesson plans, and even draft emails in seconds, one might wonder whether traditional Information Literacy remains essential. The answer is a simply "Yes", perhaps more than ever before. While AI dramatically changes how we access, create, and interact with information, it does not replace the critical human skills needed to evaluate, interpret, contextualize, and ethically use that information. In fact, the rise of AI-generated contents make strong information literacy skills even more crucial for navigating an increasingly complex information landscape.

detail.abstract: Information literacy has become a serious focus in scientific research and political advocacy within Brazilian Librarianship and Information Science. Since the early 2000s, Brazil has come a long way: it shifted from a simple, user education approach to studies about critical thinking, multiple perspectives, and real social commitment. Shaped by real challenges such as regional inequalities, political turbulence, and the rush to go digital, Brazilian research can't be separated from social justice, fixing education, and keeping democracy strong.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts.

declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by the Social Science and Humanities Research Council of Canada (File number 890-2020-0120).

detail.abstract: In early 2020, multiple Canadian police services were implicated in a scandal exposing how a rights-infringing technology-Clearview AI-could make its way into police use without any safeguards or accountability mechanisms in place. Focusing on the province of Ontario's 43 municipal police services, this study examines how effectively police services communicate accountability for technology use in the wake of this scandal. The study examines current proactive police communication practices addressing governance of camera-based and artificial intelligence-enhanced technology use, primarily via analysis of police service websites. We analyze proactive communication content for the depth of policy information provided to the public, and what policy elements are being communicated (if any). The study points to patterns that support or undermine the efficacy of police transparency and suggests how these can be more effectively addressed.

title: The C2S Reliability Framework

detail.title: The C2S Reliability Framework

declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:

As these systems assume increasingly consequential advisory roles, the central challenge is no longer computational capability alone, but institutional trust. Decisions affecting human lives, national security, and strategic infrastructure require analytical systems that are not only accurate, but also transparent, explainable, and scientifically accountable.

This monograph introduces the C2S Reliability Framework, a conceptual model proposing that causal artificial intelligence can strengthen personnel reliability in high-consequence domains by supporting—rather than replacing—human institutional judgment. Building upon the principles established in SynsID and The Survival Blueprint, the framework argues that artificial intelligence should function as an evidence-integration system capable of organizing complex behavioral, developmental, physiological, and operational information into transparent decision-support models.

Particular attention is given to the emergence of foundation models capable of interpreting biological information, including the Cell2Sentence (C2S-Scale) family developed by Yale University, Google Research, and Google DeepMind. These technologies demonstrate the growing capacity of large language models to analyze complex biological systems. Their significance within this monograph, however, lies not in direct behavioral prediction but in illustrating how future multimodal AI systems may contribute to broader institutional evaluation frameworks.

The C2S Reliability Framework therefore rejects both biological determinism and fully autonomous decision-making. Instead, it proposes a human-centered model in which explainable causal AI assists qualified professionals by integrating multiple independent sources of objective evidence while preserving accountability, transparency, ethical safeguards, and due process.

This framework is presented as a conceptual contribution intended to stimulate interdisciplinary discussion regarding the future relationship between artificial intelligence, institutional governance, and human reliability in environments where individual decisions may carry irreversible consequences.

title: When Should You Stop Showing Someone an Ad? Neural SDE Fatigue Modeling for Multi-Channel Ad Campaigns
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: When Should You Stop Showing Someone an Ad? Neural SDE Fatigue Modeling for Multi-Channel Ad Campaigns
detail.abstract: If you show someone the same ad ten times, the first few might help, but eventually they start ignoring it, or worse, develop a negative reaction. This is ad fatigue, and it causes ad campaigns to waste money and annoy users. Standard attribution models (Last-Touch, Linear, Time-Decay) ignore fatigue entirely: they just credit the channels that were shown, with no awareness of how many times a user has already been exposed. That means campaigns keep showing ads long after they've stopped being effective. This paper asks: can a learned model detect when a user has become fatigued and stop showing ads at the right moment? We build a simulation where the true fatigue dynamics are known (users have a hidden "fatigue state" that builds up with each impression and decays between ad sessions), and we test whether a Neural SDE (a neural network that models continuous-time dynamics) can learn those dynamics from data. It turns out that simple models are surprisingly hard to beat. Heuristic baselines (Linear, FirstTouch) correctly identify fatigued impressions 74% of the time (F1 = 0.739) and achieve iROAS efficiencies of 0.71 relative to the oracle. The Neural SDE goes in the opposite direction: it flags almost everything as fatigued (recall = 99.6%), which means it stops ads very early and saves 57% of impressions. But its precision is only 38% and its iROAS efficiency drops to 0.68. The Neural SDE is not worse overall. It saves substantially more budget than any baseline, which can matter when impression costs are high. But for pure conversion efficiency, the learned model does not beat rules-of-thumb. The deeper lesson is that fatigue is not the binding constraint. The same signal-to-noise problem identified in our earlier work [Clark, 2026a,b] applies here too: with binary conversion outcomes and a 5% base rate, the data just does not contain enough signal to learn fine-grained fatigue dynamics reliably.
